n-m-h3-conic-01.title: Checking a solution about the area of triangle PF₁F₂
n-m-h3-conic-01.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-01.goal: Realize that even a solution whose calculations are all correct can make the conclusion meaningless if you do not check whether the problem's condition can actually hold, and find the range in which the condition holds.
n-m-h3-conic-01.material: A workbook has this problem and answer: "Let F₁ and F₂ be the two foci of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1. For a point P on the ellipse with ∠F₁PF₂ = 90°, find the area of triangle PF₁F₂. (Answer: 16)" Below is the solution that gets this answer.
n-m-h3-conic-01.thinking.0: Tell apart whether each line of the solution is a calculation or an acceptance of a condition
n-m-h3-conic-01.thinking.1: Test whether the given condition can actually hold by trying an extreme position
n-m-h3-conic-01.thinking.2: Find the range of the parameter for which the condition holds
n-m-h3-conic-01.prereq.0: The definition of an ellipse and the coordinates of its foci
n-m-h3-conic-01.prereq.1: The Pythagorean theorem and product formulas
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.prompt: Every line of the solution below is correct as a calculation. But the answer 16 to this problem is hard to believe. Choose the earliest line that makes the answer hard to believe.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether each line came from the previous line by calculation or simply accepts a condition taken from the problem.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put the result of the line that accepts a condition together with the result of another line already obtained earlier, and plug in numbers to see whether both can hold at the same time.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.line.0: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1, a=5 and b=4, so c²=a²−b²=9, c=3, and F₁(−3, 0), F₂(3, 0).
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.line.1: By the definition of an ellipse, PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a = 10, and F₁F₂ = 6.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.line.2: Since ∠F₁PF₂ = 90°, by the Pythagorean theorem PF₁² + PF₂² = F₁F₂² = 36.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.line.3: Since (PF₁ + PF₂)² = PF₁² + PF₂² + 2·PF₁·PF₂, we get 100 = 36 + 2·PF₁·PF₂, so PF₁·PF₂ = 32.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.line.4: The area of triangle PF₁F₂ is ½·PF₁·PF₂ = 16.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s1.explain: It is line 3. This line took the "∠F₁PF₂=90°" written in the problem as given and set up an equation. But since PF₁+PF₂=10 from line 2, PF₁²+PF₂² is smallest when the two lengths are equal, so it must be at least 5²+5²=50. It cannot be 36, so no such point P exists on the ellipse. Lines 4 and 5 are calculations that follow from the result of line 3, so even though the calculations are correct, they are meaningless.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.prompt: Explain, using numbers that appear in the solution, why you cannot believe the answer 16. Also write what the correct thing to say about this problem is.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about the smallest value PF₁²+PF₂² can take when PF₁+PF₂ is fixed at 10.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.hint.1: Draw a figure to predict where ∠F₁PF₂ is largest as P moves along the ellipse, and estimate the angle there.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use numbers from the solution (36, 10, 50, etc.) directly in your explanation?
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you state your conclusion in the form "the condition cannot hold" rather than "the calculation is wrong"?
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you realize that this can also be checked with a figure or an extreme position (the endpoint of the minor axis)?
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.model.0: If PF₁+PF₂=10, the sum of squares is smallest when the two lengths are equal, so it is at least 5²+5²=50. But line 3 said 36, so that is a contradiction. Such a point P does not exist, and 16 is a meaningless value.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.model.1: At the endpoint of the minor axis (0, 4), PF₁=PF₂=5 and F₁F₂=6, so 25+25>36, which means ∠F₁PF₂ is less than 90° at this point. This angle is largest there on the ellipse, so there is no point where it is 90°. So the area cannot be found.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.model.2: The answer 16 is not correct. If the sum is 10, the sum of squares is at least 50, but it is 36, so it does not fit. There is no such point.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s2.model.3: 16 is not right. If the sum of the two lengths is 10, the sum of squares cannot be 36, so such a P does not exist.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.prompt: Now change the ellipse to x²/25 + y²/b² = 1 (0 < b < 5). Find and enter three different values of b for which a point P with ∠F₁PF₂ = 90° actually exists on the ellipse.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.hint.0: First look at how the distance between the two foci changes as b gets larger.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.hint.1: For each value of b, estimate whether the angle at the point on the ellipse where ∠F₁PF₂ is largest reaches 90°.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.fail.c1: It must be a number in the range 0<b<5.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.ok.c2: For this b, a point with ∠F₁PF₂=90° exists on the ellipse.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.fail.c2: For this b, ∠F₁PF₂ does not reach 90° anywhere on the ellipse.
n-m-h3-conic-01.s.s3.explain: For the foci to see a point P on the ellipse at 90°, ∠F₁PF₂ must be at least 90° at the endpoint of the minor axis, where the angle is largest. This happens when c ≥ b, that is, when 25−b² ≥ b². So b² ≤ 12.5, and for 0<b<5, a point P exists when b is at most about 3.54. b=3.5 works, but 3.6 does not.

n-m-h3-conic-02.title: What else do we need to determine the equation of a hyperbola?
n-m-h3-conic-02.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-02.goal: Judge whether there is enough information to determine the equation of a curve by comparing the number of unknowns with the number of independent equations.
n-m-h3-conic-02.material: A workbook contains the problem "Find the equation of the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 (a>0, b>0) with foci (5, 0) and (−5, 0)." The teacher said, "This problem is missing one condition." You want to complete the problem by filling in the missing condition.
n-m-h3-conic-02.thinking.0: Count the equations that the given information produces
n-m-h3-conic-02.thinking.1: Separate what you already know from new information
n-m-h3-conic-02.thinking.2: Show the information is insufficient with a counterexample (a different curve with the same foci)
n-m-h3-conic-02.prereq.0: The standard form x²/a²−y²/b²=1 of a hyperbola, and the meanings of foci, vertices, and asymptotes
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information that, added to the information that the foci are (5, 0) and (−5, 0) as the only addition, determine a and b uniquely. (a>0, b>0)
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write out one by one whether each piece of information gives a new equation relating a and b.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.hint.1: First work out which equation relating a and b already holds when only the foci are known.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.o.b: The distance between the two foci is 10.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.r.b: This is already known from the coordinates of the foci (±5, 0), so it is not new information. There is still only one of the equations needed relating a and b.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.o.c: The slope of one of the asymptotes is 4/3.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.o.d: The curve is symmetric about the origin.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.r.d: This always holds for any curve of the form x²/a²−y²/b²=1. It is not new information about a and b.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.o.e: The curve does not meet the y-axis.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.r.e: Substituting x=0 gives −y²/b²=1, so a hyperbola of this form never meets the y-axis. It is not new information about a and b.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s1.explain: The foci information gives just one equation, a²+b²=25. The vertex (3, 0) gives a=3, so b=4 is determined, and the asymptote slope 4/3 gives b/a=4/3, so a=3 and b=4 are determined. The distance between the foci being 10, symmetry about the origin, and not meeting the y-axis are already known or always true, so they add no equation.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.prompt: Make two hyperbolas of different shapes that have foci (5, 0) and (−5, 0) and are of the form x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, and enter (a, b). (If you write decimals, use two decimal places.)
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.hint.0: Plug the value of c into the equation that holds among a, b, and c for a hyperbola.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one value of a that satisfies that equation and check what b becomes.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be positive.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.ok.c2: This is a hyperbola whose foci are (±5, 0).
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.fail.c2: With this (a, b), the foci are not (±5, 0).
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.explain: If the foci are the same, c=5, so a²+b²=25. Not only (3, 4) and (4, 3) but also pairs such as (2, about 4.58) are all possible, so there are infinitely many hyperbolas of different shapes.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why different hyperbolas come out even though the foci are the same.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Count how many equations relating a and b there are and how many unknowns there are.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compute a²+b² for each of the two pairs you made and compare them.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say that there is only one equation holding between a and b?
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give two or more examples of (a, b) satisfying that equation?
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.model.0: If the foci are (±5, 0), then c=5, and for a hyperbola only one equation arises: a²+b²=c²=25. There are two unknowns, a and b, so b changes depending on how a is chosen, and there are infinitely many curves.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s2.because.model.1: We are only given a²+b²=25, so (3, 4) works, (4, 3) works, and so do many others. So the foci alone do not determine it uniquely.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.prompt: This time, choose a method that can be used for curves other than hyperbolas too. When you receive new information, what is the most reliable way to decide whether that information alone determines the curve uniquely?
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.hint.0: Put side by side the number of equations obtained from the two pieces of information used so far and the number of unknowns.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how one new piece of information changes those counts.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.o.a: Decide by looking at whether the new information contains specific numbers.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.r.a: Even if there are numbers, they may just restate something already known (for example, the distance between the foci). The presence of numbers cannot be the criterion.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.o.b: Check whether it gives one more equation relating a and b that differs from the focus condition.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.o.c: Check whether the curve can be drawn using the new information.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.r.c: Being able to draw a figure does not mean the numbers are determined. You have to decide whether they are determined using equations.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.o.d: Decide by looking at whether the new information is expressed in the same way as the foci.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.r.d: The way something is expressed has nothing to do with the amount of information. What matters is which equation it adds.
n-m-h3-conic-02.s.s3.explain: To be determined uniquely, you need as many independent equations as there are unknowns. The foci gave one equation and a and b are two unknowns, so you must check whether the new information gives one more equation different from what is already known. However, even with two equations the solution may not be unique, so in the end solve to confirm.

n-m-h3-conic-03.title: How does the locus of point P change when point F moves?
n-m-h3-conic-03.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-03.goal: Confirm from the definitions that in the same construction, changing the position of point F changes the locus into a circle, an ellipse, or a hyperbola, and build the habit of not carrying the conclusion from one case over unchanged to another.
n-m-h3-conic-03.material: In a plane there are a circle with center O and radius 6, and a point F. For a point Q moving on the circle, let P be the point where the perpendicular bisector of segment FQ meets line OQ. We will investigate the figure P traces as Q moves on the circle, changing the position of F.
n-m-h3-conic-03.thinking.0: Revise your judgment each time the condition changes
n-m-h3-conic-03.thinking.1: Find the locus using the sum and difference of distances
n-m-h3-conic-03.thinking.2: Notice the danger of generalizing from a special case (F=O)
n-m-h3-conic-03.prereq.0: Definitions of ellipses and hyperbolas (sum of distances, difference of distances)
n-m-h3-conic-03.prereq.1: The property that a point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is the same distance from the two endpoints
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time as the position of point F changes. At each step, choose a judgment based only on what you know so far.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, draw a figure showing where point P lies on segment OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.hint.1: Use PF=PQ to check whether the sum or difference of PO and PF simplifies to a constant value.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.info: First consider the case where F is the same point as the center O. A point on the perpendicular bisector of segment FQ is the same distance from F and Q, so PF=PQ. Point P lies on line OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: As Q goes once around the circle, what figure does P trace?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If F=O, then PO=PQ and PO+PQ=OQ=6, so PO=3. P is a point 3 away from O, so it traces a circle of radius 3.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A circle with center O and radius 6
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You just restated the circle that Q traces. P is not Q; it is a point on the perpendicular bisector of FQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A circle with center O and radius 3
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You saw that P is at a constant distance from O.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: An ellipse with O and some point as its foci
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: We are not yet in a situation with two foci. F and O are the same point.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: When Q moves, P moves too.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.info: F has been moved to a point inside the circle, 4 away from O. It is still true that PF=PQ. If you draw the figure, P lies on segment OQ (between O and Q).
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the locus of P now?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.after: Since P is on segment OQ, PO+PF=PO+PQ=OQ=6. The sum of the distances from the two points O and F is a constant 6, so it is an ellipse with foci O and F and major axis of length 6.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Still a circle centered at O: because Q is on the circle
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: When F leaves O, PO is no longer constant. You carried over the conclusion from the previous step unchanged.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A hyperbola with a constant difference of distances from O and F
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You did not check whether PO and PF are added or subtracted. Use the fact that P is on segment OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: An ellipse with a constant sum of distances from O and F
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You saw that the sum is constant, since PO+PF=PO+PQ=OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: A parabola with points equidistant from F and a line
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The equal distances are the relationship between F and Q (PF=PQ), and it is the distance to point Q, not to a line.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.info: This time F has been moved to a point outside the circle, 9 away from O. If you draw the figure, P is not on segment OQ but on the extension of line OQ (on the Q side or the O side). It is still true that PF=PQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the locus of P now?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.after: On the extension on the Q side, PO=OQ+PQ, so PO−PF=6, and on the extension on the O side, PF−PO=6. Either way, |PO−PF|=6 is constant, so it is a hyperbola with foci O and F and transverse axis of length 6 (OF=9>6).
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A hyperbola with a constant difference of distances from O and F
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: An ellipse with a constant sum, as in the inside case
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You carried over the result from the inside case unchanged. If P is not on segment OQ, PO+PQ is not OQ.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Check whether PO is constant. If F is away from O, it is not constant.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The perpendicular bisector and line OQ meet for almost every Q.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s1.reflect: As the position of F changed, the same construction gave a circle, an ellipse, and a hyperbola in turn. Carrying the inside result over unchanged to the outside is wrong. Depending on whether point P is on segment OQ or on its extension, it changed whether the sum or the difference of PO and PF is constant.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain why the locus of P differs when F is inside the circle and when F is outside the circle, using PO, PF, and the radius 6 of the circle.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.hint.0: Say where P is on line OQ in the inside case and in the outside case.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.hint.1: In each case, connect the relationship between PO and PQ to the length 6.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write that PO+PF=6 inside and |PO−PF|=6 outside?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain that the sum and the difference split apart because the position of P (on the segment or on the extension) differs?
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.model.0: If F is inside, P is on segment OQ, so PO+PF=PO+PQ=6, the sum is constant, and it is an ellipse. If F is outside, P is on the extension, so the difference of PO and PQ is 6, the difference of PO and PF is a constant 6, and it is a hyperbola.
n-m-h3-conic-03.s.s2.model.1: If F is inside the circle, the sum of the distances from O and F is 6, so it is an ellipse, and if F is outside the circle, the absolute value of the difference of the distances is a constant 6, so it is a hyperbola. This is because whether P is on the segment or on the extension changes.

n-m-h3-conic-04.title: Building lines tangent to a hyperbola yourself
n-m-h3-conic-04.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-04.goal: Build several tangent lines yourself, discover that there is a range of slopes for which a tangent line exists, and explain this using the discriminant.
n-m-h3-conic-04.material: There is a hyperbola x²/4 − y²/9 = 1. You will find out about lines y = mx + k tangent to this curve by building them yourself.
n-m-h3-conic-04.thinking.0: Substitute and set up the discriminant
n-m-h3-conic-04.thinking.1: Build tangent lines yourself and find the pattern
n-m-h3-conic-04.thinking.2: State the range in which they exist
n-m-h3-conic-04.prereq.0: The discriminant of a quadratic equation
n-m-h3-conic-04.prereq.1: The positional relationship between a line and a conic (simultaneous equations)
n-m-h3-conic-04.prereq.2: The meaning of the asymptotes of a hyperbola
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.prompt: Build three different lines y = mx + k tangent to the hyperbola x²/4 − y²/9 = 1 and enter (m, k). (Use decimals to three decimal places.)
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute the equation of the line into the equation of the hyperbola to make an equation in x.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what state that equation must be in for the line to touch the curve at exactly one point.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.ok.c1: Substituting the line gives a quadratic equation in x.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.fail.c1: With this slope, substituting the line does not give a quadratic equation.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.ok.c2: The quadratic equation has a double root (tangent).
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.fail.c2: This line is not tangent to the hyperbola (the discriminant is not 0).
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s1.explain: Substituting y=mx+k into 9x²−4y²=36 gives (9−4m²)x²−8mkx−4k²−36=0. The discriminant is 144(k²+9−4m²), so for tangency, k²=4m²−9. For example, if m=2.5, then k²=16, so k=±4.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.prompt: Recall the lines you built earlier. Choose all the slopes for which a line y = mx + k tangent to this hyperbola exists.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the condition for the discriminant of the equation you set up earlier to be 0 as an equation in k².
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.hint.1: For each slope m, decide whether k² would be negative.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.r.a: A horizontal line y=k either crosses each of the hyperbola's two branches once or meets neither. It can never be tangent.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.r.d: It seems you assumed that a small slope has a tangent line. If you carry over the ellipse tangent formula k²=a²m²+b² unchanged, you get k=±√13, but this line meets the hyperbola at two points.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s2.explain: For tangency, k²=4m²−9≥0 is needed, and excluding the case parallel to an asymptote (slope ±3/2), 4m²>9, that is, |m|>3/2. Slopes 2 and −3 work; for 0 and 1, k² is negative, so they do not.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.prompt: A line with slope 1 cannot be tangent to this hyperbola. Explain why, and explain the range of slopes m for which a tangent line exists.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute m=1 and find the k that makes the discriminant 0.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.hint.1: Work out what range m must be in so that k² is not negative.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain the reason using the discriminant (or the sign of k²)?
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the boundary of the range is connected to the slope of the asymptotes?
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.model.0: Substituting y=x+k makes the discriminant 144(k²+5), which can never be 0. To be a tangent line, k²=4m²−9≥0 is needed, so the absolute value of m must be greater than 3/2.
n-m-h3-conic-04.s.s3.model.1: With slope 1, k²=−5, so there is no real k and hence no tangent line. The slopes for tangent lines need 4m²−9 to be at least 0, but ±1.5, which are parallel to the asymptotes, must be excluded, so |m|>1.5.

n-m-h3-conic-05.title: If k changes, does the type of curve change too?
n-m-h3-conic-05.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-05.goal: In an equation of a conic that contains a letter, find and verify directly the intervals where the type of figure changes depending on the sign of the denominators.
n-m-h3-conic-05.material: For real k, investigate how the figure represented by the equation x²/(9−k) + y²/(4−k) = 1 changes with k. If you put in k=2, it becomes x²/7 + y²/2 = 1, which is an ellipse.
n-m-h3-conic-05.thinking.0: Read the sign structure of the equation
n-m-h3-conic-05.thinking.1: Build an example that satisfies the whole range
n-m-h3-conic-05.thinking.2: Check that the equation may represent no figure at all
n-m-h3-conic-05.prereq.0: Standard forms of ellipses and hyperbolas
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.prompt: If you put in k=6, you get x²/3 + y²/(−2) = 1. What figure does this equation represent?
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite the term with the negative denominator in subtraction form.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the rewritten equation with the standard form and check which term is positive.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.o.a: It is an ellipse, because the equation is written as a sum of two terms.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.r.a: You missed that the sign of a denominator can change when you put in k. You only looked at the outward appearance of the equation.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.o.b: It is a hyperbola whose transverse axis is in the y-axis direction, because the negative is on the y² side.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.r.b: If the negative denominator is on the y² side, the x² term is positive, so it opens in the x-axis direction. Check which term is positive.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.o.c: It is no figure at all, because one denominator is negative.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.r.c: If one denominator is negative, the equation turns into a subtraction. It is not that there are no points; the type of curve changes.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.o.d: It is a hyperbola, because one denominator becomes negative and the equation takes subtraction form.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s1.explain: y²/(−2) is −y²/2, so the equation is x²/3 − y²/2 = 1. The x² term is positive, so it is a hyperbola opening in the x-axis direction.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter three different values of k for which the equation x²/(9−k) + y²/(4−k) = 1 becomes a hyperbola of the form x²/A − y²/B = 1 (A>0, B>0).
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write what the signs of the two denominators must be for the equation to take subtraction form.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.hint.1: Turn that sign condition into inequalities in k and find the range.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The denominator of the x² term is positive.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The denominator of the x² term is not positive.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The y² term takes subtraction form.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The y² term does not change to subtraction form.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.explain: If the denominator 9−k of the x² term is positive and the denominator 4−k of the y² term is negative, the equation takes the form x²/(9−k) − y²/(k−4) = 1. That is, every k with 4<k<9 works (k=4 and 9 do not work because a denominator is 0).
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.prompt: When k=2 it was an ellipse, but when k=6 it became a hyperbola. Explain which part of the equation changed and how.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the signs of the two denominators for k=2 and for k=6 and compare them.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the sign changes of the two denominators at k=2 and k=6?
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you pinpoint exactly which denominator changed sign?
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.model.0: When k=2, the two denominators are 7 and 2, both positive, so it has the form of a sum (ellipse). When k=6, the denominator 4−k on the y² side becomes −2, a negative, so the equation changes to subtraction form (hyperbola).
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s2.because.model.1: When k goes past 4, 4−k becomes negative. Then the sign in front of the y² term changes, so the ellipse becomes a hyperbola. 9−k stays positive.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.prompt: If you put in k=10, the equation becomes x²/(−1) + y²/(−6) = 1. Which statement about the figure this equation represents is correct?
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite the left side by clearing the denominators.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the range of values the left side can take with the right side, 1.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.o.a: No point (x, y) satisfies this equation.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.o.b: It is an ellipse, because even though both denominators changed, it is still in the form of a sum.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.r.b: Even when both denominators are negative, it is still in the form of a sum, but you did not check that the left side cannot be greater than 0, so it cannot equal 1 on the right.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.o.c: It is a hyperbola opening in the x-axis direction, because 9−k is negative.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.r.c: Both denominators are negative, so it is not in subtraction form. Look at the signs once more.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.o.d: It is a circle, because the two terms look the same.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.r.d: The denominators have different values, so it cannot be a circle, and you also did not check the signs.
n-m-h3-conic-05.s.s3.explain: The left side is −x²−y²/6, which is at most 0. It cannot equal 1 on the right, so no real (x, y) satisfies this equation. Depending on whether the denominators are positive or negative, it splits into an ellipse, a hyperbola, or nothing at all.

n-m-h3-conic-06.title: Where do the focus and directrix go when a parabola is shifted?
n-m-h3-conic-06.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-06.goal: Read the direction of a translation correctly from the equation, move the focus and directrix by the same translation, and write an explanation for a younger student.
n-m-h3-conic-06.material: Your junior Haeun sent you a note while trying to find the focus and directrix of the parabola (y−1)² = −8(x+2).
n-m-h3-conic-06.thinking.0: Reading how the signs in the equation correspond to the direction of the shift
n-m-h3-conic-06.thinking.1: Choosing a way to verify (the vertex)
n-m-h3-conic-06.thinking.2: Rewriting the explanation to fit the person you are explaining to
n-m-h3-conic-06.prereq.0: The focus and directrix of the parabola y²=4px
n-m-h3-conic-06.prereq.1: Translations and how the equation changes
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.prompt: This is the note your junior Haeun sent. Choose the first line that goes wrong.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.hint.0: First find the point in the new equation where both sides are 0. Compare it with where that role was played in the old equation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether each line's calculation follows from the previous line or is a new judgment.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.0: For y² = −8x, 4p = −8, so p = −2, the focus is (−2, 0), and the directrix is x = 2.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.1: (y−1)² = −8(x+2) has x+2 and y−1, so it is y² = −8x translated by +2 in the x-direction and −1 in the y-direction.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.2: Moving the focus the same way gives (−2+2, 0−1) = (0, −1).
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.3: Moving the directrix the same way gives x = 2+2 = 4.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the focus is (0, −1) and the directrix is x = 4.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s1.explain: It is line 2. Putting x+2 in place of x shifts by −2 in the x-direction, and putting y−1 in place of y shifts by +1 in the y-direction. The signs are opposite. Everything from line 3 on is a calculation following the direction in line 2, so if the direction is wrong, all of it is wrong. Line 1 is correct.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose the most reliable way to check whether Haeun's direction of translation is right.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what feature the point corresponding to the old vertex has in the new equation of the shifted figure.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.hint.1: First recall whether the focus and directrix are on the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.a: Substitute the focus found, (0, −1), to see if it satisfies the new equation (y−1)² = −8(x+2).
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.a: The focus is not a point on the curve, so it does not need to satisfy the equation when substituted. So this check cannot tell you the direction of the translation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.b: Compare whether the coefficient −8 in the new equation is the same as the coefficient in the original equation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.b: The coefficient only tells you the shape (the direction it opens and its width). It does not tell you which way the position was shifted.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.c: Find the point where both sides of the new equation are 0 and see whether it is where the old vertex (0, 0) moved to.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.o.d: Sketch the graph roughly and see whether the direction it opens is the same as before.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.r.d: A translation does not change the direction it opens, so it looks the same even if the direction of the translation is wrong.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s2.explain: The vertex was the point (0, 0) where both sides of the old equation were 0, so the point (−2, 1) where both sides of the new equation are 0 is where the vertex moved. So the translation is −2 along the x-axis and +1 along the y-axis. The focus and directrix are not points on the curve, so you cannot check them by substituting into the equation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.prompt: Haeun is a first-year high school student who has just learned translations. Write a reply to send to Haeun. It must include where it went wrong, the correct direction of translation, the correct focus and directrix, and how to check it.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.hint.0: Decide the order of the reply: where it went wrong, the corrected translation, focus and directrix, how to check.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.hint.1: Using the corrected translation, move the vertex, focus, and directrix of the original equation.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you point out where it went wrong in words Haeun can understand?
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you show how the focus and directrix moved from their old positions?
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the way to check included in the reply?
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.model.0: Haeun, the direction is reversed on line 2. If x+2 is put in place of x, the graph is shifted by −2 in the x-direction, and with y−1 it is shifted by +1 in the y-direction. The point in the new equation where both sides are 0 is (−2, 1), so you can tell that the vertex moved from (0, 0) to there. So the focus (−2, 0) moves to (−4, 1), and the directrix x=2 moves to x=0.
n-m-h3-conic-06.s.s3.model.1: Haeun, the direction of translation on line 2 is wrong. (x+2) shifts 2 to the left, and (y−1) shifts 1 up. You can check by plugging in that the vertex is (−2, 1). So the focus is (−4, 1) and the directrix is x = 0.

n-m-h3-conic-07.title: The sum of two paths through a point on a parabola
n-m-h3-conic-07.topic: Conic sections: definitions and tangent lines of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas; correspondence between figures and equations
n-m-h3-conic-07.goal: Using the position of points, see that the lower bound from the triangle inequality is not always a value that is reached, and find the minimum again using the definition of a parabola (distance to the focus = distance to the directrix).
n-m-h3-conic-07.material: The parabola y² = 8x has focus F(2, 0) and directrix x = −2. Seoyun claims, "For a point P on the curve and any point A, the minimum of PA + PF is always AF by the triangle inequality."
n-m-h3-conic-07.thinking.0: Examine the condition for equality in an inequality
n-m-h3-conic-07.thinking.1: Rewrite in a different form using the definition
n-m-h3-conic-07.thinking.2: Split into cases depending on the position of the point
n-m-h3-conic-07.prereq.0: The definition of a parabola (focus and directrix)
n-m-h3-conic-07.prereq.1: The triangle inequality and its equality condition
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.prompt: For the parabola y² = 8x with focus F(2, 0) and a point A(4, 2), you moved the point P on the curve to find the minimum of PA+PF. Which value and reason fit best?
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.hint.0: Pick several points P on the curve, compute PA+PF directly, and make a table.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.hint.1: Recall the definition and check whether you can rewrite PF as another length for a point on the parabola.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.o.a: 6, because it equals the distance from A to the directrix.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.o.b: 2√2, because PA+PF ≥ AF and there is a P for which equality holds.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.r.b: Equality in the triangle inequality holds only when P is on segment AF. You did not check whether such a P is on the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.o.c: 4, because it equals the x-coordinate of A.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.r.c: You only looked at the coordinates of point A. There is no explanation of what distances this value is the sum of.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.o.d: 2+2√5, because it is the value at the vertex P=(0, 0).
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.r.d: You only found the value at one point and did not check whether it is the minimum.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s1.explain: For a point on the parabola, PF equals the distance from P to the directrix x=−2. So PA+PF is the sum of PA and "the distance from P to the directrix," which is at least 6, the distance from A to the directrix. It equals 6 at a point on the curve at the same height as A, such as P=(0.5, 2). 2√2 is AF, but A and F are both inside the curve, so segment AF does not cross the curve and it cannot be reached.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.prompt: This time choose point A(x, y) with integer coordinates (−10 to 10), and find and enter three different points A for which the minimum of PA+PF equals AF as P moves on the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.hint.0: First say where P must be for equality in the triangle inequality to hold.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.hint.1: Split into the cases where A is inside and outside the curve, and draw whether segment AF meets the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.ok.c1: These are integer coordinates within the range.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The coordinates must be integers from −10 to 10 inclusive.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Segment AF meets the curve, so there is a P with PA+PF=AF.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.fail.c2: For this point, there is no P on the curve for which it equals AF.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s2.explain: PA+PF ≥ AF, and equality holds only when P is on segment AF. F is inside the curve, so if A is on the curve or outside it (y² ≥ 8x), segment AF meets the curve. If A is inside (y² < 8x), the segment does not meet the curve, so the minimum is greater than AF.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.prompt: At A(4, 2), the minimum came out greater than AF. Explain why Seoyun's claim "the minimum of PA+PF is always AF" is wrong.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.hint.0: Say where P would have to be for equality to hold in the inequality Seoyun used.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether that condition is met at A(4, 2) using the positions of segment AF and the curve.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state the equality condition of the triangle inequality?
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the result differs depending on the position of point A (inside/outside the curve)?
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.model.0: PF equals the distance from P to the directrix, so PA+PF is at least 6, the distance from A to the directrix. This 6 is much greater than AF=2√2. Seoyun's claim is not always true, since there are cases where AF is the minimum.
n-m-h3-conic-07.s.s3.model.1: Equality in the triangle inequality PA+PF≥AF holds only when P is on segment AF. If A and F are both inside the curve, segment AF does not meet the curve, so there is no such P. So the minimum is greater than AF.

n-m-h3-diffc-01.title: How should we read a slope whose denominator is 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.topic: Differentiation: implicit differentiation and tangent lines at points where the slope is undefined
n-m-h3-diffc-01.goal: Examine whether a tangent line exists at a point where the denominator of the slope obtained by implicit differentiation is 0, and find and fix the wrong conclusion in a solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.material: This is Hayoon's solution for finding the tangent line at the point P(2, −1) on the curve C: x²+xy+y²=3. (x² and y² mean x squared and y squared. That point P is on C was checked with 4−2+1=3.)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.0: Find the wrong line in the solution
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.1: Interpret the tangent line where the slope is undefined as a shape of the graph
n-m-h3-diffc-01.thinking.2: Choose the conditions to check before concluding
n-m-h3-diffc-01.prereq.0: Implicit differentiation (treat y as a function of x and differentiate both sides with respect to x)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.prereq.1: Finding the equation of a tangent line at a point on a curve
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Hayoon's solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line from the top and check by direct calculation whether it follows from the line right before it.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the conclusion on the last line says the same thing as the fact obtained in the earlier line (what is undefined).
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.0: Differentiating both sides with respect to x gives 2x + (y + x·y′) + 2y·y′ = 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.1: Solving for y′ gives y′ = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y).
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.2: Substituting P(2, −1), the denominator x+2y is 2+2·(−1)=0, so the slope is undefined.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.line.3: Therefore no tangent line exists at the point P.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. The calculations on lines 1 to 3 are correct. But "the slope expression is undefined" means "there is no number called the slope," not that there is no tangent line. The numerator 2x+y=3 is not 0, so the slope can grow without bound, that is, a tangent line parallel to the y-axis can occur.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.prompt: If there is a tangent line to the curve C at the point P, write its equation, and write the reason you judged so.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate what value the numerator takes while the denominator is 0, and think about how large the slope becomes.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.hint.1: Sketch what a line whose slope grows without bound looks like in the coordinate plane, and write the equation of that line through the point P.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Looking at the direction of the tangent line ...
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the denominator is 0 but the numerator is not 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you substitute x=2 into the equation of the curve and look at how the curve and the line meet?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you state the difference between "there is no slope" and "there is no tangent line"?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.model.0: The denominator is 0 and the numerator is 3, so the slope grows without bound. So the tangent line is the line x=2, parallel to the y-axis. Substituting x=2 into the curve gives y²+2y+1=0, so y=−1 is the only solution, which means the line just touches the curve at the point P, which fits too.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.model.1: There is a tangent line. The slope is undefined because the tangent line is vertical, and its equation is x=2. I also checked that the numerator 2x+y is 3, not 0, so it is not of the form 0/0.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It is enough to check the numerator, even without using the method of substituting x=2 into the curve.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.prompt: What must you check before concluding "there is a vertical tangent line" at a point where the denominator of the slope expression is 0?
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.hint.0: In the form y′ = (numerator)/(denominator), compare how the fraction looks different when the denominator is 0 and the numerator's value differs.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.hint.1: Are the forms 0/0 and 3/0 the same situation? Think about what each one says.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.a: Whether, when the denominator is 0, the numerator is also nonzero (that is, whether it is not of the form 0/0)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.a: You thought of checking the numerator as well.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.b: Whether the value of y is not negative when the point is on the curve
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.b: The sign of y has nothing to do with whether a tangent line exists. You may have confused the sign of a coordinate with the direction of a tangent line.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.c: Whether the twice-differentiated value y″ is not 0
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.c: The second derivative only tells you the direction in which the curve bends; it does not decide whether a tangent line exists.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.o.d: Whether the curve can be written in the form y = (an expression in x)
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.r.d: A tangent line exists even if an implicit function cannot be written in the form y=f(x). This condition is not needed.
n-m-h3-diffc-01.s.s3.explain: Even if the denominator is 0, if the numerator is not 0, the slope grows without bound and a vertical tangent line appears. If the numerator is also 0, it is of the form 0/0, so this expression alone cannot decide it, and you must look at the shape of the curve at that point by another method.

n-m-h3-diffc-02.title: At the moment the velocity is 0, does the point turn around?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.topic: Differentiation: velocity and acceleration, conditions for a change of direction
n-m-h3-diffc-02.goal: Understand, through the change of sign of the velocity, the difference between the moment the velocity is 0 and the moment the direction of motion changes, and build and check velocity expressions that meet the conditions yourself.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.material: The velocity of a point P moving on a number line at time t (t≥0) is v(t), and v(1)=0. Minsu said, "At the moment the velocity is 0, the point definitely changes direction." (Changing direction means going from moving right to moving left, or from moving left to moving right. If the velocity is positive, it moves right; if negative, left.)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.0: Choose the exact condition for a change of direction
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.1: Build and verify velocity expressions that satisfy the conditions
n-m-h3-diffc-02.thinking.2: Sort out what can be judged from the values of velocity and acceleration alone
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.0: The relationship among position, velocity, and acceleration (velocity is the derivative of position, acceleration is the derivative of velocity)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.1: The relationship between the sign of velocity and the direction of motion
n-m-h3-diffc-02.prereq.2: Sign changes of a factored expression
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the statement that means the same as "point P changes direction at time t₀."
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.hint.0: First write which way the point moves when the velocity is positive and when it is negative.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what the sign of the velocity must do for the direction to change, and compare with the case where it becomes 0 and then returns to the same sign.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.o.a: The acceleration at t₀ is not 0
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.a: Even if the acceleration is not 0, if the velocity is not 0 the direction stays the same. You may have mixed up velocity and acceleration.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.o.b: The position at t₀ is greater than the positions at all times just before and after
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.b: This only considers when the position is largest (the right end). It leaves out the case of turning back at the left end.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.c: v(t₀)=0 is only one feature of the moment of changing direction, not the same statement. Think about the case where v=0 but the sign stays the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.o.d: The signs of the velocity just before and just after t₀ are different
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.r.d: You saw the change of direction through the change of sign of the velocity.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s1.explain: The direction changes when the sign of the velocity changes from positive to negative or from negative to positive. The velocity being 0 is a necessary condition that occurs at the moment the sign changes, but it is not sufficient.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.prompt: When the velocity is given by v(t)=(t−1)^m (t−p)^n, enter two or more different triples (m, n, p) that satisfy all of the following: point P does not change direction at t=1, and does change direction at t=p. (m and n are natural numbers from 1 to 6, and p is a natural number from 2 to 9.)
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.hint.0: Try several values of m and n and make a table of the signs of (t−1)^m and (t−p)^n just before and after t=1 and t=p.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split into the cases where the exponent is even and odd, and compare whether the sign is the same or different just before and after that point.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c1: m, n, and p are natural numbers within the ranges.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c1: They must be natural numbers with 1≤m≤6, 1≤n≤6, 2≤p≤9.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The sign of the velocity is the same just before and after t=1.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The sign of the velocity changes just before and after t=1, so the point changes direction.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The sign of the velocity is different just before and after t=p.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The sign of the velocity is the same just before and after t=p, so the point does not change direction.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.explain: If the exponent of (t−1) is even, this factor has the same sign just before and after t=1, and if the exponent of (t−p) is odd, the sign is different just before and after t=p. The other factors do not change sign near that point (p≥2). For (1, 1, 3), the sign also changes at t=1, and for (2, 2, 3), it does not change at t=3.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the examples you found and write why the point does not change direction at t=1 even though v(1)=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write v(t) with your chosen (m, n, p), and compare the signs when you plug in a value slightly less than 1 and a value slightly greater than 1.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Connect whether (t−1)^m is positive or negative just before and after t=1 to whether m is odd or even.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. Just before and after t=1, the sign of (t−1)^m is ...
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In your chosen example, did you actually work out the sign of the velocity before and after t=1?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare with the case where the exponent is odd?
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.model.0: I chose (2, 1, 3). In v=(t−1)²(t−3), (t−1)² is at least 0 on both sides of t=1, so its sign does not change, and (t−3) stays negative. So v is 0 at t=1 but its sign stays the same, so the direction does not change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The exponent m is even, so (t−1)^m does not become less than 0 as t passes 1. The velocity touches 0 and comes back with the same sign, so the direction stays the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It includes both the even exponent and the fact that the sign does not change.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.prompt: When the velocity v is a differentiable function and the acceleration is a(t)=v′(t), choose all the correct statements.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.hint.0: Set up simple velocity expressions yourself, such as v=(t−1)² and v=(t−1)³, calculate v′(1) for each, and compare with whether the direction changes.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.hint.1: For each statement, find one counterexample to check whether it holds "always."
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.a: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)≠0, the point changes direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.a: You thought that if the acceleration is not 0, the graph of the velocity passes through 0 and its sign changes.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.b: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)=0, the point does not change direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.b: Even if a(t₀)=0, in cases such as v=(t−1)³ the direction changes. You missed that when the acceleration is 0, this alone cannot decide it.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.c: If v(t₀)=0 and a(t₀)=0, the point definitely changes direction at t₀
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.c: Even if a(t₀)=0, in cases such as v=(t−1)² the direction stays the same.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.o.d: If the point changes direction at t₀, then v(t₀)=0 necessarily
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.r.d: You thought that for the direction to change, the velocity must change continuously and pass through 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-02.s.s3.explain: If v(t₀)=0 and v′(t₀)=a(t₀)≠0, then v passes through 0 and changes sign. Conversely, if a(t₀)=0, the sign may not change, as with (t−1)², or may change, as with (t−1)³, so you must look at the sign of the velocity directly. For the direction to change, the continuous v must change sign, so v=0 at that moment.

n-m-h3-diffc-03.title: Can we find the slope of a composite function from the values in a table?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.topic: Differentiation: derivative of a composite function and tables of function values and derivative values
n-m-h3-diffc-03.goal: When finding the derivative of a composite function, decide at which point the derivative of the outer function should be read, and sort out what can be found from the values in the table alone.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.material:
The values of two differentiable functions f and g are as in the table below. Values not in the table are unknown. (f∘g)(x) means f(g(x)), and (g∘f)(x) means g(f(x)).
 x=1: f(1)=3, f′(1)=4, g(1)=2, g′(1)=−3
 x=2: f(2)=5, f′(2)=7, g(2)=1, g′(2)=6
n-m-h3-diffc-03.thinking.1: Distinguish what can be found from what cannot
n-m-h3-diffc-03.thinking.2: Explain the cause of a wrong calculation
n-m-h3-diffc-03.prereq.0: The chain rule for composite functions (f∘g)′(x)=f′(g(x))g′(x)
n-m-h3-diffc-03.prereq.1: Reading a table to find function values
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the values used to find (f∘g)′(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the derivative of the composite function f(g(x)) as a product of an outer part and an inner part, and look at what value the outer part takes as its input.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact that when x=1, the result of putting 1 into g becomes the input of f to decide which entries to read from the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.a: You read the slope of f at x=1. The outer function f must use its slope at the value of the inner function, g(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.b: You read the derivative of the outer function at the value of the inner function, g(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.c: g(1) is needed to decide at which point the outer function is differentiated.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.d: You thought of the part where the derivative of the inner function is multiplied.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.e: g′(2) is the slope at x=2, so it is not used in the value being found at x=1.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.r.f: The function value f(2) is a height, not a slope, so it is not used in calculating a derivative.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.explain: (f∘g)′(1)=f′(g(1))·g′(1). Since g(1)=2, read f′(2)=7 and multiply by g′(1)=−3 to get −21. The key point is to use f′(g(1)), not f′(1).
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s1.acc.0: g(1)=2 is the value used to decide at which point to read f′, so it does not appear directly in the multiplication, but multiplying only f′(2) and g′(1) is the same calculation.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the values that are determined by the values in the table alone.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each composite function, first find and write down the value of the inner function.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the derivative of the outer function at that input is in the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.a: We need the slope g′(3) at g(f(1))=g(3), but it is not in the table. Using g′(1) from the table uses a different input point.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.b: The slope f′(2) at the outer function's input g(1)=2 is in the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.c: We need the slope g′(5) at g(f(2))=g(5), but it is not in the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.r.d: The slope f′(1) at the outer function's input g(2)=1 is in the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s2.explain: The derivative of a composite function can be found only if the table has the slope of the outer function read at the value of the inner function. For (f∘g)′, the values of g, 2 and 1, are both x-values in the table, so it is possible, and for (g∘f)′, the values of f, 3 and 5, are x-values not in the table.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.prompt: Find the value of (f∘g)′(2). Also write why it is wrong to calculate f′(2)·g′(2)=42.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.hint.0: First read the value of g(2) from the table and decide at which point the outer function is differentiated.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.hint.1: In the calculation that gave 42, compare the point at which you read the derivative of f with the value that actually goes into f.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you first find g(2) and decide which point to read from the outer function?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which point's slope was mixed into the value 42?
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.model.0: g(2)=1, so f′ must be read at 1, giving (f∘g)′(2)=f′(1)·g′(2)=4×6=24. f′(2)·g′(2) reads the slope of f at x=2, but the value going into f is not 2 but g(2)=1, so it is wrong.
n-m-h3-diffc-03.s.s3.model.1: The derivative of a composite function is f′(g(2))g′(2). Since g(2)=1, f′(1)=4 and g′(2)=6, and the product is 24. 42 is wrong because it used f′(2)=7.

n-m-h3-diffc-04.title: What happens if the slope is 0 and the amount of bending is 0 too?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.topic: Differentiation: interpreting graphs, extreme values, and the second derivative
n-m-h3-diffc-04.goal: As information is added one piece at a time, revise judgments about extreme values, and understand that when the value of the second derivative is 0, you must look directly at the sign change of the derivative.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.material: A polynomial function f satisfies f′(0)=0 at x=0. Each time a piece of information is revealed, check your judgment about what shape the graph has at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.thinking.0: Revise your judgment according to new information
n-m-h3-diffc-04.thinking.1: Notice cases where a test does not work
n-m-h3-diffc-04.thinking.2: Check extreme values from the sign change of the derivative
n-m-h3-diffc-04.prereq.0: The relationship between extreme values and sign changes of the derivative
n-m-h3-diffc-04.prereq.1: The second derivative and concavity of a graph
n-m-h3-diffc-04.prereq.2: The meaning of an inflection point (a point where concavity changes)
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment based only on what you know so far.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, decide which test it is used for and whether the conditions are right for that test to give a conclusion.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the facts that f′ and f″ are each 0 say the same thing as the signs on the left and right of that point.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.info: f′(0)=0. (At x=0, the tangent line is parallel to the x-axis.)
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we say that f has an extreme value at x=0?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.after: f′(x)=0 only tells you a candidate for an extreme value. You need to know more about the sign of f′ just before and after x=0, or the sign of f″.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is a local minimum: if the tangent line is horizontal, the graph meets it from below
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You treated every point with a horizontal tangent line as a local minimum. A horizontal tangent line can occur at a local maximum, a local minimum, or an inflection point.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is a local maximum: if the tangent line is horizontal, it is the top of the graph
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You treated every point with a horizontal tangent line as a local maximum.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We do not know yet: it may or may not be an extreme value, so we need to know more
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought that a horizontal tangent line alone cannot settle that it is an extreme value.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this information, what is your judgment now?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The test that f″(0)>0 gives a local minimum and f″(0)<0 gives a local maximum tells you nothing when f″(0)=0. f(x)=x⁴, −x⁴, and x³ all have f′(0)=f″(0)=0, but their shapes differ.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is not an extreme value: if f″(0) is 0, it is not an extreme value
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You read f″(0)=0 as evidence that it is not an extreme value. All it means is that the test "positive second derivative means a local minimum, negative means a local maximum" cannot be used.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It cannot be decided from this information: the test using the second derivative stops working
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You noticed that if f″(0)=0, f″ cannot be used to decide whether it is a local maximum or minimum.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a local minimum: the slope is 0 and the bending is 0, so it is the flattest
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You asserted a local minimum from the feeling of being "flat." A flat point is not necessarily a low point.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Finally, what is the shape of f at x=0?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.after: f′(x)=4x³ is negative for x<0 and positive for x>0, so f has a local minimum at x=0. Also f″(x)=12x²≥0, so the concavity does not change, and it is not an inflection point.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It has a local minimum, and this point is not an inflection point
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read together that the sign of f′ changes from negative to positive and that f″ is at least 0 and does not change sign.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It has no extreme value, and this point is an inflection point
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You decided it was an inflection point only because f″(0)=0. For it to be an inflection point, the sign of f″ must change.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It has a local minimum, and this point is also an inflection point
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought that f″(0)=0 means an inflection point. f″(x)=12x² is at least 0, so its sign does not change.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, f′(0)=0 alone made it look like an extreme value, and when f″(0)=0 appeared, the test stopped working. Even so, you can reach a conclusion by directly checking whether the sign of f′ changes. A value being 0 is different from a sign changing.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose the function with f′(0)=0 and f″(0)=0 that has no extreme value at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.hint.0: Find the derivative of each function and compare its sign to the left and right of x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.hint.1: Split them into functions where the sign of f′ changes and functions where it does not.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.r.a: x⁴ has f′(0)=f″(0)=0 but has a local minimum at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.r.b: −x⁶ has f′(0)=f″(0)=0 but has a local maximum at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.r.c: x⁶ also has a local minimum at x=0. Look at whether the exponent is even.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.r.d: For x³, f′(x)=3x² does not change sign, so there is no extreme value.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s2.explain: For x³, f′(x)=3x²≥0, so f′ has the same sign before and after x=0, and there is no extreme value. For the other three functions, the sign of f′ changes, so they have extreme values. This means f′(0)=f″(0)=0 alone cannot tell which case it is.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.prompt: When f′(0)=0 and f″(0)=0, write what you must check, and how, to decide whether there is an extreme value at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write what it looks like to say there is an extreme value in terms of the sign of f′.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately the method that can no longer be used when f″(0)=0 and the method that can still be used.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that you compare the sign of f′ to the left and right of x=0?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that f″(0)=0 does not mean there is no extreme value?
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.model.0: If f″(0)=0, the second derivative cannot tell you whether it is a local maximum or minimum. So you have to look directly at whether the sign of f′ changes to the left and right of x=0. If it changes, there is an extreme value, and if it does not change, there is none.
n-m-h3-diffc-04.s.s3.model.1: If the second derivative value is 0, the test stops working, so draw a sign chart of f′(x). If f′ changes from negative to positive (minimum) or from positive to negative (maximum) around 0, it is an extreme value, and if the sign stays the same, it is not.

n-m-h3-diffc-05.title: If the inner function has a corner, does the composite function have one too?
n-m-h3-diffc-05.goal: Test the claim "if the inner function is not differentiable, the composite function is not differentiable either" with examples, and confirm the conditions under which the composite function becomes differentiable with examples you build yourself.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.material: g(x)=|x| is not differentiable at x=0. (The slope to the left of x=0 is −1, and the slope to the right is 1.) Minseo claims, "If the inner function g is not differentiable at x=0, then for any differentiable function f, the composite function h(x)=f(g(x))=f(|x|) is not differentiable at x=0."
n-m-h3-diffc-05.thinking.0: Find a counterexample to the claim
n-m-h3-diffc-05.thinking.1: Build and check an example that satisfies the conditions
n-m-h3-diffc-05.thinking.2: Explain the result in a situation where the chain rule cannot be used
n-m-h3-diffc-05.prereq.0: The absolute value function |x| is not differentiable at x=0
n-m-h3-diffc-05.prereq.1: The definition of the derivative (left and right limits)
n-m-h3-diffc-05.prereq.2: The chain rule for composite functions
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the f for which h(x)=f(|x|) becomes differentiable at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each f, write h(x)=f(|x|) out directly in terms of |x|.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.hint.1: Near x=0, use |x|=x for x>0 and |x|=−x for x<0 to compare the shape of h on the left and right.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.r.a: h(x)=x²+|x|, and x² cannot hide the corner of |x|. For this f, the slope at x=0 is not 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.r.b: h(x)=|x|³, so the slopes on both sides of x=0 approach 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.r.c: h(x)=3|x|+2, and the corner shape remains.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.r.e: h(x)=(|x|−1)²=x²−2|x|+1, and because of −2|x| it has a corner at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s1.explain: The right derivative of h at x=0 is f′(0) and the left derivative is −f′(0). For them to be equal, f′(0)=0 is needed. x³ and x²+3 have f′(0)=0, so they are differentiable, and the others have f′(0) equal to 1, 3, and −2 respectively, so they have corners.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.prompt: Let f(x)=ax³+bx²+cx. Enter two or more different triples (a, b, c) that make h(x)=f(|x|) differentiable at x=0. Here a and b are not 0, and all are integers from −9 to 9 inclusive.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write f(|x|) as an expression and separate the terms in which |x| remains as an odd power from the terms with even powers, where |x| disappears.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find which term leaves |x| as is and gives a corner at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.ok.c1: All three coefficients are integers within the range.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, and c must be integers from −9 to 9 inclusive.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.fail.c2: a and b must not be 0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The left and right slopes at x=0 are equal.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.fail.c3: If the coefficient of x is not 0, h has a corner at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s2.explain: In h(x)=a|x|³+bx²+c|x|, a|x|³ and bx² are differentiable at x=0, and c|x| has a corner if c≠0. So c must be 0. That is, f′(0)=c=0. (1, 2, 1) has c≠0, so it has a corner; (0, 2, 0) and (1, 0, −2) have a=0 and b=0 respectively, so they violate condition c2, and the last one violates c3 as well.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain that Minseo's claim is wrong using the examples above, and write what condition f must satisfy for f(|x|) to be differentiable at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.hint.0: Put side by side the f's that were differentiable in the previous step and those that were not, and compare the slope of f at x=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.hint.1: Express the right slope and the left slope of h at x=0 in terms of the slope of f.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give one specific f and show that h(x) is differentiable at x=0?
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say how the left slope and right slope become equal?
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.model.0: If f(x)=x²+3, then h(x)=x²+3, which is differentiable at x=0. Even though |x| has a corner, the composite has none. The right slope of h is f′(0) and the left slope is −f′(0), so if f′(0)=0 the two slopes are equal and it is differentiable. So Minseo's claim is wrong.
n-m-h3-diffc-05.s.s3.model.1: A counterexample is f(x)=x³. h(x)=|x|³ has slope 0 at x=0. In general, if f′(0)=0, the left and right derivatives are 0 and 0, so it is differentiable, and if f′(0) is not 0, it has a corner.

n-m-h3-diffc-06.title: How should you tell a younger student what it means for the second derivative to be positive?
n-m-h3-diffc-06.topic: Differentiation: interpreting graphs, the second derivative and convexity
n-m-h3-diffc-06.goal: Find the wrong sentence in a senior student's explanation, check it with a counterexample, and rewrite it as a correct sentence that a younger student can understand.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.material: Your junior Haeun asked, "If f″(x)>0, does the graph go up as it goes to the right?" Your senior Jihu answered as below. Check this write-up and then rewrite it so that Haeun can understand. (f″ is the derivative of the derivative of f.)
n-m-h3-diffc-06.thinking.0: Find the wrong sentence in the explanation
n-m-h3-diffc-06.prereq.0: The sign of the derivative and increasing/decreasing of a function
n-m-h3-diffc-06.prereq.1: The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative
n-m-h3-diffc-06.prereq.2: The meaning of convex downward (concave up) and convex upward (concave down)
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one wrong sentence in Jihu's answer.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.hint.0: Follow how each sentence continues from the previous one, one by one.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which function's sign you need to know in order to say "the value increases."
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.line.0: If f″(x)>0, the derivative f′(x) increases.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.line.1: f′(x) increasing means that the slope of the tangent line keeps getting larger.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.line.2: So on an interval where f″(x)>0, the value of f(x) also gets larger as you go to the right.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.line.3: In this case the graph is convex downward.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s1.explain: Sentence 3 is wrong. Whether the value of f(x) increases or decreases is decided by the sign of f′(x). f″>0 only tells you that f′ is increasing, so on an interval where f′ is negative, f(x) can be decreasing and still have f″>0.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.prompt: Which function and interval most clearly show that sentence 3 is wrong?
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.hint.0: A counterexample is a case where "the first condition is true but the conclusion is false." For each function, check separately the sign of f″ and whether f is increasing.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, also find the sign of f′.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.r.a: On this interval f″=2>0 and f is increasing, so it does not contradict sentence 3.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.r.b: f″=2>0 but f′=2x<0, so f decreases. This is an example that contradicts sentence 3.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.r.c: f″=−2<0, so it is not a case of f″>0.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.r.d: f″=6x>0 and f is increasing, so it does not contradict sentence 3.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s2.explain: For f(x)=x² with x<0, f″(x)=2>0 but f′(x)=2x<0, so f(x) decreases. The graph is convex downward but goes downhill.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite sentence 3 so that Haeun can understand. It should include what f″(x)>0 tells you, and what decides whether f(x) increases or decreases.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write in two columns what f″>0 tells you and what it does not tell you.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.hint.1: Look at the counterexample from the previous step and check whether the value that decides "going up or down" is the sign of f, f′, or f″.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If f″(x)>0, then ... but whether f increases ...
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you describe what f″>0 tells you in terms of slope or convexity?
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write that the sign of f′ decides increasing and decreasing?
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you give an example so that Haeun can follow just by looking at the symbols?
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.model.0: If f″(x)>0, the slope of the tangent line keeps getting larger and the graph is convex downward. But whether f(x) increases or decreases is decided by the sign of f′(x). For example, f(x)=x² has f″=2>0 for x<0, but f′=2x<0, so it decreases.
n-m-h3-diffc-06.s.s3.model.1: f″>0 means that f′ is increasing, that is, the slope is getting larger. Whether it goes up to the right is decided by whether the slope is positive, that is, whether f′>0. If the slope is negative and getting larger, it is going down and still has f″>0.

n-m-h3-diffc-07.title: Second derivative of a curve given by a parameter
n-m-h3-diffc-07.topic: Differentiation: the second derivative of a function given parametrically
n-m-h3-diffc-07.goal: For a curve given by a parameter, find and fix the error in a solution that differentiates dy/dx again, and choose the correct formula.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.material: This is Seoyeon's solution for finding the second derivative d²y/dx² at t=2 on the curve x=t², y=t³−3t (t>0). (t² is t squared and t³ is t cubed.)
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.0: Find the first line that goes wrong in the solution
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.1: Find the value again with the correct method
n-m-h3-diffc-07.thinking.2: Compare the structure of the expressions to choose the correct formula
n-m-h3-diffc-07.prereq.1: The chain rule for composite functions
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Seoyeon's solution.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.hint.0: Confirm that dy/dx on line 2 is an expression in t, and think about how to write the process of differentiating it with respect to x using the chain rule.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.hint.1: Describe in words which derivative each line is finding, and test whether it follows legitimately from the previous line with a simple example such as x=t², y=t³.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first wrong line. dy/dx is an expression in t, so to differentiate it with respect to x, you must first differentiate it with respect to t and then divide by dx/dt. Differentiating y and x twice each and dividing is not that calculation. Line 4 just uses the result of line 3.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.prompt: Find the value of d²y/dx² at t=2 using the correct method, and write how you found it.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.hint.0: Simplify dy/dx as an expression in t, then differentiate that expression with respect to t.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.hint.1: To differentiate with respect to x, use dx/dt to think about what you must divide the derivative with respect to t by.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you first simplify dy/dx as an expression in t?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you differentiate that expression with respect to t and then divide by dx/dt?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check by plugging in the value 15/32 directly?
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.model.0: dy/dx=(3t²−3)/(2t)=(3/2)(t−1/t), and differentiating this with respect to t gives (3/2)(1+1/t²). Dividing this by dx/dt=2t gives d²y/dx². At t=2, (3/2)(5/4)=15/8, divided by 4, gives 15/32.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s2.model.1: d²y/dx²=(d/dt(dy/dx))÷(dx/dt). Putting t=2 into d/dt{(3/2)(t−1/t)}=(3/2)(1+1/t²) gives 15/8, and dividing by dx/dt=4 gives 15/32.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.prompt: Choose the correct formula for finding d²y/dx² for a curve given by a parameter.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write what d²y/dx² can be read as "differentiating what with respect to what."
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.hint.1: Use the chain rule to think about what you must multiply or divide by to change differentiation with respect to t into differentiation with respect to x.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.a: Divide y differentiated twice with respect to t by x differentiated twice with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.a: This is the method Seoyeon used. The ratio of the twice-differentiated values with respect to t is different from dy/dx differentiated with respect to x.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.b: Divide dy/dx differentiated once with respect to t by x differentiated once with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.b: This expresses the process of differentiating dy/dx with respect to x using the chain rule.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.c: Divide dy/dx differentiated once with respect to t by x differentiated twice with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.c: You put the second derivative of x in the denominator. To change to differentiation with respect to x, you divide by dx/dt once.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.o.d: Divide dy/dx differentiated once with respect to t by the square of x differentiated once with respect to t
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.r.d: You squared the denominator. In the chain rule, the only thing you divide by to change differentiation with respect to t into differentiation with respect to x is dx/dt, once.
n-m-h3-diffc-07.s.s3.explain: d²y/dx²=d/dx(dy/dx)=[d/dt(dy/dx)]·(dt/dx)=[d/dt(dy/dx)]÷(dx/dt). At t=2, the formulas above give 6, 15/16, and 15/128 respectively, which differ from the correct value 15/32.

n-m-h3-diffc-08.title: Does a tangent line meet the curve only at the point of tangency?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.topic: Differentiation: equations of tangent lines, tangent lines of cubic curves
n-m-h3-diffc-08.goal: Build your own example of a tangent line to a cubic curve that meets the curve again at a point other than the point of tangency, and tell apart the points of tangency where this does not happen.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.material: The tangent line to the curve y=x³−3x at the point A(1, −2) is y=−2. For the graph of a quadratic function, you saw that the tangent line meets the curve only at the one point of tangency. Is that so for this curve too?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.thinking.0: Set up the equation for the intersection points
n-m-h3-diffc-08.thinking.1: Build an example that satisfies the conditions yourself
n-m-h3-diffc-08.thinking.2: Find the points of tangency that are exceptions
n-m-h3-diffc-08.prereq.0: Finding the equation of a tangent line
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.prompt: If you find all the x-coordinates of the points where the tangent line y=−2 meets the curve y=x³−3x, what do you get?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.hint.0: The points where the tangent line and the curve meet are the solutions of the equation setting the two expressions equal. Set up the equation.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact that x=1 is a solution to factor the left side.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.r.a: You thought that since it is a tangent line, it meets the curve only at the point of tangency. Solve the equation x³−3x=−2 directly.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.r.b: You treated x=1 and −1 as a pair. Plug x=−1 into the equation to check.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.r.c: This is the result of factoring x³−3x+2=0 as (x−1)²(x+2)=0.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.r.d: You missed the double root x=1. x=1 is the point of tangency, so it lies on the tangent line.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s1.explain: x³−3x+2=(x−1)²(x+2), so the solutions are x=1 (double root, the point of tangency) and x=−2. At the point (−2, −2), the tangent line meets the curve again.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.prompt: Enter two or more different pairs (a, b) such that the tangent line to the curve y=x³−3x at the point (a, a³−3a) also meets the curve at a point (b, b³−3b) other than the point of tangency. (a and b are integers from −6 to 6 inclusive, and b≠a)
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a value for the x-coordinate a of the point of tangency, find the equation of the tangent line, and write the equation obtained by setting it equal to the curve.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.hint.1: Use the solution you already know in that equation (the point of tangency) to find the remaining solutions.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.var.a: x-coordinate a of the point of tangency
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.var.b: x-coordinate b of the point where it meets again
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from −6 to 6 inclusive.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a point different from the point of tangency.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.fail.c2: b must be different from a.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The point (b, b³−3b) lies on the tangent line.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The point (b, b³−3b) does not lie on the tangent line.
