n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.explain: Setting the equation of the tangent line at the point (a, a³−3a) equal to the curve gives (x−a)²(x+2a)=0, so the x-coordinate of the point where it meets again is b=−2a. (1, −2), (2, −4), and (−3, 6) are examples; (1, 1) is the point of tangency itself, and (1, −1) is not a point on the tangent line.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Looking at the (a, b) pairs you found, write the relationship expressing b in terms of a, and explain why that relationship holds.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the values of a and b from your examples side by side in a table and compare how many times a the value b is.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Consider that the combined equation is cubic and what kind of root x=a is (a single root or a double root), and write the three roots.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. Setting the tangent line equal to the curve gives ...
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that the cubic equation formed from the tangent line and the curve has a double root at the point of tangency?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you find b using the fact that the sum of the three roots is 0, or using factoring?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.model.0: b=−2a. Setting the tangent line equal to the curve gives a cubic equation of the form x³−3x=m(x−a)+a³−3a, and the point of tangency x=a is a double root, so it can be written as (x−a)²(x−b). The coefficient of x² is 0, so the sum of the three roots is a+a+b=0, giving b=−2a.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s2.because.model.1: I checked that it becomes (x−a)²(x+2a)=0. The point of tangency is a double root, so there is a factor (x−a)², and there is no x² term, so the remaining root is −2a, that is, b=−2a.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.prompt: Among the points on the curve y=x³−3x, for which x-coordinate does the tangent line at that point not meet the curve anywhere other than the point of tangency?
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.hint.0: Using the relationship you found in the previous step, find the x-coordinate of the point where it meets again for the point of tangency in each choice.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what happens when the point where it meets again becomes the same as the point of tangency.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.r.a: If a=−1, the tangent line meets the curve again at x=2.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.r.b: You considered the case where the x-coordinate of the point where it meets again becomes the same as the point of tangency.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.r.c: If a=1, the tangent line meets the curve again at x=−2.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.r.d: If a=2, the tangent line meets the curve again at x=−4.
n-m-h3-diffc-08.s.s3.explain: The x-coordinate of the point where it meets again is −2a, so this equals the point of tangency only when −2a=a, that is, a=0. The tangent line y=−3x meets the curve at the one point x=0, from x³=0. This point is also an inflection point of the curve.

n-m-h3-dist-01.title: Checking Gayoung's variance solution
n-m-h3-dist-01.topic: Probability distributions: expected value and variance of a discrete random variable
n-m-h3-dist-01.goal: Find the first line that goes wrong in a solution for variance, find the correct value, and check whether the result makes sense.
n-m-h3-dist-01.material: A random variable X takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 in order. Gayoung solved as below to find the variance V(X). (E(X²) is "the expected value of X squared," and {E(X)}² is "the square of the expected value.")
n-m-h3-dist-01.thinking.0: Follow the lines of the solution one by one and find the wrong line
n-m-h3-dist-01.thinking.1: Check whether the result fits the shape of the distribution
n-m-h3-dist-01.prereq.0: The expected value E(X) of a discrete random variable
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Gayoung's solution.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check in order from the top whether each line legitimately follows from the line right before it.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write the definitions of E(X) and E(X²) in words, and compare whether each line was calculated according to those definitions.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.line.1: The variance is found by V(X)=E(X²)−{E(X)}².
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.line.2: E(X²) is just E(X) squared, so E(X²)=1.6²=2.56
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. E(X²) is not "the square of the expected value"; it is the value obtained by first squaring each value of X, then multiplying by the probabilities and adding. Lines 4 and 5 continue from the result of line 3, so those calculations themselves are correct, but the conclusion is wrong.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.prompt: Fix the wrong line and find the values of E(X²) and V(X). Also write in one sentence why Gayoung's result V(X)=0 makes no sense for this distribution.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.hint.0: Square each of the values 0, 1, 2, 3 of X and multiply by the same probabilities.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put into words what a variance of 0 means about the values of X.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. E(X²) is ... and V(X) is ...
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate E(X²) directly using the square of each value?
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you say that E(X²) and {E(X)}² are different numbers?
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you say for what kind of distribution a variance of 0 is possible?
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.model.0: E(X²)=0²×0.1+1²×0.4+2²×0.3+3²×0.2=0.4+1.2+1.8=3.4. V(X)=3.4−1.6²=3.4−2.56=0.84, and since X takes different values 0, 1, 2, 3, the variance cannot be 0.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.model.1: You have to square each value, multiply by the probability, and add, so E(X²)=3.4 (=17/5) and V(X)=0.84. A variance of 0 would mean X always takes just one value, but that is not so here.
n-m-h3-dist-01.s.s2.model.2: E(X²)=3.4 and the variance is 0.84. A variance of 0 means all the values are the same, which is not the case here.

n-m-h3-dist-02.title: When can we call it a binomial distribution if we draw three balls?
n-m-h3-dist-02.topic: Probability distributions: conditions for a binomial distribution to hold
n-m-h3-dist-02.goal: Pick out the information that is absolutely necessary to judge whether it can be treated as a binomial distribution, and show with numbers how the probability changes when that information changes.
n-m-h3-dist-02.material: A box contains 3 white balls and 2 black balls. Seoyun said, "The number X of white balls when 3 balls are drawn follows the binomial distribution B(3, 3/5)." Whether Seoyun is right cannot be known from what is written so far.
n-m-h3-dist-02.thinking.0: Tell apart the information that is essential for the judgment from the information that is not
n-m-h3-dist-02.thinking.1: Check by calculation the difference that arises when the condition breaks
n-m-h3-dist-02.prereq.0: The meaning of the binomial distribution B(n,p): perform n independent trials, each with the same probability of success p
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.prompt: What must you know to judge whether Seoyun is right?
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.hint.0: First recall what properties the trials must have in order to use a binomial distribution.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.hint.1: Decide one by one whether each choice checks that property, or just asks about something already known.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.o.a: Count again to check that the box really has 3 white balls and 2 black balls
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.r.a: The number of balls has already been given. It is used to find the probability 3/5, but it does not tell you whether the same probability is kept every time.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.o.b: Check whether drawing 3 balls is a sufficiently large number of trials
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.r.b: A binomial distribution does not hold because the number of trials is large. Even if it is small, like n=3, it is a binomial distribution if the conditions are met.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.o.c: Check whether each drawn ball is put back in the box before the next ball is drawn
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.r.c: You are checking whether the contents of the box stay the same each time. This is the key condition for a binomial distribution.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.o.d: Check whether the order in which white balls come out is decided in advance
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.r.d: The order does not matter for the distribution of the number X of white balls. What decides whether it is a binomial distribution is whether the trials affect each other.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s1.explain: For B(3, 3/5), the probability of a white ball must be 3/5 every time a ball is drawn, with no influence between draws. If each drawn ball is put back, that holds, but if not, earlier results change later probabilities. The number of balls is already known, and the number of trials does not need to be large.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.prompt: Suppose 3 balls are drawn without putting them back. If the first ball was white, find the probability that the second ball is white, and use this to write why X cannot be B(3, 3/5) in this case.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of balls left in the box and the number of white balls after the first ball is drawn.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put that probability next to the probability for the first draw and compare them.
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If the first ball is white, the remaining balls are ...
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you count the number of remaining balls (4) and white balls (2) yourself?
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you say how the probability changing connects to "not independent"?
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you explain what happens when the balls are put back?
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.model.0: If the first ball is white, the remaining balls are 2 white out of 4, so the probability is 2/4=1/2. It differs from the original 3/5, so the condition that the probability is the same every time breaks, and it is not B(3, 3/5).
n-m-h3-dist-02.s.s2.model.1: If the balls are not put back, the result of the earlier draw changes the next probability. If a white ball is drawn first, the probability that the next is white is 2 out of 4 (0.5), which differs from 3/5, so the trials are not independent and it cannot be a binomial distribution.

n-m-h3-dist-03.title: Two games with the same mean: is the spread the same too?
n-m-h3-dist-03.topic: Probability distributions: variance of a sum and of a multiple of random variables
n-m-h3-dist-03.goal: Judge by comparing the distributions directly whether having the same mean means the spread is the same too, and explain the reason using variance.
n-m-h3-dist-03.material: Let X be the number shown when a standard six-sided die is rolled. There are two games. In Game A, you roll the die once and your score is twice the number shown (2X), and in Game B, you roll the die twice and your score is the sum of the two numbers (X₁+X₂). In both games the mean score is 7 points. Youngsu said, "Since the means are the same, the spread of scores should be the same too."
n-m-h3-dist-03.thinking.0: Choose a comparison method that tests the claim
n-m-h3-dist-03.thinking.1: Build evidence for a counterexample using concrete probabilities
n-m-h3-dist-03.thinking.2: Generalize using the rules for how variance changes
n-m-h3-dist-03.prereq.0: Expected value and variance of a discrete random variable
n-m-h3-dist-03.prereq.1: Variance of the sum of two independent random variables V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable comparison for testing Youngsu's claim?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.hint.0: Youngsu's claim is about the "spread," not the mean. What data would show that?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, consider whether it could reveal a difference between the two games.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.o.a: Recalculate to check that the means of the two games really are the same, 7 points
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.r.a: It was already given that the means are the same. Checking the same value again will not tell you about the spread.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.o.b: Use the fact that the mean of one die roll is 3.5 to compare the two games
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.r.b: This only tells you that the mean of 7 points in both games comes from this value. It does not reveal the spread.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.o.c: Put side by side the scores possible in the two games and the probability of each score
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.r.c: You are comparing the whole distribution of scores. This is a way to see directly whether the shape of the distribution can differ even when the means are the same.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.o.d: Roll the die many times and see whether the average scores of the two games get close to 7 points
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.r.d: It shows whether the average gathers near 7, but it tells you nothing about the spread.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s1.explain: The mean is just one summary of a distribution. If you put the scores and probabilities side by side, you can see right away whether the shape of the distribution can differ even with the same mean. Recomputing the mean or only checking whether it gathers near the mean cannot test Youngsu's claim.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.prompt: Find the probability that the score is 2 or 12 in each game (the combined probability of the two cases), and explain that Youngsu's claim is not right.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write down which die numbers give 2 points and 12 points in Game A.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.hint.1: In Game B, count all the ordered pairs of two numbers that give 2 points and 12 points, and find how many of the 36 outcomes they are.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. In Game A, to get 2 points ...
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you count the ways to get 2 points and 12 points in Game B as ordered pairs yourself?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you say that the shape of a distribution can differ even when the means are the same?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you say how the difference between the two probabilities shows the difference in spread?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.model.0: In Game A, a roll of 1 or 6 gives 2 or 12 points, so it is 2/6=1/3. In Game B, there are only two outcomes, (1,1) and (6,6), so it is 2/36=1/18. With the same mean, the probabilities of the extreme scores differ a lot, so the spread cannot be called the same.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s2.model.1: The probability of getting 2 or 12 points is one third in A and one eighteenth in B. Even though the mean is 7 in both, A gives far more extreme scores more often, so the variances differ.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.prompt: Let V be the variance of the number X shown on one roll of the die. What are the variances of the Game A score 2X and the Game B score X₁+X₂ (the two rolls do not affect each other)?
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.hint.0: 2X is one result doubled, and X₁+X₂ is two different results added. Think about the two separately.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.hint.1: Put a simple number in for V (for example V=1), find the two variances for each choice, and compare whether they match the spread of the two games you saw in the previous step.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.o.a: The variance of 2X is 2V, and the variance of X₁+X₂ is 2V
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.r.a: You treated 2X as the same as "X added twice." Adding the same value twice is different from adding the results of two separate rolls.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.o.b: The variance of 2X is 4V, and the variance of X₁+X₂ is 2V
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.r.b: For 2X, every value is doubled, so the variance becomes 2² times as large; for the sum of two independent results, the variances add, so it is 2 times as large.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.o.c: The variance of 2X is 4V, and the variance of X₁+X₂ is 4V
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.r.c: You applied the rule that multiplying by a constant squares the factor in the variance to the sum of two rolls as well. For an independent sum, the variances simply add.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.o.d: The variance of 2X is 2V, and the variance of X₁+X₂ is 4V
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.r.d: You swapped the variance of a multiple and the variance of a sum.
n-m-h3-dist-03.s.s3.explain: V(2X)=2²V=4V, and for the sum of two independent random variables, V(X₁+X₂)=V+V=2V. The means are both 7, but the variances differ: 4V and 2V. (The variance of a die roll is V=35/12, so they are 35/3 and 35/6.)

n-m-h3-dist-04.title: Is the expected value the value that comes up most often?
n-m-h3-dist-04.topic: Probability distributions: the meaning of expected value
n-m-h3-dist-04.goal: Sort out the definition and meaning of expected value, and build and check a distribution in which the expected value is neither a possible value nor the value with the greatest probability.
n-m-h3-dist-04.material: There is a random variable X taking the values 0, 1, 2. Once you decide the probabilities of the three values in the probability distribution table, the expected value E(X) is determined.
n-m-h3-dist-04.thinking.0: Sort statements about expected value into true and false
n-m-h3-dist-04.thinking.1: Build a distribution that meets the conditions and use it as a counterexample
n-m-h3-dist-04.prereq.0: The probability distribution table of a discrete random variable
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the correct statements about the expected value E(X).
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, think about whether you can test it by making a probability distribution table.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.hint.1: First test with a simple distribution where the values are only 0 and 1 and the two probabilities are equal.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.o.a: E(X) is one of the values X can take
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.r.a: Even if X can only take integer values, E(X) can be a decimal. For example, the mean number of heads in a coin toss can be a value like 0.5.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.o.b: E(X) is the sum of each value multiplied by its probability.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.o.c: E(X) is the value of X with the greatest probability.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.r.c: You treated the expected value and "the value with the greatest probability" as the same thing. The most probable value is a separate idea, and the two are usually different.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.o.d: If a trial is repeated many times, the mean of the observed values gathers near E(X).
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.r.d: You correctly described where the mean settles as the trial is repeated.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s1.explain: E(X) is the sum of value × probability, and it is the value the mean settles toward when the trial is repeated many times. There is no guarantee that it is a value X can actually take, and no guarantee that it is the value with the greatest probability.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.prompt: Suppose X takes the values 0, 1, 2. Choose their probabilities as whole-number percentages (p0, p1, p2). Conditions: ① each of the three probabilities is at least 1% and they sum to 100% ② the value with the greatest probability is 2 alone ③ E(X)≤1.2 (the expected value is at least 0.8 less than 2, the most probable value). Make 3 different examples (with different values of p2).
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.hint.0: First choose p0, p1, p2 so that they add up to 100, and make p2 the largest.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compute E(X)=(p1+2·p2)/100 and check whether it is at most 1.2. If it is too big, try increasing p0 or p1.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.hint.2: Change p2 to different values such as 45 and 39, and choose p0 and p1 again each time.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The probabilities are whole numbers of at least 1% and they sum to 100%.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The three probabilities must be whole numbers of at least 1% and must sum to 100.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Only the value 2 has the greatest probability.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.fail.c2: P(X=2) must be greater than each of the other two probabilities (it must not be equal to either).
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s2.explain: E(X)=(p1+2·p2)/100. For example, for (40, 15, 45), E(X)=1.05, and the value with the greatest probability is 2. E(X)=1.05 is not a value X can take, and it also differs from 2, the value with the greatest probability. Examples that only reorder (p0, p1, p2) do not need to be counted as the same example.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of your examples and, using its numbers, explain why it is wrong to read E(X) as "the value that comes up most often" or "the value that actually comes up."
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.hint.0: Find E(X) for your chosen example and compare it with the values X can take: 0, 1, 2.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write down how the value with the greatest probability relates to the value of E(X).
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate E(X) yourself for the example you chose?
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why E(X) is a value that cannot actually occur?
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say how the value with the greatest probability differs from E(X)?
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.model.0: For example, for (40, 15, 45), E(X)=0.15 + 0.9 = 1.05. This is not a value X can take, and the value with the greatest probability is 2. So E(X) is neither the value that comes up most often nor a value that can come up.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.model.1: For (37, 24, 39), E(X)=1.02, but X can only be 0, 1, or 2, so 1.02 can never occur. The value with the greatest probability is 2, at 39%, so it differs from the expected value.
n-m-h3-dist-04.s.s3.model.2: For (25, 36, 39), E(X)=1.14 is not a value X can take, and it also differs from 2, the most likely value.

n-m-h3-dist-05.title: If the Probability Is 0, Can It Really Never Happen?
n-m-h3-dist-05.topic: Probability distributions: the probability of a single point for a continuous random variable
n-m-h3-dist-05.goal: Decide whether a value can occur when its probability at a single point of a continuous random variable is 0, and explain that judgment, and the effect of including or excluding endpoints, in words a friend can understand.
n-m-h3-dist-05.material: A bus arrives equally likely at any moment between 0 and 10 minutes from now. The waiting time X (minutes) can be any value from 0 to 10 inclusive. The probability of an interval is proportional to its length: P(a≤X≤b)=(b−a)/10. Jia wrote up the following.
n-m-h3-dist-05.thinking.0: Find the flaw in the reasoning of a solution
n-m-h3-dist-05.thinking.1: Explain a difficult concept using simple words and examples
n-m-h3-dist-05.thinking.2: Decide whether including or excluding an endpoint changes the probability
n-m-h3-dist-05.prereq.0: The meaning of a continuous random variable and a probability density function (probability is the area over an interval)
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the incorrect line in Jia's write-up.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.hint.0: Check in order whether each line follows legitimately from the line before it.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.hint.1: Find the lines that say "the probability is 0" and "it cannot happen," and test whether the reasoning connecting them is valid by thinking about a bus that actually arrives.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.line.0: X can take every value from 0 to 10, and P(a≤X≤b)=(b−a)/10.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.line.1: P(X=4) is the probability of an interval of length 0, so it is (4−4)/10=0.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.line.2: Since the probability is 0, the bus arriving at exactly 4 minutes is something that cannot happen.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. For a continuous random variable, even if the probability at a single point is 0, that value is not necessarily impossible. There are infinitely many values between 0 and 10, so each one has probability 0, yet some value does occur. Lines 4 and 5 follow correctly.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.prompt: Write a text message explaining to Jia. Say which part of her reasoning needs to be fixed, and how P(X≤4) and P(X<4) compare in size, using simple words and an example.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine how small the chance is of picking out exactly one value between 0 and 10.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.hint.1: Restate the same idea in terms of area: what is the area of a single line with no width?
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The probability of exactly 4 minutes is ...
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use words and an example that a middle school friend could understand?
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that "probability 0" does not mean "impossible"?
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say why the probability is the same whether or not the endpoint is included?
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.model.0: There are infinitely many values between 0 and 10 minutes, so the chance of hitting exactly 4 minutes is so tiny, close to 0, that it becomes 0. But that doesn't mean the bus never arrives at 4 minutes, because it does arrive at some moment. Whether 4 minutes is included or not, the probability it adds is 0, so P(X≤4) and P(X<4) are equal.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.model.1: Because it's continuous, even if a single point has probability 0, the bus can still come at that moment. It's like a single point on a line having area 0 while the line still has points on it. Adding or removing one point doesn't change the probability, so P(X≤4)=P(X<4)=0.4.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s2.model.2: P(X=4)=0, but the arrival time is one definite value, so it isn't impossible for that value to come up. A single point has no width, so adding or removing it doesn't change the probability, and the two probabilities are equal.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.prompt: Which of the following is correct?
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how each statement depends on the value of P(X=a).
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.hint.1: For a die roll X (discrete), find P(X≤3) and P(X<3) and compare them.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.o.a: Even for a continuous random variable, P(X≤a) is always greater than P(X<a).
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.r.a: You thought that "≤" includes more cases, so its probability must be greater. For a continuous random variable, the probability at a single point is 0, so the two are equal.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.o.b: For a continuous random variable, if P(X=a)=0, then X cannot equal a.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.r.b: You treated probability 0 as the same as impossible. For a continuous random variable, a value with probability 0 can actually occur.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.o.c: For a continuous random variable, the probability is the same whether or not the endpoints of an interval are included.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.r.c: The probability at a single point is 0, so including or excluding an endpoint does not change the probability.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.o.d: For a discrete random variable as well, P(X≤a)=P(X<a) always holds.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.r.d: For a discrete random variable, P(X=a) can be nonzero, so the two may not be equal.
n-m-h3-dist-05.s.s3.explain: For a continuous random variable, P(X=a)=0, so P(a≤X≤b)=P(a<X<b)=P(a≤X<b)=P(a<X≤b). For a discrete random variable, P(X=a)>0 is possible, so including or excluding an endpoint can change the probability.

n-m-h3-dist-06.title: If You Flip a Coin Many Times, Will Exactly Half Be Heads?
n-m-h3-dist-06.topic: Probability distributions: the binomial distribution and the number of trials
n-m-h3-dist-06.goal: Check step by step how the probability of "exactly half" and the probability of "near half" move differently as the number of trials grows, and revise your first idea.
n-m-h3-dist-06.material: Let X be the number of heads when a fair coin is flipped. Information is revealed one piece at a time. (Probabilities for large numbers of flips were found with a calculator.)
n-m-h3-dist-06.thinking.0: Revise your judgment as information grows
n-m-h3-dist-06.thinking.1: Distinguish the probability of an exact value from the probability of a range
n-m-h3-dist-06.prereq.0: The binomial distribution B(n,1/2) and P(X=k)=nCk (1/2)ⁿ
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.prompt: At each step, choose a judgment based on what you know so far.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, consider whether the answer to the same question should change.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write side by side the probabilities of getting 4, 5, and 6 heads in 10 flips, and see how such neighboring counts change as the number of flips grows.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how likely is it to get exactly 5 heads?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.after: C(10,5)/2¹⁰=252/1024≈0.246. Even though this is the most likely count, its probability is only about 25%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: About 50%: because exactly half is the most natural outcome
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought that getting half is the most natural outcome, so its probability should be 50%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: About 25%: because it is the middle count, but it shares probability with neighboring counts such as 4 and 6
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You saw that even the most likely middle count shares probability with its neighboring counts.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Under 5%: because hitting it exactly is rare
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought that hitting the exact count is very rare.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.info: This time you flip the coin 100 times, and the question is the probability of getting exactly 50 heads.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does it compare with the roughly 25% for 10 flips?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.after: C(100,50)/2¹⁰⁰≈0.080. As the number of flips grows, the probability of "exactly half" actually gets smaller.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It gets smaller: because there are far more neighboring counts with similar probability
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You saw that more neighboring counts have probability similar to the middle count, so the share of the single middle value shrinks.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It gets larger: because the more you flip, the closer you get to half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You thought that the more you flip, the more exactly half comes up.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It stays about the same: because it is still half and half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked only at the fact that it is half and half and did not see the effect of the changed number of flips.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Now the question is the probability that, in 100 flips, the proportion of heads is between 40% and 60% inclusive (40 to 60 heads). In 10 flips, the probability of getting 4 to 6 heads is about 66%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What happens to this probability for 100 flips?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.after: The probability of 40 to 60 heads is about 0.965. The probability of exactly 50 went down, but the probability of landing near half actually goes up.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Lower than 66%: because the probability of exactly half also went down
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You thought that since the probability of exactly half decreased, the probability near half must have decreased too.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: About 8%: because the probability for 100 flips was 8%
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You mistook the probability of exactly 50 for the probability of a range.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Over 90%: because results cluster near half
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You looked at the combined probability of the range near half, not of the exact value.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s1.reflect: At first it is easy to think that "the more you flip, the more exactly half comes up." But as the number of flips grows, the probability of exactly half goes down, while the probability that the proportion of heads lands near half goes up. You need to read "an exact value" and "a range" as different things.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.prompt: Write how the probability of getting exactly half heads and the probability of landing near half each change as the number of flips grows. If your thinking differs from your first idea, include that too.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write side by side the probability of "exactly half" for 10 flips and for 100 flips.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write down how the probability of "near half" differed between the two cases.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Compared with 10 flips, for 100 flips the probability of exactly ...
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the probability values in the two cases?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish the probability of an exact value from the probability of a range?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say how your first idea changed?
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.model.0: As the number of flips grows, the probability of exactly half drops from about 25% for 10 flips to about 8% for 100 flips. But the probability of landing near half actually rises: for 100 flips, the probability of 40 to 60 heads is over 96%.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.model.1: At first I thought that flipping many times would give exactly half, but that was wrong. The probability of exactly half goes down, while the probability that the proportion of heads gathers near half goes up.
n-m-h3-dist-06.s.s2.model.2: The more you flip, the smaller the share of the single outcome of exactly half becomes, but the probability of landing close to half grows.

n-m-h3-dist-07.title: Building a Binomial Distribution from a Mean and Variance
n-m-h3-dist-07.topic: Probability distributions: the mean and variance of the binomial distribution
n-m-h3-dist-07.goal: Use the relationship between the mean and variance of a binomial distribution to rule out impossible combinations, and build binomial distributions that meet given conditions to find a rule.
n-m-h3-dist-07.material: You want to describe some data with a binomial distribution B(n,p). Here n is a natural number and p is a number between 0 and 1. The mean of a binomial distribution is np and the variance is np(1−p).
n-m-h3-dist-07.thinking.0: Check the hidden conditions (n is a natural number, 0<p<1)
n-m-h3-dist-07.thinking.1: Build your own examples that meet the conditions and find a rule
n-m-h3-dist-07.prereq.0: The mean np and variance np(1−p) of the binomial distribution B(n, p)
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.prompt: Which of the following pairs of mean and variance can actually occur for a binomial distribution B(n, p)?
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.hint.0: Set the mean equal to np and the variance equal to np(1−p), then see what is left when you divide the variance by the mean.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check for each option whether the p you find is between 0 and 1 and n is a natural number.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.r.a: Here the variance is greater than the mean. Since the variance is np(1−p), it cannot be greater than the mean np.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.r.b: If you find p and then n=np÷p, n is not a natural number. You overlooked the condition that n is a natural number.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.r.c: If the variance equals the mean, then 1−p=1, so p=0. Then the mean would be 0, which does not fit.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.r.d: Variance ÷ mean = 1−p determines p, and n also comes out as a natural number, so this is possible.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s1.explain: Variance ÷ mean = 1−p. For (8, 6), 1−p=3/4, p=1/4, and n=8÷(1/4)=32, so it is possible. For (10, 12), 1−p>1 so p<0; for (8, 5), p=3/8 and n=64/3, which is not a natural number; and for (6, 6), p=0.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.prompt: Build 3 different binomial distributions B(n, p) with mean 12 and variance at most 8. Write n as a natural number and p as a whole-number percentage (p%). (e.g. for p=25%, write 25)
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.hint.0: Start by writing pairs of n and p that satisfy mean np=12 (p as a whole-number percentage).
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.hint.1: For each pair, compute the variance 12(1−p) and check whether it is at most 8.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.ok.c1: n is a natural number and p is between 1% and 99%.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number and p must be a whole-number percentage from 1 to 99.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The variance np(1−p) is at most 8.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s2.explain: From np=12, p=q/100. For the variance np(1−p)=12(1−p) to be at most 8, p must be at least 1/3. Examples where both n and p fit the conditions are (30, 40%), (25, 48%), (24, 50%), (20, 60%), (16, 75%), and (15, 80%).
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.prompt: Looking at your three distributions, write what relationship exists between p and the variance when the means are equal.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write p and the variance for the three distributions side by side, like a table.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.hint.1: See whether the variance gets larger or smaller as p gets larger.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. When the mean is the same, 12, as p gets larger the variance ...
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually calculate the variance of the three distributions?
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the relationship between p and the variance together with the condition that the means are equal?
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use the fact that the variance can be written as 12(1−p)?
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.model.0: When the mean np is the same, 12, the variance is 12(1−p), so the larger p is, the smaller the variance. For example, p=40% gives 7.2 and p=75% gives 3.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.model.1: All three distributions have mean 12, but the variance got smaller as p got larger. For example, 6 when p=50% and 2.4 when p=80%: the higher the success probability, the less spread out it is.
n-m-h3-dist-07.s.s3.model.2: When the means are equal, the larger p is, the smaller the variance 12(1-p) becomes.

n-m-h3-dist-08.title: A Solution That Gave Probability 2: Which Line Went Wrong?
n-m-h3-dist-08.topic: Probability distributions: the domain of a probability density function
n-m-h3-dist-08.goal: Recognize that you cannot integrate outside the interval where a probability density function is nonzero, find the line that went wrong, and find the correct probability.
n-m-h3-dist-08.material: A continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x)=kx (0≤x≤2), and f(x)=0 for all other x. Here is Minjun's solution for finding the constant k and P(1≤X≤3).
n-m-h3-dist-08.thinking.0: Find the first line in a solution that goes wrong
n-m-h3-dist-08.thinking.1: Check whether a result is within the range possible for a probability
n-m-h3-dist-08.prereq.0: Properties of a probability density function (total area 1)
n-m-h3-dist-08.prereq.1: Definite integrals or areas of shapes
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Minjun's solution.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.hint.0: Check from the top whether each line follows legitimately from the line before it.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, compare the graph used over that interval of x with the f(x) given in the problem.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.line.0: f(x)=kx (0≤x≤2) and f(x)=0 elsewhere, and the total area is 1.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.line.1: Using the area of a triangle, (1/2)×2×2k=2k=1, so k=1/2.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.line.2: P(1≤X≤3) is the area between the graph of y=x/2 and the x-axis from x=1 to x=3.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. For a probability density function, f(x)=0 when x is greater than 2, so the graph of y=x/2 is used only up to x=2. So the area from x=2 to 3 should not be added. Lines 4 and 5 simply carry over the wrong interval from line 3.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.prompt: Fix the incorrect line and find the value of P(1≤X≤3). Also write why Minjun's answer of 2 cannot be a probability.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.hint.0: First sketch where the graph is nonzero.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about the range of values a probability can take.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. f(x) is nonzero only when x is ..., so ...
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check the interval where f(x) is nonzero before solving?
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate 3/4 yourself (by integration or as a trapezoid)?
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check your answer using the fact that a probability cannot exceed 1?
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.model.0: When x is greater than 2, f(x)=0, so you only need to compute from x=1 to 2, and the area is (1/2)×(1/2+1)×1=3/4. Minjun's answer of 2 is impossible because a probability cannot be greater than 1, yet it exceeds 1.
n-m-h3-dist-08.s.s2.model.1: P(1≤X≤3)=P(1≤X≤2)=∫₁² x/2 dx=3/4. Since the total area is 1, the area of an interval cannot be 2.

n-m-h3-est-01.title: Checking a Solution for the Probability That 9 Bottles Average at Least 503 mL
n-m-h3-est-01.topic: Statistical estimation: the distribution of the sample mean
n-m-h3-est-01.goal: Compare the mean and standard deviation of the sample mean's distribution with the population's values, find and fix the wrong line in a solution, and explain why a probability for the sample mean differs from the probability for an individual value.
n-m-h3-est-01.material: At a beverage factory, the volume of one bottle follows a normal distribution with mean 500 mL and standard deviation 6 mL. Haeun, who works in quality control, randomly sampled 9 bottles and found the probability that the mean volume X̄ is at least 503 mL. Part of the standard normal table: P(0≤Z≤0.5)=0.1915, P(0≤Z≤1.5)=0.4332, P(0≤Z≤3)=0.4987. (Z is a random variable that follows the normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.)
n-m-h3-est-01.thinking.0: Read carefully to tell a single value from the sample mean
n-m-h3-est-01.thinking.1: Compare the mean and standard deviation of the sample mean with the population's values
n-m-h3-est-01.thinking.2: Explain how the corrected probability differs, and in which direction, from the probability for an individual value
n-m-h3-est-01.prereq.0: How to standardize a normal distribution and read the standard normal table
n-m-h3-est-01.prereq.1: The relationship between the mean and standard deviation of the sample mean and those of the population
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Haeun's solution.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and sort out whether it is about "a single bottle" or "the mean of 9 bottles."
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the two values, the mean and the standard deviation of the distribution of X̄, one by one with the values for the distribution of a single bottle.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.line.0: The population is normal with mean 500 and standard deviation 6, and the sample mean of 9 bottles is X̄.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.line.1: The mean of X̄ is 500, the same as the population mean.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.line.2: The standard deviation of X̄ is 6, the same as the population standard deviation.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The standard deviation of the sample mean X̄ is the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size: 6/√9=2. So X̄ follows a normal distribution with mean 500 and standard deviation 2, and P(X̄≥503)=P(Z≥1.5)=0.5−0.4332=0.0668. Lines 4 and 5 carry over the 6 from line 3, so their results are wrong (0.3085 corresponds to the probability that a single bottle is at least 503).
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.prompt: Use the corrected solution to find P(X̄≥503). Then explain in one or two sentences how this probability differs from the probability that a single bottle's volume is at least 503 mL, and why.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write the standard deviation of X̄, then find the standardized value of 503.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare it with the standardized value for a single bottle, and think about how the spread has changed.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The standard deviation of X̄ is ..., so ... compared with a single bottle ...
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the corrected standard deviation being 2, not 6, to √9?
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain, with a reason, why the probability became smaller than for a single bottle (about 0.31)?
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you put into words the idea that when you average 9 bottles, high ones and low ones offset each other?
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.model.0: The standard deviation of the sample mean is 6÷√9=2. P(X̄≥503)=P(Z≥1.5)=0.5−0.4332=0.0668. When you average 9 bottles, high bottles and low bottles offset each other, so the mean is less spread out than a single bottle, and the probability of being at least 503 is much smaller.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.model.1: X̄ follows N(500, 2²), so Z=(503−500)/2=1.5 and the probability is about 6.68%. For a single bottle the standard deviation is 6, but for the mean it shrinks to 2 and clusters more tightly around 500, so the probability of being at least 503 is smaller.
n-m-h3-est-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: The key point is the statement that the standard deviation shrank from 6 to 2.

n-m-h3-est-02.title: What Do You Need to Know to Find the Length of a Confidence Interval?
n-m-h3-est-02.topic: Statistical estimation: confidence interval for a population mean
n-m-h3-est-02.goal: Distinguish what determines the length of a confidence interval for a population mean from what determines its position, and build your own survey plan that satisfies a length condition.
n-m-h3-est-02.material: You want to estimate the population mean m of teenagers' average daily reading time (in hours). The population follows a normal distribution and the population standard deviation σ is known. If the sample size is n and the sample mean is x̄, the 95% confidence interval is x̄−1.96×σ/√n ≤ m ≤ x̄+1.96×σ/√n. The research team has not started the survey yet, and first wants to calculate only the "length of the confidence interval."
n-m-h3-est-02.thinking.0: Sort out the information that is needed from the information that is not
n-m-h3-est-02.thinking.1: Distinguish the factors that affect length from those that affect position
n-m-h3-est-02.thinking.2: Build several plans that meet a condition and verify them
n-m-h3-est-02.prereq.0: The confidence interval formula for a population mean from a normal distribution with known population standard deviation
n-m-h3-est-02.prereq.1: The z-value for a given confidence level in the standard normal distribution (about 1.96 for 95%)
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.prompt: Before starting the survey, choose all the information you must know to calculate the length of the 95% confidence interval. (Do not choose what is not needed.)
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.hint.0: Subtract the lower endpoint from the upper endpoint directly and write the expression for the length first.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the letters into those that remain in that expression and those that disappear.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.o.a: The value of the sample mean x̄
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.r.a: x̄ determines the center of the interval. You can check whether x̄ remains in the distance between the two endpoints by subtracting the lower endpoint from the upper endpoint in the expression.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.r.b: n appears in σ/√n and changes the length of the interval. Think about how the interval changes when the sample is larger.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.o.c: The standard deviation s computed from the sample
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.r.c: The population standard deviation σ is already known, so s does not appear in the expression for the length. Check which letters appear in the expression.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.r.d: σ appears in the length expression σ/√n. If you do not know the spread, you cannot say how wide the interval is.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.o.e: The value of the population mean m
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.r.e: The population mean is the very value we are trying to estimate, so it is not yet known, and it does not appear in the expression for the length of the interval either.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s1.explain: Subtracting the lower endpoint from the upper endpoint makes x̄ disappear and leaves only 2×1.96×σ/√n. The 95% confidence level is already fixed, so the length is determined by σ and n, and the sample mean only determines the position of the interval. The population mean m is the value being estimated, and the sample standard deviation s is not used in the length expression because σ is known.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.prompt: Assume σ is at least 4, and make survey plans so that the length of the 95% confidence interval is at most 2 hours. Enter σ and the sample size n for each. The two plans must have different values of σ; make 2 plans. (n is a natural number at most 400.)
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.hint.0: Turn the condition that the length 2×1.96×σ/√n is at most 2 into an inequality in √n.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose σ first, then choose an n that satisfies that condition. Do it once more with a different σ.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.ok.c2: n is a natural number at most 400.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.fail.c2: n is not a natural number at most 400.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The length of the interval is at most 2.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The length of the interval is greater than 2.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s2.explain: For the length 2×1.96×σ/√n to be at most 2, √n must be at least 1.96σ. With σ=5, n=100 the length is 1.96, and with σ=10, n=400 the length is 1.96. When σ is large, n has to be much larger. σ=5, n=25 gives a length of 3.92, which does not work.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.prompt: With the same plan (σ=2, n=64, 95% confidence), a survey was done twice and the sample means were 2.7 and 3.2. Find the two confidence intervals, and compare their lengths and positions.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.hint.0: For each sample mean, add and subtract the value of 1.96×2/√64 to write the interval.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.hint.1: Find the difference between the upper and lower endpoints for each interval, then also compare the midpoints.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. For 2.7 it is ... to ..., for 3.2 it is ... to ..., and the length is ...
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate the interval 2.21 to 3.19 yourself for sample mean 2.7?
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the lengths of the two intervals with numbers?
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you connect the fact that the length is determined by σ, n, and the confidence level, while x̄ only determines the position?
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.model.0: For sample mean 2.7, 2.7±1.96×2/8=2.7±0.49, that is, 2.21 to 3.19, and for 3.2 it is 2.71 to 3.69. Both intervals have the same length, 0.98, and depending on the sample mean only the position shifts, by 0.5.
n-m-h3-est-02.s.s3.model.1: The length is the same, about 0.98, and only the center (the sample mean) differs, so the interval shifts 0.5 to the right. The length is determined only by σ, n, and the confidence level, and the sample mean determines only the position of the interval.

n-m-h3-est-03.title: A Survey of 900 Respondents or a Random Survey of 60: Which Should You Trust?
n-m-h3-est-03.topic: Statistical estimation: bias in sample surveys
n-m-h3-est-03.goal: Distinguish a sample being large from a sample being representative of the population, and explain why bias that comes from the way a sample is chosen does not go away when the sample size grows.
n-m-h3-est-03.material: You want to find the average daily study time of all 1200 students in a school. Method A posted a survey link on the school website and took the mean of the 900 students who responded on their own: 3.1 hours. Method B asked 60 students chosen with random numbers from the student roster, and all of them answered: the mean is 2.4 hours.
n-m-h3-est-03.thinking.0: Evaluate sample size and sampling method separately
n-m-h3-est-03.thinking.1: Spot bias from a selection process such as voluntary response
n-m-h3-est-03.thinking.2: Judge the strength of the evidence and explain it
n-m-h3-est-03.prereq.0: The meaning of population and sample
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the survey that is more trustworthy for estimating the average study time of all students.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether, in each method, every student in the school has the same chance of ending up in the sample.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think, using an example, about whether "the sample is large" and "the sample represents all students" mean the same thing.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.o.a: B: because it was drawn from the roster with random numbers, so every student had the same chance
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.o.b: A: because the sample of 900 is much larger, so the sample mean is close to the population mean
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.r.b: It is true that a larger sample reduces the scatter caused by chance. But if who ends up in the sample is skewed in one direction, that bias does not shrink with size.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.o.c: Neither can be used: because only some students, not all, were surveyed
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.r.c: A sample survey is, by design, a way of estimating the whole from a part. The question is whether the way the part is chosen represents the population.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.o.d: Use both: just average the two means, 3.1 and 2.4
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.r.d: Mixing biased data with other data leaves the bias in. You first have to ask which data represents the population.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s1.explain: In the website survey, students who are interested or have time respond on their own, so the chance of being chosen from the population differs from student to student. This kind of selection bias does not disappear even if the number of respondents increases. In B, the sample is small at 60, so scatter due to chance is larger, but every student was chosen with the same chance, so the sample mean scatters around the population mean, which makes it the more trustworthy basis for the estimate.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.prompt: Method A has a much larger sample of 900, yet it is hard to trust its mean of 3.1 hours as an estimate of the average for all students. Explain why, relating it to the sample getting larger.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine how students who see the survey link but do not respond might differ from those who do.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether that difference shrinks if you double the respondents from 900.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. A includes only ... students, so ... even if the sample gets larger ...
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you point out who ends up in the sample in A (the selection process)?
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the bias remains even when the sample gets larger?
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you connect it to why B is trustworthy (the same chance)?
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.model.0: The website survey includes only students who respond on their own, so certain students, such as those very interested in studying, may be over-represented. This bias stays the same whether there are 900 respondents or 9000, so it is hard to trust even though the sample is large.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.model.1: A is a sample made up only of people who responded voluntarily, so it does not represent all students. No matter how many in the sample, if the way of choosing is skewed in one direction, the mean stays off from the population mean.
n-m-h3-est-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: Both "voluntarily" and "does not represent" are meaningful expressions.

n-m-h3-est-04.title: Can a Skewed Waiting Time Be Treated as Normal Once You Take Its Mean?
n-m-h3-est-04.topic: Statistical estimation: the distribution of the sample mean
n-m-h3-est-04.goal: Judge, as information is revealed one piece at a time, when a normal distribution can be used for the sample mean if the population is not normal, and explain why the judgment changes.
n-m-h3-est-04.material: At a snack bar, the waiting time (in minutes) from ordering until the food arrives has mean 10 minutes and standard deviation 10 minutes. Most customers wait a short time, but a few wait a very long time, so the distribution is skewed with a long right tail and is not normal. Part of the standard normal table: P(0≤Z≤1)=0.3413, P(0≤Z≤1.2)=0.3849.
n-m-h3-est-04.thinking.0: Revise a judgment when new information appears
n-m-h3-est-04.thinking.1: Distinguish the formulas for the sample mean's mean and standard deviation from the shape of its distribution
n-m-h3-est-04.thinking.2: Explain the conditions under which a normal approximation is possible
n-m-h3-est-04.prereq.0: The mean and standard deviation of the sample mean (m, σ/√n)
n-m-h3-est-04.prereq.1: How to read the standard normal table
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first check whether what is being calculated is "one customer's waiting time" or "the mean of several customers."
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.hint.1: Separate what a formula can tell you (the mean and standard deviation) from what concerns shape (whether it is normal).
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.info: A staff member says, "Let's treat the waiting time as N(10, 10²) and calculate the probability that one customer waits 20 minutes or more as P(Z≥1)=0.5−0.3413=0.1587."
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which is the most appropriate judgment about this calculation?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The waiting-time distribution is not normal, so 0.1587 from the normal table is only an approximation, not the true value, and there is little reason to trust it.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 0.1587 is exact because we know the mean and standard deviation.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought that knowing the mean and standard deviation tells you the shape of the distribution too. With a different shape, the probability can differ even with the same mean and standard deviation.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is not normal, so 0.1587 is hard to trust as it stands.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not normal, so this probability cannot be found by any method.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If you know the shape, you can find it another way. The key point right now is that the value calculated with a normal distribution is hard to trust as it stands.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.info: This time it is about X̄, the mean waiting time of 36 randomly sampled customers. The mean of the sample mean is 10 and its standard deviation is 10/√36=5/3. The staff member says, "Let's calculate the probability that X̄ is at least 12 minutes as P(Z≥1.2)=0.5−0.3849=0.1151."
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Which is the most appropriate judgment about this calculation?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Even if the population is not normal, when the sample size n is large enough (usually 30 or more), the distribution of the sample mean X̄ is close to a normal distribution with mean m and standard deviation σ/√n. So 0.1151 can be used as an approximation.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The population is not normal, so the distribution of X̄ cannot be normal either.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You treated the distribution of one customer and the distribution of the mean of 36 as the same. Taking a mean can change the shape of the distribution.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Even with 36, the skewed shape of the population stays as it is in the distribution of X̄.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even as the sample gets larger, the distribution of individual values stays the same, but the distribution of the means changes shape.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The sample is large enough that the distribution of X̄ is close to normal.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.info: The staff member suggests using the same method for the mean of 3 customers: "Let's say X̄ follows a normal distribution with mean 10 and standard deviation 10/√3."
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which is the most appropriate judgment about this suggestion?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The mean m and standard deviation σ/√n of the sample mean hold even when n is small. But the claim that the shape is close to normal applies when n is large enough, so with a skewed population and n=3, the approximation can be rough.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The formulas can be used, but treating it as normal is still hard to trust.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: As long as n is greater than 1, treating it as normal is good enough.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You shortened "the approximation gets better as the sample grows" to "a little bigger is enough." A skewed distribution needs a larger sample.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: n is small, so even the mean and standard deviation formulas cannot be used.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The mean and standard deviation formulas hold even for a small sample. What changes is the shape of the distribution.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you may have thought you could calculate with just the mean and standard deviation. Look back and see whether your judgment shifted to this: for a single value, the shape is the problem; when the sample gets large, the distribution of the mean gets close to normal; but when the sample is small, you need to be careful again.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.prompt: Summarize, with reasons, when it is acceptable to use a normal distribution to calculate probabilities for the sample mean X̄ when the population is not normal.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.hint.0: Compare why the judgments differed in the earlier steps for 36 customers and for 3 customers.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write in a sentence what has to become large for the shape of the sample mean's distribution to change.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If the sample size is ..., the distribution of ... is ...
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state the condition on the sample size clearly?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the population does not need to be normal?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish one person's value from the sample mean?
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.model.0: Even if the population is not normal, when the sample size is large enough (usually 30 or more), the sample mean is close to a normal distribution with mean m and standard deviation σ/√n, so you can use the normal table to find an approximate value.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.model.1: If you take a large sample, the distribution of the mean approximates a normal shape. So when n is large it can be used regardless of the population's shape, and when n is small the skewed shape remains, so it is hard to trust.
n-m-h3-est-04.s.s2.model.2: The larger n is, the closer the sample mean's distribution is to normal, so the mean of 36 customers can use a normal approximation, but with as few as 3 it is hard to trust.

n-m-h3-est-05.title: Explaining the Difference Between Two Cities' Sample Means Correctly to a Friend
n-m-h3-est-05.goal: When two sample means differ only slightly, calculate the confidence intervals to check for overlap, then rewrite the claim in words that do not declare a winner and explain it to a friend.
n-m-h3-est-05.material: Local newspaper article: "High school students in City A use their smartphones for an average of 3.4 hours a day, longer than City B (3.1 hours). City A students use theirs longer." In both cities, 100 students were randomly sampled, usage time follows a normal distribution, and the population standard deviation is known to be 1.5 hours in both cities.
n-m-h3-est-05.thinking.0: Calculate confidence intervals yourself and compare them
n-m-h3-est-05.thinking.1: Distinguish the difference in point estimates from the overlap of intervals
n-m-h3-est-05.thinking.2: Rewrite a correction to suit the person receiving it
n-m-h3-est-05.prereq.0: Confidence interval for a population mean from a normal distribution with known population standard deviation
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.prompt: Find the 95% confidence interval for each city's population mean and enter the values rounded off at the third decimal place (so, to two decimal places). (City A: lower and upper limits; City B: lower and upper limits)
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.hint.0: First find the standard deviation of the sample mean for one city, 1.5/√100.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply that value by 1.96 to get the margin of error, then add and subtract it from the sample mean for each city.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.fail.c1: City A's interval is not correct. Check 3.4 ± 1.96×1.5/√100.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.fail.c2: City B's interval is not correct. Check 3.1 ± 1.96×1.5/√100.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s1.explain: Sample mean ± 1.96×1.5/√100 = ± 0.294, so City A is 3.106 to 3.694 and City B is 2.806 to 3.394. If you do not divide by √n, as in 3.4±1.96×1.5, the interval is too wide, and if you use z=1.645, you get a 90% interval.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.prompt: Looking at the two confidence intervals, choose the most appropriate judgment about the article.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.hint.0: Draw the two intervals on a number line and check whether they overlap.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether a value in the overlapping part could be the population mean of both cities.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.o.a: City A is longer, because its sample mean is 0.3 hours larger.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.r.a: You compared only the sizes of the sample means. A sample mean changes from sample to sample, so once you allow for error, the ordering could be reversed.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.o.b: It is hard to say for sure that City A is longer; the intervals overlap, so they could still be equal.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.o.c: The two cities are the same, because the two intervals overlap, so the population means can be considered equal.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.r.c: You read the overlap as evidence of "the same." Overlap means that being equal remains possible; it does not confirm that they are equal.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.o.d: It cannot be judged; with only 100 students per city, no comparison is meaningful.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.r.d: A small sample does not make the interval useless. It still tells you what range the means lie in.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s2.explain: The two intervals, 2.806 to 3.394 and 3.106 to 3.694, overlap from 3.106 to 3.394. Overlap is only a quick check; more precisely, you should look at whether the 95% interval for the difference of the two means contains 0. Here the interval for the difference is about −0.12 to 0.72, which contains 0, so it is hard to conclude that City A is longer. But it has also not been proven that the two means are equal.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.prompt: A friend read this article and posted in the group chat, "A city kids definitely use their phones longer than B city kids." Based on the interval calculations above, write a correcting message in two or three sentences, in words a high school friend can understand.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.hint.0: Begin the first sentence by acknowledging the article's numbers (3.4 and 3.1).
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.hint.1: Then, in simple words, continue with what possibility the overlap of the intervals leaves open.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The article says 3.4 hours and 3.1 hours, but ...
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in simple words your friend can understand?
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the overlap of the intervals as your evidence at least once?
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you stay balanced, saying "hard to be sure" rather than "wrong"?
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.model.0: Just because it's 3.4 hours for A and 3.1 for B, it's too early to say A is longer. They only surveyed 100 students each, and the 95% confidence intervals, about 3.11 to 3.69 for A and about 2.81 to 3.39 for B, overlap. In reality, the two cities could be about the same.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.model.1: The 0.3-hour difference in sample means is within the margin of error. Since the two confidence intervals overlap, it's hard to say A uses theirs longer, and they could be equal.
n-m-h3-est-05.s.s3.model.2: The difference is only 0.3 hours, so they might be similar, and I can't say for sure. The two intervals overlap.

n-m-h3-est-06.title: Drawing Two Balls: What Is the Probability the Sample Mean Is at Least 5?
n-m-h3-est-06.topic: Statistical estimation: the distribution of the sample mean
n-m-h3-est-06.goal: For samples of size 2 drawn with replacement, list all ordered pairs whose sample mean meets a condition without missing any, and explain why you must distinguish order to calculate the probability correctly.
n-m-h3-est-06.material: A bag contains 4 balls marked 1, 3, 5, and 7, one number per ball. You draw one ball, record its number, put it back, and then draw another and record it. Let a be the first number drawn and b the second, and call (a, b) one sample; the sample mean is X̄=(a+b)/2. On each draw, all 4 balls are equally likely.
n-m-h3-est-06.thinking.2: Check the error of counting while ignoring order
n-m-h3-est-06.prereq.0: Sampling with replacement and counting outcomes
n-m-h3-est-06.prereq.1: The meaning of the sample mean
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.prompt: Make 4 different samples (a, b) in which the first and second numbers are different and the sample mean is at least 5, and enter them. ((a, b) and (b, a) with the order swapped count as different samples.)
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.hint.0: Take a as 1, 3, 5, 7 one at a time, and find the b for which a+b is at least 10.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the pair with a and b swapped also meets the condition.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.ok.c1: a is a number on the balls (1, 3, 5, 7).
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.fail.c1: a is not one of the numbers on the balls: 1, 3, 5, 7.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.ok.c2: b is a number on the balls (1, 3, 5, 7).
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.fail.c2: b is not one of the numbers on the balls: 1, 3, 5, 7.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.fail.c3: a and b are the same.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.ok.c4: The sample mean is at least 5.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.fail.c4: The sample mean is less than 5.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s1.explain: The ordered pairs with a≠b and a+b≥10 are exactly 4: (3,7), (7,3), (5,7), (7,5). (3,7) and (7,3) are different samples with the first and second swapped. (3, 5) has mean 4, so it does not work, and (5, 5) is left out of this condition because its two numbers are the same.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.prompt: Including the cases where a and b are the same, choose the probability that the sample mean X̄ is at least 5.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find the total number of samples that can be made when a and b are placed in order.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether all those samples are equally likely, and count the samples that meet the condition, including those from the previous step.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.o.a: 1/4: count only the 4 samples with different numbers
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.r.a: You left out the samples with a and b the same, (5,5) and (7,7), whose means are also at least 5. The problem said to include the cases that are the same.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.o.b: 2/5: 4 of the 10 samples when order is ignored
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.r.b: This is the result of ignoring order and counting {3,7} as one case. These 10 cases do not come up with equal probability.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.o.c: 3/8: 6 of the 16 samples when order is distinguished
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.o.d: 1/2: half of the samples have a mean greater than the population mean 4
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.r.d: You thought that above and below the population mean 4 are exactly half and half. There are also samples with X̄=4, and you have to remove their share.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s2.explain: The 16 ordered samples (a, b) are all equally likely, each with probability 1/16. The ones with mean at least 5 are the 4 above plus (5,5) and (7,7), 6 in all, so 6/16=3/8. If you ignore order and count 10 cases, {3,7} counts the two cases (3,7) and (7,3) as one, and the probability comes out wrong.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain why the probability changes if you ignore order and count {3, 7} as one case, by saying with what probability each of (3, 7) and (7, 3) occurs.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find the probability of getting 3 first and 7 second as the product of the probabilities of drawing each ball.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.hint.1: Also find the probability of 7 first and 3 second, and compare with the probability of getting {5,5}.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the probability of each of (3,7) and (7,3)?
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which case's probability is missed when {3,7} is counted as one case?
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say that the probability of {3,7} is greater than that of (5,5)?
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.model.0: (3,7) and (7,3) are different samples, with the first and second numbers different, and each occurs with probability 1/16. So the single case {3,7} has probability 2/16. If you ignore order and count it as 1 case, you treat it the same as {5,5} at 1/16, and the probability comes out wrong.
n-m-h3-est-06.s.s3.model.1: The 16 ordered cases are all equally likely. Drawing 3 first and 7 second is a different case from the reverse, so the probability of getting {3,7} as the two cases combined is 1/8, twice the probability of (5,5).

n-m-h3-est-07.title: A Survey That Picks a Whole Class: Can You Trust the Sample Mean?
n-m-h3-est-07.topic: Statistical estimation: bias in sample surveys
n-m-h3-est-07.goal: Understand that every student having an equal chance of being chosen is different from the sample representing the population well, and build and explain a hypothetical situation that exposes the weakness.
n-m-h3-est-07.material: A high school has 20 classes of 30 students each, 600 students in all. You are planning how to choose 30 students to survey for average daily sleep time.
n-m-h3-est-07.thinking.0: Check whether the chances of being chosen are equal
n-m-h3-est-07.thinking.1: Build a counterexample situation that meets the conditions
n-m-h3-est-07.thinking.2: Explain the weakness of a sampling method and how to improve it
n-m-h3-est-07.prereq.0: The meaning of random sampling and population
n-m-h3-est-07.prereq.1: That the sample mean is a value used to estimate the population mean
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the methods in which all 600 students have the same probability of being chosen for the sample.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one student and write, as an expression, the probability that the student ends up in the sample under each method.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.hint.1: Also take a first-year, a second-year, and a third-year student in turn and check that the probabilities are the same.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.o.a: Number the full list of students and pick 30 using random numbers.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.r.a: Each student is chosen with probability 30/600, all the same. Check whether you missed this method.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.o.b: Draw one class at random from the 20 classes and pick all 30 students in it.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.r.b: Each student is chosen with probability 1/20, the chance that their class is chosen, all the same. Check whether you missed this method.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.o.c: Draw 30 at random from the 200 third-year students.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.r.c: First- and second-year students have no chance of being chosen at all. It is fair only within the third year, not for all students.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.o.d: Pick the first 30 students you meet in the hallway at lunchtime.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.r.d: Students who are often in the hallway are more likely to be met, so the probability of being chosen differs from student to student.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s1.explain: In A, 30 are chosen out of 600, so each student has probability 30/600, and in B, one class out of 20 is chosen, so each student is chosen with probability 1/20=30/600. In C the probability for first- and second-year students is 0, and in D the probability of being met differs by student. However, B gives equal chances yet the students chosen together can resemble each other, so it cannot be considered the same method as A.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the school has only two classes of 30 students each. If you draw one class at random and use its 30 students as the sample, then whichever class is chosen, the sample should be off from the schoolwide average sleep time by at least 1 hour. Make 2 different pairs of the two classes' average sleep times a and b (in hours, from 4 to 10 inclusive) and enter them.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.hint.0: When the two classes have the same number of students, first write the schoolwide mean in terms of a and b.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the difference between the chosen class's mean and the schoolwide mean, and choose the difference between a and b so that it is at least 1.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.var.b: Mean of the other class, b (hours)
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are between 4 and 10 inclusive.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.fail.c1: a or b is not between 4 and 10 inclusive.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Whichever class is chosen, it is off from the schoolwide mean by at least 1 hour.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Depending on which class is chosen, there is a case where it is off from the schoolwide mean by less than 1 hour.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s2.explain: Since the two classes have the same number of students, the schoolwide mean is (a+b)/2, and whichever class is chosen, the amount it is off is the same, |a−b|/2. For this to be at least 1, |a−b|≥2. For example, if the classes average 6 hours and 8 hours, the schoolwide mean is 7 hours, and choosing one class gives 6 or 8 hours, each off by 1 hour from 7.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.prompt: Compare the whole-class method with the method of picking 30 of the 600 students using random numbers. Using the example you made above, explain the weakness of choosing a whole class, and write one way to reduce this weakness.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.hint.0: In the example you made, write with numbers how the sample mean changes depending on which class is chosen.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how many classes' students end up in a single sample when 30 are picked with random numbers.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Students in the same class ... so ... To reduce this ...
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain the weakness using the two class means you made above?
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that even with equal chances of being chosen, the sample mean can be far off?
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does your improvement go in the direction of mixing students from several classes?
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.model.0: Students in the same class have similar habits, so if you pick a whole class, the sample mean can be far from the schoolwide mean depending on which class is chosen. For example, with a 6-hour class and an 8-hour class, whichever is chosen is off by 1 hour. You can reduce this by picking with random numbers from the full list, or by picking a few students from every class.
n-m-h3-est-07.s.s3.model.1: Students within one class resemble each other, so even if you pick 30, the information is not worth 30 students. If the classes have different means, the result varies a lot depending on which class is chosen (the error gets larger), and it improves if you pick randomly and evenly from many classes.

n-m-h3-est-08.title: Checking the z-Value in a Solution for a 90% Confidence Interval
n-m-h3-est-08.topic: Statistical estimation: confidence interval for a population mean
n-m-h3-est-08.goal: Check the relationship between the confidence level and probabilities in the standard normal table, find and fix the wrong line in a solution, and confirm the error by calculating what confidence level the wrong z-value actually corresponds to.
n-m-h3-est-08.material: From a normally distributed population with population standard deviation σ=8, a random sample of 64 has sample mean x̄=50. Jiho found the 90% confidence interval for the population mean m. Part of the standard normal table: P(0≤Z≤1.28)=0.3997, P(0≤Z≤1.645)=0.4500, P(0≤Z≤1.96)=0.4750, P(0≤Z≤2.58)=0.4950. (Z is a random variable that follows the normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.)
n-m-h3-est-08.thinking.0: Find the first error in a solution
n-m-h3-est-08.thinking.1: Convert the confidence level to the middle probability to get the z-value
n-m-h3-est-08.thinking.2: Trace back a wrong value and check it
n-m-h3-est-08.prereq.0: How to read the standard normal table
n-m-h3-est-08.prereq.1: The confidence interval formula for a population mean
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Jiho's solution.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.hint.0: First draw a picture of which part of the standard normal distribution the 90% confidence level refers to.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.hint.1: Split that part in half at 0 and compare it with the table's form P(0≤Z≤z).
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.line.0: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n=8/√64=1.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.line.1: The confidence level is 90%, so use the z for which P(Z≤z)=0.90.
