n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.line.2: P(0≤Z≤z)=0.90−0.50=0.40, so from the table z=1.28.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. A 90% confidence level means the probability between −z and z: P(−z≤Z≤z)=0.90. By symmetry, P(0≤Z≤z)=0.45, and from the table z=1.645. Lines 3, 4, and 5 follow line 2, so their results are wrong. The correct interval is 50±1.645×1, that is, 48.355 ≤ m ≤ 51.645.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.prompt: Find the 90% confidence interval with the corrected solution. Then, using the table, calculate P(−1.28≤Z≤1.28) for Jiho's z=1.28, write what confidence level this value corresponds to, and show why Jiho's interval is not a 90% interval.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.hint.0: First write the value of P(0≤Z≤z) so that P(−z≤Z≤z)=0.90, then find z in the table.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.hint.1: For 1.28, add P(0≤Z≤1.28) twice (once for each side).
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. P(−z≤Z≤z)=0.90, so z=..., and the interval is ... With Jiho's z=1.28, ...
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you get half of the middle probability 0.90, which is 0.45, and find z=1.645?
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you correctly calculate the endpoints as 50±1.645×1?
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you compute both sides for 1.28 (2×0.3997) and confirm it is about 80%?
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.model.0: If P(−z≤Z≤z)=0.90, then P(0≤Z≤z)=0.45, so z=1.645. The interval is 50±1.645×1, so 48.355 to 51.645. For Jiho's z=1.28, P(−1.28≤Z≤1.28)=2×0.3997=0.7994, about 80%, so it is not a 90% confidence interval.
n-m-h3-est-08.s.s2.model.1: z is 1.645 and the confidence interval is [48.355, 51.645]. If you use 1.28, the combined probability for both sides is 0.7994, only about 80%, so the interval is too narrow and its confidence level falls short of 90%.

n-m-h3-integc-01.title: Can You Trust a Value Found by Integration by Parts?
n-m-h3-integc-01.topic: Integration: errors in integration by parts and checking with the sign of the integrand
n-m-h3-integc-01.goal: Find and fix the first wrong line in an integration-by-parts solution, and explain how to check the sign of a definite integral using the sign of the integrand, and the limits of that check.
n-m-h3-integc-01.material: Seojin solved ∫_0^π x sin x dx using integration by parts. (∫_0^π is the definite integral from 0 to π. [F]_0^π = F(π) − F(0).)
n-m-h3-integc-01.thinking.0: Check each line of a solution
n-m-h3-integc-01.thinking.1: Predict the sign of a definite integral from the sign of the integrand
n-m-h3-integc-01.thinking.2: Examine the range where the checking method applies (intervals where the sign changes)
n-m-h3-integc-01.prereq.1: Derivatives and antiderivatives of trigonometric functions
n-m-h3-integc-01.prereq.2: Definite integrals and the sign of the integrand
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Seojin's solution.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line that gives a newly found function (u', v), check that function against the original condition.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.hint.1: On the line where v is found, differentiate v yourself and check whether it equals v'.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.line.0: For ∫_0^π x sin x dx, let u=x and v'=sin x.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.line.2: By the integration by parts formula, ∫_0^π x sin x dx = [x cos x]_0^π − ∫_0^π 1·cos x dx.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.line.3: [x cos x]_0^π = π·cos π − 0 = −π, and ∫_0^π cos x dx = [sin x]_0^π = 0.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first to go wrong. The derivative of cos x is −sin x, so the v with v'=sin x is −cos x, not cos x. From line 3 on, the wrong v is simply plugged into the formula, so the formula and the arithmetic are right but the result is wrong.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.prompt: Fix the incorrect line and find the value of ∫_0^π x sin x dx. Then, using the sign of x sin x on 0≤x≤π, write in one or two sentences why Seojin's −π cannot be the value.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find v with v'=sin x again, put it into the formula from line 3, and evaluate at the limits.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check in a table whether x and sin x are each at least 0 on 0≤x≤π, and think about what sign the definite integral of a function that is at least 0 has.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If we fix v, ..., and the value is .... But x sin x is ...
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you correct v to −cos x and put it back into the formula?
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you cite that sin x is at least 0 on 0≤x≤π as your reason?
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you connect the property that if the integrand is at least 0, the definite integral is at least 0?
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.model.0: If v'=sin x, then v=−cos x. [−x cos x]_0^π + ∫_0^π cos x dx = π + 0 = π. On 0≤x≤π, x≥0 and sin x≥0, so x sin x≥0, which means the definite integral cannot be negative (−π).
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s2.model.1: If you correct v to −cos x, the value is π. On the interval x sin x is always at least 0, so like an area it cannot come out less than 0, and −π is negative, which is a contradiction.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.prompt: Now the same function is used, but the interval is changed to [0,2π]. Choose the correct statement about the method of checking the sign of a definite integral using the sign of the integrand.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.hint.0: Check the sign of sin x on [π,2π] and picture the shape of the graph of x sin x.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.hint.1: When there are both positive and negative parts, think about what the sign of the sum depends on.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.o.a: x sin x is at least 0 on [0,2π], so the value must also be positive.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.r.a: Check the sign of sin x on [π,2π]. You did not examine whether the sign stays the same when the interval changes.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.o.b: Even if the sign changes, the positive part comes first, so the value is always positive.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.r.b: You looked only at the order without comparing the sizes of the positive and negative parts. The negative part could be larger.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.o.c: The sign of x sin x changes within the interval, so the sign alone cannot determine the sign of the value.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.r.c: You noted that the sign check is a tool that can be used on an interval where the sign is of one kind.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.o.d: Even if the interval is extended, the added part cancels, so the value is π, the same as on [0,π].
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.r.d: You assumed the added interval [π,2π] would cancel without checking its integral directly.
n-m-h3-integc-01.s.s3.explain: On [π,2π], sin x≤0, so x sin x≤0. So the sign is not one kind over the whole interval, and the positive part and the negative part cut into each other. In fact, [−x cos x + sin x]_0^{2π} = −2π, which is negative. The sign check tells you the sign of the value only when the sign does not change within the interval.

n-m-h3-integc-02.title: Making Different Cubic Functions with Definite Integral 4
n-m-h3-integc-02.topic: Integration: properties of definite integrals — cancellation of odd-degree terms on a symmetric interval
n-m-h3-integc-02.goal: Use the fact that definite integrals of odd-degree terms over a symmetric interval are 0 to build different functions with the same definite integral, and explain the structure.
n-m-h3-integc-02.material: Consider the definite integral of the cubic function f(x)=ax³+bx²+cx+d over [−1,1]. (x³ means x cubed, and ∫_{-1}^{1} is the definite integral from −1 to 1.)
n-m-h3-integc-02.thinking.0: See whether parts of an expression cancel on a symmetric interval
n-m-h3-integc-02.thinking.1: Build different functions that give the same definite integral
n-m-h3-integc-02.thinking.2: Check the conditions under which this method can be used (symmetric interval, odd degree)
n-m-h3-integc-02.prereq.0: Computing definite integrals of polynomial functions
n-m-h3-integc-02.prereq.1: How the sign of a function's value differs at x and −x
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the functions whose definite integral over [−1,1] is 0.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.hint.0: Split each expression into terms and mark which terms change how when you substitute −x for x.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one expression whose definite integral is not 0 and compute the integral of each term over [−1,1] to check.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.r.a: Even-degree terms have the same value at x and −x, so they do not cancel. Compute the definite integral of each of the two terms.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.r.b: You saw that there are only odd-degree terms, so the values at x and −x are opposite.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.r.c: The constant term 1 has the same value at x and −x, so it does not cancel. Check the integral of the constant term.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.r.d: The x term cancels but the x² term does not. You judged the whole expression from only one term.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.r.e: You saw that there are only odd-degree terms, so the values at x and −x are opposite.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s1.explain: For terms whose values at x and −x are opposite (x, x³, x⁵, …), the area on the left and the area on the right over [−1,1] differ only in sign, so the definite integral is 0. For x⁴−x² it is 2/5−2/3, for x³+1 it is 2, and for x²+x it is 2/3, none of which is 0.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.prompt: Let f(x)=ax³+bx²+cx+d (a, b, c, d are integers from −20 to 20 inclusive) with ∫_{-1}^{1} f(x)dx = 4, and make three different f that actually have an x³ term and an x term (a≠0, c≠0). Enter a, b, c, d for each.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.hint.0: First compute what you get when you integrate ax³ and cx separately over [−1,1].
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.hint.1: First choose (b, d) so that the remaining expression 2b/3+2d equals 4, then fill in a and c with nonzero numbers.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.ok.c1: All four coefficients are integers within the range.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The four coefficients must be integers from −20 to 20 inclusive.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.fail.c2: If a is 0, there is no x³ term.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.fail.c3: If c is 0, there is no x term.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.fail.c4: The definite integral over [−1,1] is not 4.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.explain: Over [−1,1], ∫ax³dx=0 and ∫cx dx=0, so ∫f(x)dx = 2b/3 + 2d. If this is 4, then b+3d=6. Examples are (1,0,2,2), (3,3,−1,1), and (−2,6,5,0). (1,3,2,2) gives 2+4=6, not 4, and examples with a=0 or c=0 are excluded by the conditions.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.prompt: After finding three or more different f, you see that the definite integral stays the same even though a and c change freely. Explain why.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compute the integral of each of ax³ and cx over [−1,1].
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write as an expression whether the integral of the remaining terms uses only b and d.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you connect why x³ and x have definite integral 0 over [−1,1] to the symmetry of the interval?
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you confirm with an expression that the integral is determined by the remaining b and d alone?
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.model.0: ax³ and cx have opposite signs at x and −x, so over [−1,1] their definite integrals cancel and are 0. So the value is determined only by the integrals of bx² and d, 2b/3+2d.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The definite integrals of the odd-degree terms ax³ and cx are 0, so a and c cannot affect the value. Only the even-degree b and the constant term d have an effect.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.prompt: This property can be used when the interval is symmetric about 0, like [−1,1]. Choose the definite integral for which this method is appropriate.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.hint.0: First check whether the interval is centered at 0, with equal lengths on the left and right.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.hint.1: Then check whether replacing x with −x in the integrand changes only the sign.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.r.a: You noted that the interval is symmetric about 0 and the integrand has only odd-degree terms.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.r.b: The integrand is an even function, so no cancellation happens. Compute the actual value.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.r.c: The interval [0,2] is not symmetric about 0. Even for an odd function, the interval must be symmetric for the left and right to cancel.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.r.d: The interval [−1,3] is not symmetric about 0. You need to treat the symmetric part and the non-symmetric part separately.
n-m-h3-integc-02.s.s3.explain: ∫_{-2}^{2}(x³−4x)dx is 0 because the interval is symmetric and the integrand has only odd-degree terms. [0,2] and [−1,3] are not symmetric, so you cannot say right away that the integral is 0, and x²−4 is an even function, so it does not cancel (the value is −32/3).

n-m-h3-integc-03.title: Volume Made by Rotating the Region Between Two Curves: Where Did It Go Wrong?
n-m-h3-integc-03.topic: Integration: volume of a solid made by rotating the region between two curves (shape of the cross-section)
n-m-h3-integc-03.goal: In a solution for the volume of the solid of revolution of the region between two curves, find and fix the line that got the cross-section shape wrong, and identify which region's volume the wrong expression actually gives.
n-m-h3-integc-03.material: Soyoung found the volume of the solid made by rotating the region enclosed by the two curves y=x and y=x² once around the x-axis. (x² means x squared.)
n-m-h3-integc-03.thinking.0: Draw the shape of the cross-section at one point
n-m-h3-integc-03.thinking.1: Work backward to find the region the wrong expression represents
n-m-h3-integc-03.thinking.2: Confirm the error by directly comparing cross-section areas
n-m-h3-integc-03.prereq.0: Volume of a solid of revolution about the x-axis
n-m-h3-integc-03.prereq.1: Sketching the region between two curves
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Soyoung's solution.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.hint.0: Pick a single point such as x=1/2 and sketch how far the region is from the x-axis there and where it extends.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.hint.1: Decide whether the rotated cross-section is a solid disk or a disk with a hole.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.line.0: The curves y=x and y=x² meet at x=0 and x=1, and on 0≤x≤1, x≥x².
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.line.1: When this region is rotated about the x-axis, the cross-section at x is a circle with radius x−x².
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.line.2: So the volume is V = π∫_0^1 (x−x²)² dx.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first to go wrong. When the region between two curves is rotated about the x-axis, the cross-section is a washer, a disk with a hole (outer radius x, inner radius x²). It is not a circle whose radius is the difference of the two radii. From line 3 on, the calculation follows the wrong cross-section from line 2, so the arithmetic is right but the result is wrong.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.prompt: Fix the incorrect line and find the volume. Then, using the cross-section at x=1/2, explain in one or two sentences why Soyoung's expression is not correct.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.hint.0: Sketch the cross-section at x to check whether it is a large circle of radius x with a small circle of radius x² removed.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.hint.1: At x=1/2, write down and compare the areas of the large circle, the small circle, and Soyoung's circle.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The cross-section at x is ...
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the outer radius and inner radius of the cross-section at x and find its area?
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you compare Soyoung's cross-section area with the correct one at x=1/2?
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you realize that (x−x²)² and x²−x⁴ are different?
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.model.0: The cross-section at x is a washer with outer radius x and inner radius x², so its area is π(x²−x⁴). V=π∫_0^1 (x²−x⁴)dx=π(1/3−1/5)=2π/15. At x=1/2 the correct cross-section is π(1/4−1/16)=3π/16, but Soyoung's expression is a circle of radius 1/4, which is only π/16.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s2.model.1: The cross-section made by rotating the region between two curves is the large disk minus the small disk, so it is π(x²)−π(x²)², and the volume is 2π/15. Squaring the difference of the radii is not the same as the difference of the areas of the large and small circles.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.prompt: The expression Soyoung found, π∫_0^1 (x−x²)² dx, is the volume of rotating which region once about the x-axis?
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.hint.0: π∫_0^1 (some function)² dx stacks solid disks whose radius is "the value of that function." Find which curve's height that function is.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.hint.1: For each option, write down the shape of the cross-section at x when it is rotated about the x-axis.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.o.a: The region enclosed by y=x and y=x²
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.r.a: This region produces a cross-section with a hole, so you would have to integrate π(x²−x⁴). Check the cross-section at x=1/2.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.o.b: The region enclosed by y=x, the x-axis, and x=1
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.r.b: The cross-section of this region is a solid circle of radius x, so it becomes π∫x²dx.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.o.c: The region enclosed by y=x², the x-axis, and x=1
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.r.c: The cross-section of this region is a solid circle of radius x², so it becomes π∫x⁴dx.
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.o.d: The region enclosed by y=x−x² and the x-axis
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.r.d: You noted that this is the region that produces solid circles whose radius is the curve's height x−x².
n-m-h3-integc-03.s.s3.explain: y=x−x² is at least 0 on 0≤x≤1, and when the region between this curve and the x-axis is rotated about the x-axis, the cross-section is a solid circle of radius x−x². Soyoung's expression gives the volume of this region (π/30), and the volume of the region in the problem (between the two curves) is 2π/15.

n-m-h3-integc-04.title: Definite Integrals Without an Antiderivative
n-m-h3-integc-04.topic: Integration: definite integrals using substitution and symmetry of the interval (finding the value without an antiderivative)
n-m-h3-integc-04.goal: Revising your judgment as information grows, confirm that a symmetry relation obtained by substitution determines the value of a definite integral without finding an antiderivative.
n-m-h3-integc-04.material: Follow, step by step, the process of finding the value of the definite integral I=∫_0^{π/2} sin x/(sin x+cos x) dx. (∫_0^{π/2} is the definite integral from 0 to π/2.)
n-m-h3-integc-04.thinking.0: Estimate the size of a result roughly
n-m-h3-integc-04.thinking.1: Count the number of equations and the number of unknowns
n-m-h3-integc-04.thinking.2: Watch the direction of the interval after a substitution
n-m-h3-integc-04.thinking.3: Judge the conditions under which the same method works
n-m-h3-integc-04.prereq.0: Integration by substitution (changing the limits in a definite integral)
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, count "how many unknowns and how many equations there are."
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether your first estimate and the value found later are not very different.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.info: You want to find I=∫_0^{π/2} sin x/(sin x+cos x) dx. It is hard to find an antiderivative of this expression directly. The values of the integrand h(x)=sin x/(sin x+cos x) are h(0)=0, h(π/4)=1/2, h(π/2)=1, and the length of the interval is π/2 (about 1.57).
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which estimate of the size of I is most appropriate?
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The height rises from 0 to 1 with a middle value of 1/2, so the area is roughly around (1/2)×1.57≈0.8. This estimate can be used later to check whether the value you find is right.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I is about 1.57: because you treat the height as 1 and multiply by the length 1.57
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The height is 1 only at the end of the interval. This estimate treats the height as 1 over the whole interval.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: I is about 0.8: because the height varies from 0 to 1, the average is about 1/2
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You estimated the change in height by an average. It is not the exact value, but it can be used to gauge the size.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I is 0: because h(0)=0 at the starting point
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The value being 0 at one point does not make the definite integral 0. Look at the values over the whole interval.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Look also at J=∫_0^{π/2} cos x/(sin x+cos x) dx. Adding the two fractions makes the numerator equal to the denominator, so I+J=∫_0^{π/2} 1 dx=π/2.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can I be determined from this information alone?
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.after: There is only one equation, I+J=π/2, so I and J cannot be determined separately. You need to find one more relation between I and J.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It can be determined: I+J=π/2, so I=π/4.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You split it in half without checking whether I=J. I+J=π/2 is just one relation between I and J.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It cannot be determined: I+J=π/2 does not help at all in finding I.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The value of I+J is useful information. It gave one relation between I and J.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Not enough yet: you need to know one more relation between I and J.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You noted that there are two unknowns, I and J, but only one equation.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.info: In J, let x=π/2−t. Then dx=−dt, and as x goes from 0 to π/2, t goes from π/2 to 0. Since sin(π/2−t)=cos t and cos(π/2−t)=sin t, J=∫_{π/2}^{0} sin t/(sin t+cos t)·(−dt)=∫_0^{π/2} sin t/(sin t+cos t) dt, which equals I.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, what is the value of I?
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.after: I=J and I+J=π/2, so I=π/4 (about 0.785). This agrees well with the first estimate of 0.8.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You used the two equations I=J and I+J=π/2 together. It also agrees with the first estimate of 0.8.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You mistook the value of I+J for the value of I. J contains the same amount as well.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You mistook the height at one middle point for the value of the definite integral. You have to multiply the height by the length of the interval.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s1.reflect: At first only an estimate was possible, and even after getting the equation for I+J, it was important that "splitting in half" was still too early. Only after the substitution gave the relation J=I was I determined. By using symmetry of the interval in a definite integral, you can find the value without finding an antiderivative.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.prompt: When you substitute x=π/2−t in J, dx=−dt, yet J becomes +I rather than −I. Explain why, focusing on the limits of integration (upper and lower).
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.hint.0: Find the value of t corresponding to x=0 and to x=π/2, and write the upper and lower limits of the new integral.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write what happens to the sign when you put a definite integral whose upper limit is less than its lower limit back into the normal direction.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The minus sign from dx=−dt ...
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write yourself that after the substitution the lower limit is π/2 and the upper limit is 0?
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the step of changing ∫_{π/2}^{0} into −∫_0^{π/2}?
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.model.0: As x goes from 0 to π/2, t goes from π/2 to 0, so the upper and lower limits of the integral are swapped. Reversing the interval changes the sign, and together with the minus from dx=−dt the signs cancel, so J=+I.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s2.model.1: After the substitution, the interval is reversed, from π/2 to 0. Setting the reversed interval right creates one minus sign, and that and the minus from dx=−dt eliminate each other, so the sign ends up positive.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.prompt: Choose the definite integral whose value can be found with the same method used to find I (replace x with π/2−x and add the paired expression).
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, write what happens to the interval and the denominator when x is replaced with π/2−x.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the numerator and denominator become equal when you add the original expression and the replaced expression.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.r.a: If the interval is [0,π/3], then x and π/2−x are not paired within the same interval, so the method above does not work as it is.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.r.b: The denominator is not symmetric, so even if you add the paired expression the fraction does not simplify to a single number.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.r.c: You saw that replacing x with π/2−x swaps sin³ and cos³, and that the sum of the two expressions is 1.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.r.d: The denominator becomes 0 inside the interval (at x=3π/4), so the definite integral is not even defined.
n-m-h3-integc-04.s.s3.explain: In c, the interval [0,π/2] maps to itself under x→π/2−x, and the denominator sin³x+cos³x is symmetric, so adding the paired expression gives 1. So the value is π/4. The problem in a is the interval, in b the symmetry of the denominator, and in d the point where the denominator is 0 (3π/4).

n-m-h3-integc-05.title: Definite Integrals of Periodic Functions: What Do You Need to Know?
n-m-h3-integc-05.topic: Integration: properties of definite integrals — definite integrals of periodic functions and choosing the information needed
n-m-h3-integc-05.goal: When finding a definite integral of a periodic function, sort out the information that is needed (the period, the value over one period) from what is not, and confirm that the key is whether the length of the interval is a multiple of the period.
n-m-h3-integc-05.material: There is a continuous function f. You want to find the value of the definite integral ∫_2^{11} f(x)dx. (∫_2^{11} is the definite integral from 2 to 11.)
n-m-h3-integc-05.thinking.0: Distinguish needed information from unneeded information
n-m-h3-integc-05.thinking.1: Build your own examples that meet the conditions
n-m-h3-integc-05.thinking.2: Investigate cases that the given information does not determine
n-m-h3-integc-05.prereq.0: The interval-splitting property of definite integrals
n-m-h3-integc-05.prereq.1: The meaning of a periodic function
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.prompt: f is a function that is continuous on all real numbers. Choose all the pieces of information below that are absolutely necessary to determine the value of ∫_2^{11} f(x)dx. (Knowing everything necessary is enough; do not choose what is not needed.)
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find the length of the interval [2,11], and divide it by 3 to see what happens.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.hint.1: Remove each piece of information one at a time and check whether the value is still determined without it.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.r.a: The interval [0,2] does not overlap [2,11]. Think about how this value would be used for the value on [2,11].
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.r.b: You saw that this is information that the same shape repeats every 3 units, so it connects the values on different intervals.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.r.c: The fact that f is even only means it is symmetric left and right about 0; it is not used to divide [2,11] into repeating intervals.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.r.d: You saw that you need the value of the definite integral over one repeating interval to determine the whole value.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.r.e: The function's value at a single point does not affect the value of a definite integral.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s1.explain: The length of [2,11] is 9, which is 3 times the period 3. No matter where the period interval starts, the definite integral over one repeating interval is the same, so ∫_2^{11} f = 3×6 = 18. For that you need the periodicity (b) and the value of the definite integral over one period (d), and nothing else is needed.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.prompt: Using only the information that the period is 3 and ∫_0^3 f(x)dx=6, find two intervals [p,q] for which the value of ∫_p^q f(x)dx can be determined, and enter p and q. (p and q are integers, p is not a multiple of 3, 0<p, 4≤q−p≤20, q≤40)
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.hint.0: First, using periodicity, think about what the definite integral over the interval [1,4], of length 3, would be.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.hint.1: Choose (p, q) so that the length of the interval divided by 3 is a whole number, and check that p is not a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers within the range.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be integers with 0
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.ok.c2: p is not a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The length of the interval is between 4 and 20 inclusive.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The length q−p of the interval is not between 4 and 20 inclusive.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The length of the interval is a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.fail.c4: The length of the interval is not a multiple of 3, so the value is not determined.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.explain: If the length of the interval is a multiple of 3, it is made of several whole period intervals laid end to end, so regardless of the starting point the value is (length/3)×6. (1,7) gives 6, (2,11) gives 18, and (4,19) gives 30. (1,8) has length 7, which is not a multiple of 3, so the value is not determined; (3,9) is excluded because p is a multiple of 3; and (1,4) has length 3, which is less than 4.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why the value is determined even if the starting point p is not a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Split [p,q] into consecutive intervals of length 3. How many pieces does it split into?
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Using periodicity, think about what the definite integrals over the length-3 intervals [1,4] and [2,5] would each be.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. If the length is a multiple of 3, ...
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the definite integral over an interval of length 3 is 6 even in an example where p is not a multiple of 3?
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that an interval of length 9 splits into 3 period intervals?
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.model.0: If the length of the interval is a multiple of 3, it can be split into several period intervals, and wherever the start is, the definite integral over one period interval is the same 6. So regardless of the starting point, the value is (length/3)×6.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s2.because.model.1: If the length q−p is some multiple of 3, then [p,q] is several length-3 intervals joined together, and an interval of length 3 has integral 6 wherever it starts, so it doesn't matter whether p is a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.prompt: The same information is given (period 3, ∫_0^3 f(x)dx=6). Choose the correct statement about ∫_2^{10} f(x)dx.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.hint.0: Split [2,10] into consecutive intervals of length 3 and find the length of the part left over at the end.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the values for different f that both satisfy period 3 and ∫_0^3 f=6 (the constant function f=2 and one more).
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.o.a: It is determined: the average height over one period is 2, so for length 8 it is 16.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.r.a: If it does not split exactly into whole period intervals, you cannot calculate with the average. This interval contains 2.67 periods.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.o.b: It is determined: the two period intervals give 12, and the remainder is taken as 0.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.r.b: There is no basis for the integral of the leftover part of length 2 being 0.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.o.c: It is not determined: after removing two period intervals, the value of the leftover part of length 2 cannot be known.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.r.c: You noted that length 8 is not a multiple of 3, so it does not split exactly into period intervals.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.o.d: It is not determined: because the starting point 2 is not a multiple of 3.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.r.d: Whether the starting point is a multiple of 3 does not matter. Recall what you checked in the previous step.
n-m-h3-integc-05.s.s3.explain: [2,10] has length 8, so it splits into two period intervals (length 6) and a leftover part of length 2. The integral of the leftover part cannot be known from the given information. For example, if f(x)=2 it is 16, and if f(x)=2+cos(2πx/3) it is about 16.83. Both have period 3 and ∫_0^3 f=6. Whether the starting point is a multiple of 3 does not matter.

n-m-h3-integc-06.title: Integration by Parts: Can You Choose u Any Way You Like?
n-m-h3-integc-06.topic: Integration: criteria for choosing u and v' in integration by parts
n-m-h3-integc-06.goal: Confirm that the difficulty of the remaining integral depends on how you choose u and v' in integration by parts, and explain the criteria for choosing in words a friend can understand.
n-m-h3-integc-06.material: Hajun did integration by parts on ∫ x eˣ dx with u=eˣ and v'=x, and the expression got more complicated. Hajun says, "Can't you choose u and v' any way you like in integration by parts?" (eˣ is e to the power x, and ln x is the natural logarithm of x.)
n-m-h3-integc-06.thinking.0: Compare how the remaining integral changes depending on the choice
n-m-h3-integc-06.thinking.1: Set a criterion for choosing (becomes simpler when differentiated / easy to integrate)
n-m-h3-integc-06.thinking.2: Explain the criterion in a friend's words
n-m-h3-integc-06.prereq.1: Derivatives and integrals of logarithmic and exponential functions
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.prompt: Hajun did integration by parts on ∫ x eˣ dx with u=eˣ and v'=x. Which of the following describes what happens with this choice?
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.hint.0: With u=eˣ and v'=x, find u' and v yourself and write the integral on the right side of the formula uv − ∫u'v dx.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the original integral and the remaining integral and see how the power of x has changed.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.o.a: The remaining integral contains x², so the power of x actually goes up.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.r.a: You saw that if u and v' are swapped, integrating v' raises the power, and as a result the remaining integral can become more complicated than the original.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.o.b: The remaining integral becomes 0, so the answer comes out right away.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.r.b: For the remaining integral to be 0, u'v would have to be 0. Find u' and v yourself and check.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.o.c: The integration by parts formula does not hold, so it cannot be solved.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.r.c: The formula holds whichever factor you take as u. What changes is the difficulty of the remaining integral.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.o.d: The remaining integral is just eˣ, so it becomes much easier.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.r.d: What remains is the product of u'=eˣ and v=x²/2. Find u' and v yourself.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s1.explain: With u=eˣ and v'=x, u'=eˣ and v=x²/2, so ∫ x eˣ dx = (x²/2)eˣ − ∫ (x²/2)eˣ dx. The remaining integral has x to a power one higher than the original, so it got harder. The formula holds, but the choice was not a good one. If you take u=x and v'=eˣ, the remaining integral is just ∫ eˣ dx.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to find ∫ x ln x dx using integration by parts. Choose the appropriate advice to give Hajun.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.hint.0: For each choice, first check whether you can find v right away.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the product of u' and v is simpler than the original integral.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.o.a: The easiest is to take u=x and v'=ln x.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.r.a: Finding v from v'=ln x is not immediate (v=x ln x−x). The remaining integral also contains ln x and does not get simpler.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.o.b: The easiest is to take u=1 and v'=x ln x.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.r.b: Finding an antiderivative of v'=x ln x is the same as the original problem, so there is no progress.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.o.c: The easiest is to take u=ln x and v'=x.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.r.c: You took the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated (ln x) as u and the factor that is easy to integrate (x) as v'.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.o.d: It makes no difference how you choose, since the remaining integral is equally hard, so choose anything.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.r.d: Depending on the choice, the remaining integral can become easier or harder. Recall Hajun's experience in the previous step.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s2.explain: With u=ln x and v'=x, u'=1/x and v=x²/2, and ∫ x ln x dx = (x²/2)ln x − ∫ (x/2) dx = (x²/2)ln x − x²/4 + C. The remaining integral is a linear expression in x, so it is simple. The criterion for a good choice is to take the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated (ln x → 1/x) as u, and the factor that is easy to integrate (x) as v'.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to Hajun. Hajun said, "Can't you choose u and v' any way you like in integration by parts?" Using ∫ x ln x dx as an example, explain in simple words how to choose well and why.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.hint.0: In ∫ x ln x dx, find which of ln x and x becomes simpler when differentiated and which is easy to integrate.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write what the remaining integral is with that choice, and use it as evidence to show Hajun.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state a criterion for choosing, in one sentence, rather than "any way"?
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you actually apply the criterion to ∫ x ln x dx?
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it in words Hajun can understand (not just a list of symbols)?
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.model.0: Hajun, the formula holds however you choose, but whether the remaining integral gets easier is different. For ∫ x ln x dx, you should take u=ln x and v'=x. ln x becomes simpler, 1/x, when differentiated, and x is easy to integrate. Then the remaining integral becomes the easy ∫ x/2 dx.
n-m-h3-integc-06.s.s3.model.1: Try u=ln x and v'=x. The criterion is to take the factor that gets simpler when differentiated as u and the factor that is easy to integrate as v'. Then the remaining integral is just x/2, which is solved quickly. If you take u=x instead, you have to start by integrating ln x, which is harder.

n-m-h3-integc-07.title: If the Definite Integral Is Smaller, Is the Function Smaller Everywhere?
n-m-h3-integc-07.topic: Integration: properties of definite integrals — does the converse of the comparison property hold?
n-m-h3-integc-07.goal: Confirm by building your own counterexample that the comparison property of definite integrals goes in one direction only, and sort out what can be said in the other direction (existence).
n-m-h3-integc-07.material: This is Minsu's reasoning about two functions f and g defined on the interval 0≤x≤2. (∫_0^2 is the definite integral from 0 to 2.)
n-m-h3-integc-07.thinking.0: Check the direction of a claim
n-m-h3-integc-07.thinking.1: Build counterexamples that meet the conditions
n-m-h3-integc-07.thinking.2: Use the contrapositive to decide what can be said for sure
n-m-h3-integc-07.prereq.0: The comparison property of definite integrals
n-m-h3-integc-07.prereq.1: Definite integrals of linear and constant functions
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line where the logic goes wrong in Minsu's reasoning.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.hint.0: In lines 1 and 2, find the "assumption" and the "conclusion" in each and compare whether they have been swapped.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether line 3 shows a proof that line 2 is always true, or just one example.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.line.0: If f(x)≤g(x) on 0≤x≤2, then ∫_0^2 f(x)dx ≤ ∫_0^2 g(x)dx.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.line.1: Conversely, if ∫_0^2 f(x)dx < ∫_0^2 g(x)dx, then f(x)<g(x) for every x in 0≤x≤2.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.line.2: For example, if f(x)=x and g(x)=3, then ∫_0^2 f(x)dx=2 < 6=∫_0^2 g(x)dx, and f(x)<g(x) on 0≤x≤2.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s1.explain: Line 2 goes wrong. The comparison property of definite integrals goes one way: "if f≤g at every x, then the integral of f is at most the integral of g." Its converse (if the integral is smaller, the function is smaller at every x) does not hold in general. Line 3 only showed one example where it happens to hold; it is not a proof that line 2 is right.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.prompt: Show with examples why Minsu's line 2 is wrong. For f(x)=px and g(x)=q (p and q are integers from 1 to 30 inclusive), find three pairs (p, q) such that ∫_0^2 f(x)dx < ∫_0^2 g(x)dx and yet there is some x in 0≤x≤2 with f(x)>g(x), and enter them.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write ∫_0^2 px dx and ∫_0^2 q dx in terms of p and q, and turn their comparison into a condition.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.hint.1: f(x)=px gets larger as x gets larger. Write a condition that compares f(2) and g(2) at the end of the interval, x=2.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers within the range.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be integers from 1 to 30 inclusive.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.ok.c3: At x=2, f(2)=2p is greater than g(2)=q.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.fail.c3: There is no x in 0≤x≤2 with f(x)>g(x).
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.explain: ∫_0^2 px dx = 2p and ∫_0^2 q dx = 2q. 2p<2q means p<q, and for f(2)=2p to be greater than g(2)=q at x=2 you need q<2p. So examples with p<q<2p, such as (3,4), (5,7), and (10,11), are counterexamples. (3,6) has q=2p, so f(2)=g(2) and f(x)≤g(x) holds at every x, so it is not a counterexample.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the (p, q) you entered, and, giving one value of x where f(x)>g(x) and the values of the two definite integrals, explain why it is a counterexample to Minsu's line 2.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one x where f(x)>g(x) and write the values of f and g there.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compute the values of the two definite integrals and compare which is larger.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you confirm, with concrete numbers, an x where f(x)>g(x)?
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the values of the two definite integrals and check the inequality?
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.model.0: If (p, q)=(3,4), then ∫_0^2 3x dx=6 and ∫_0^2 4 dx=8, so ∫f<∫g. But at x=2, f(2)=6 and g(2)=4, so f(2)>g(2). The integral of f is smaller, yet at some x f is larger, so it is a counterexample to line 2.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s2.because.model.1: For (5,7), the definite integrals are 10 and 14, so f's is smaller. But at x=2, f(2)=10 is greater than g(2)=7. So even if the integral is smaller, the function is not smaller at every x.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.prompt: Suppose ∫_0^2 f(x)dx < ∫_0^2 g(x)dx holds. What can you say for sure under this condition?
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write what the comparison of the definite integrals would be if you assumed "f≥g at every x."
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what conclusion remains if that result contradicts the given condition.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.o.a: There is at least one x in the interval where f(x)<g(x).
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.r.a: You used the contrapositive of the property that if f≥g at every x, then the integral of f must be at least the integral of g.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.r.b: You cannot determine the value at the single point x=1 from the comparison of the definite integrals. You can also build an example where f is larger at x=1.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.r.c: The counterexample made earlier breaks this claim. Even if the integral is smaller, f can be larger at some x.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.o.d: There is no x in the interval where f(x)>g(x).
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.r.d: In the counterexample, f(2)>g(2) at x=2. There can be points where f is larger.
n-m-h3-integc-07.s.s3.explain: If f(x)≥g(x) at every x, then ∫f ≥ ∫g would have to hold. The given condition ∫f<∫g contradicts this, so there is at least one x with f(x)<g(x). But you cannot tell where that x is, how many there are, or whether there are x with f>g.

n-m-h3-integc-08.title: The Area of the Same Region: Two People, Two Different Solutions
n-m-h3-integc-08.topic: Integration: area — integrating with respect to x and with respect to y (changing the representation)
n-m-h3-integc-08.goal: Explain, using the shape of the region, why integrating with respect to x and integrating with respect to y give the same area for the same region, and judge the conditions under which the second method can be used.
n-m-h3-integc-08.material: Two people found the area of the region R enclosed by the curve y=ln x, the x-axis, and the line x=e using different methods. Jian solved ∫_1^e ln x dx by integration by parts and got [x ln x − x]_1^e = (e−e)−(0−1) = 1. Soyul subtracted ∫_0^1 eʸ dy = e−1 from the area e of the rectangle 0≤x≤e, 0≤y≤1, and got e−(e−1)=1. (∫_1^e is the definite integral from 1 to e.)
n-m-h3-integc-08.thinking.0: Cut the region in a different direction
n-m-h3-integc-08.thinking.1: Check with a picture what region is being subtracted
n-m-h3-integc-08.thinking.2: Judge the conditions under which the method works (one-to-one correspondence)
n-m-h3-integc-08.prereq.1: Inverse functions and definite integrals of logarithmic and exponential functions
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.prompt: In the figure, which part's area is the ∫_0^1 eʸ dy that Soyul subtracts from e?
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.hint.0: Take a height y, draw one horizontal line across the rectangle, and find the point where the curve cuts that line.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.hint.1: On that line, tell which side of the curve, left or right, is R.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.o.a: The region R itself, whose area we want to find
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.r.a: R's area is the value obtained by subtracting this expression from e. If R were the same as this expression's region, there would be no need to subtract from e.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.o.b: The rest of the rectangle 0≤x≤e, 0≤y≤1 after removing R
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.r.b: You saw that it is the part to the left of the curve x=eʸ, that is, the part of the rectangle that is not R.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.o.c: The part below the curve y=ln x with 1≤x≤e
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.r.c: That part is exactly R. Soyul does not subtract R from e; she subtracts the remaining part.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.o.d: The part between the x-axis and the curve with 0<x<1
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.r.d: For 0<x<1 the curve is below the x-axis, so it does not belong to R, and it has nothing to do with this expression.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s1.explain: The area of the rectangle 0≤x≤e, 0≤y≤1 is e. At each height y, the point on the curve is x=eʸ, so the width of the part to its left is eʸ, and its area is ∫_0^1 eʸ dy = e−1. R is the part to the right of the curve, so its area is e−(e−1)=1.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.prompt: Following Soyul's method, find the area of the region enclosed by y=ln x, the x-axis, and the line x=e². Show the width and height of the rectangle and the definite integral you subtract, and write the result.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.hint.0: Find the height of the curve at x=e², y=ln e², to determine the height of the rectangle.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.hint.1: At each height y, express the curve's x-coordinate in terms of y, then integrate that expression from 0 to the height of the rectangle.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The rectangle has width ..., height ..., and ...
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you confirm that the height of the rectangle is ln e²=2?
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you find ∫_0^2 eʸ dy = e²−1?
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check that it matches the value found by integration by parts?
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.model.0: The rectangle has width e² and height ln e²=2, so its area is 2e². The part to the left of the curve is ∫_0^2 eʸ dy = e²−1. So the area of R is 2e² − (e²−1) = e²+1.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s2.model.1: With x=e², y goes from 0 to 2, so the rectangle's area is 2e² and the part to subtract is ∫_0^2 e^y dy=e²−1. The area is 2e²−e²+1=e²+1.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.prompt: Soyul's method can be used "when the curve can be written as a single expression of the form x=h(y)." Choose all the curves below that can be written that way on the given interval.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each curve, take one y-value and count how many x in the interval have that y-value.
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the graph goes up and down within the interval (or only increases).
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.r.a: Each y-value corresponds to two x-values (x and −x). It cannot be written as a single expression of the form x=h(y).
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.r.b: You saw that each y corresponds to only one x (x=ln y), so it can be written as a single expression of the form x=h(y).
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.r.c: Each y-value corresponds to two x-values (x and π−x). It cannot be written as a single expression of the form x=h(y).
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.r.d: You saw that each y corresponds to only one x (x= the cube root of y), so it can be written as a single expression of the form x=h(y).
n-m-h3-integc-08.s.s3.explain: y=eˣ (0≤x≤1) and y=x³ (−1≤x≤1) are increasing on their intervals, so each y corresponds to one x (they have inverse functions). For y=x² or y=sin x, there are two x for the same y, so as they stand they cannot be a single expression x=h(y), and the interval has to be split.

n-m-h3-prob-01.title: At Least One Is a Daughter: What Is the Probability Both Are Daughters?
n-m-h3-prob-01.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayes-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-01.goal: In a conditional probability solution, find and fix the place where cases that are not equally likely were counted as equally likely, and confirm that the remaining cases change depending on how the condition is worded.
n-m-h3-prob-01.material: All we know is that a family has two children. Each child is a daughter with probability 1/2, and we assume the two children's sexes do not affect each other. Seungwoo solved "the probability that both children are daughters, given that at least one is a daughter" as shown below.
n-m-h3-prob-01.thinking.0: Find the first line in a solution that goes wrong
n-m-h3-prob-01.thinking.1: Rebuild the sample space from distinguishable cases
n-m-h3-prob-01.thinking.2: Compare probabilities that change with the wording of the condition
n-m-h3-prob-01.prereq.0: The meaning of conditional probability (the proportion of some cases among the cases that fit the condition)
n-m-h3-prob-01.prereq.1: Counting outcomes when order is distinguished
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first incorrect line in Seungwoo's solution.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check from the top, one line at a time, whether each line correctly follows from the line just before it.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write out the cases called "equally likely" yourself, distinguishing the first child from the second, and compare whether they are really the same size.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.line.0: Under the condition that at least one of the two children is a daughter, find the probability that both children are daughters.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.line.1: The makeup of the two children is one of three types, "2 daughters," "1 daughter and 1 son," and "2 sons," and the three types are equally likely.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.line.2: Removing "2 sons," which does not fit the condition that at least one is a daughter, leaves two types.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.line.3: Of the two remaining types, there is one in which both children are daughters.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first place that goes wrong. "1 daughter and 1 son" contains both the case where the first child is the daughter and the case where the second child is the daughter, so when the first and second are distinguished, it is not equally likely with "2 daughters" or "2 sons." Lines 3 to 5 follow the three types from line 2 on trust, so the calculations within them are right but the result is wrong.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.prompt: Using the corrected solution, find the probability that both children are daughters, and write why the value differs from Seungwoo's. (Each child is a daughter with probability 1/2, and the two are assumed not to affect each other.)
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.hint.0: Distinguish the children as first and second, and write out all the combinations of sexes. How many are there, and are they equally likely?
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.hint.1: Count only the cases that fit the condition, and compare how many of them have both daughters.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If we distinguish the first and second child, ...
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you list all possible cases, distinguishing the first and second child?
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you keep only the cases that fit the condition and find the proportion of both-daughter cases among them?
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that "1 daughter and 1 son" is not a single case?
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.model.0: If we distinguish the first and second child, (daughter, daughter), (daughter, son), (son, daughter), and (son, son) are all equally likely. Of the 3 cases in which at least one is a daughter, 1 has both daughters, so the probability is 1/3.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.model.1: One daughter and one son splits into two cases, (first a daughter, second a son) and (first a son, second a daughter), so it must not be counted as one case. So there are 3 cases that fit the condition, and only one of them has both daughters, so the probability is one third.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: Listing with symbols such as G and B is fine.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.prompt: If the condition were not "at least one is a daughter" but "the first child is a daughter," what would the probability be that both children are daughters?
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write the cases that remain under this condition, distinguishing the first and second child.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.hint.1: Put the list of remaining cases from the previous problem next to this list and find what changed.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.r.a: You counted the cases that fit the condition incorrectly, or you mixed up "at least one daughter" and "both daughters."
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.r.b: You gave the probability over the original whole without using the condition. When there is a condition, the remaining cases change.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.r.c: You treated the previous problem's condition and this one as the same. This time only the second child's sex is left open.
n-m-h3-prob-01.s.s3.explain: If the first child is a daughter, the remaining cases are (daughter, daughter) and (daughter, son), which are equally likely. Of these, one has both daughters, so the probability is 1/2. "At least one is a daughter" also allows (son, daughter), so there are 3 remaining cases and the probability is 1/3. The remaining sample space depends on how the condition is worded.

n-m-h3-prob-02.title: Two Events That Cannot Happen Together: Are They Independent?
n-m-h3-prob-02.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayes-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-02.goal: Distinguish "cannot happen together" from "independent," and explain the reasoning using the meaning of independence (knowing one does not change the probability of the other).
n-m-h3-prob-02.material: A fair die is rolled once. Event A is "the roll is 1 or 2," and B is "the roll is 3 or 4." The two events cannot happen at the same time. Jimin looked at this and made the claim below.
n-m-h3-prob-02.thinking.0: Judge whether a claim is right using evidence
n-m-h3-prob-02.thinking.2: Explain the reason using conditional probability
n-m-h3-prob-02.prereq.1: The meaning of mutually exclusive events
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.prompt: Jimin said, "Events A and B cannot happen at the same time, so they do not affect each other. So they are independent." Which is the most appropriate assessment of Jimin's claim?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think for yourself about what happens to the chance of B once you know that A has happened.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.hint.1: If they are independent, knowing A must leave the probability of B the same as at first. Compare whether that is the case in this situation.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.a: Wrong. If you know A has happened, B can no longer happen, so the probability of B differs from what it was at first.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.b: Right. Since the two events do not happen together, one does not change the probability of the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.b: You read "cannot happen together" as "do not affect each other." That one event happening makes the other impossible is itself a strong effect.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.c: Right. Since A and B have the same probability, one does not affect the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.c: The probabilities being equal in size and independence are different matters. Independence is about whether the probability of one changes when you know the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.o.d: Wrong. Since A and B have different probabilities, one affects the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.r.d: Different probabilities do not mean the events are not independent. What you should compare is whether the probability of one changes when you know the other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s1.explain: If A and B cannot happen at the same time and each has probability greater than 0, then knowing that A has happened changes the probability of B to 0. If they were independent, P(B|A)=P(B) would have to hold, so they are not independent. On a die, when A is 1 or 2 and B is 3 or 4, P(B)=1/3, but if A happens, P(B|A)=0.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.prompt: With the same single die roll, also consider event C (an even roll) and event D (a roll of 3 or less). Choose all the pairs of events that are independent of each other.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each pair, find P(both events happen) and P(first)×P(second) and compare whether they are equal.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.hint.1: First write down the rolls belonging to each event, then find the rolls that belong to both events.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.r.a: You treated a pair that cannot happen together as independent. If one happens, the probability of the other becomes 0.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.r.d: You treated A being contained in D as "unrelated." If A happens, D certainly happens, so the probability of D changes.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s2.explain: P(A)=1/3, P(C)=1/2, and P(A∩C)=P({2})=1/6=P(A)P(C), so A and C are independent. B and C are also independent, since B∩C={4} and 1/6=1/3×1/2. For A and D, P(A∩D)=1/3 but P(A)P(D)=1/6, so they are not independent. Events can be independent even when they overlap, and events that do not overlap (when their probabilities are greater than 0) cannot be independent.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.prompt: Write an explanation to send to Jimin. Based on what it means for A and B to be independent, explain why A and B are not independent in this die example, using "the probability of B when we know A has happened."
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write which rolls remain when you know A has happened, and see whether any of them belong to B.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write the original probability of B and the probability then side by side in one sentence and compare them.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If you know A has happened, then B ...
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the meaning of independence as "knowing one event does not change the probability of the other"?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In this example, did you state both the original probability of B and its probability after learning that A happened?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say that "cannot happen at the same time" and "independent" are different?
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.model.0: If the events were independent, the probability of B would stay 1/3 even after we know A happened. But if A (1 or 2) happens, B (3 or 4) cannot happen, so its probability becomes 0. The probability changes, so they are not independent.
n-m-h3-prob-02.s.s3.model.1: At first, the probability of B is one third. But if we learn the die shows 1 or 2, then 3 or 4 is impossible, so the probability of B changes to 0. If they were independent it should not change, but it did, so they are not independent.

n-m-h3-prob-03.title: Which Study App Is More Effective?
n-m-h3-prob-03.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-03.goal: Check that the overall rates and the rates within each group can point in opposite directions, revising your judgment at each stage as more data is revealed.
n-m-h3-prob-03.material: You want to compare the "percentage of students whose grades improved" among students at a school who used study app A or app B. The numbers are revealed stage by stage.
n-m-h3-prob-03.thinking.0: Making a first judgment from the overall rates
n-m-h3-prob-03.thinking.1: Revising the judgment using conditional rates within groups
n-m-h3-prob-03.thinking.2: Interpreting the result through differences in group composition
n-m-h3-prob-03.prereq.0: Conditional probability is a ratio within the cases that satisfy the condition
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed stage by stage. At each stage, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, check which group's rate you are comparing.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the overall rate and the rate for each class, and think about which one compares students in the same situation.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.info: At one school, students chose study app A or B themselves and used it for one semester. Of the 200 students who used A, 132 improved their grades, and of the 200 students who used B, 152 improved.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which app seems more effective at improving grades?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The overall rate looks higher for B. But if we don't know whether the two groups of students are of the same kind, it is too early to conclude anything about the apps' effect from these numbers alone.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: B: because the percentage of students whose grades improved is higher
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You compared the overall rates (66% and 76%) as they are. This is the first judgment that comes to mind.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A: even if fewer students who used A improved, it is because struggling students probably used it
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You assumed without evidence that the A users are struggling students. We cannot know the makeup of the students right now.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Too early to tell: because we don't know what kind of students used each app
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You recognized that more information is needed besides the rates.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.info: The students were split into an advanced class and a basic class and counted again. App A: 36 of 40 in the advanced class and 96 of 160 in the basic class improved. App B: 136 of 160 in the advanced class and 16 of 40 in the basic class improved.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, which app seems more effective?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.after: In the advanced class it is 36/40=90% vs 136/160=85%, and in the basic class it is 96/160=60% vs 16/40=40%. A's rate is higher in both classes, yet B looked higher overall. The overall rate and the class-by-class rates can point in opposite directions.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: B: its overall rate is higher, so the numbers split by class do not matter
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even though data split by class was given, you looked only at the overall rate. You did not use comparisons between students in the same class.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A: A's rate is higher in the advanced class (90% and 85%) and in the basic class (60% and 40%)
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You compared students in the same class to look at the effect of the app separately.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: About the same: A leads in one class and B leads in the other, so they cancel out
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: A leads in both classes, but you read it as B leading in one class. Compare the numbers again.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The students chose the apps themselves. Of the 200 students who used A, 160 were in the basic class, while of the 200 students who used B, only 40 were in the basic class.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Finally, which conclusion is most appropriate to draw from this data?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The basic class is a group with a low rate of grade improvement no matter which app is used, and those students are concentrated in A, which pulled down A's overall rate. Within the same class A leads, but since the students chose the apps themselves, there is a limit to concluding that this is the effect of the app.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A seems more effective. Its overall rate is lower only because many basic-class students used it; within the same class A leads, but it is too early to be certain
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You judged by comparing within the same class, and you also mentioned the limitation that the data comes from students' own choices.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: B seems more effective. Its overall rate of improved grades is higher, but it is too early to be certain
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You followed only the overall rate. You did not use the information that basic-class students are concentrated in A, which lowered its overall rate.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: We can't say either way. Splitting by class reversed the result, so the data as a whole can't be trusted, and it is too early to be certain
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You discarded everything because the data reversed. Comparisons within the same class still give information.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s1.reflect: At first you judged from the overall rates that B was better, but once the students were split into groups, the conclusion reversed. "The rate of improvement among students who used app A" and "the rate of improvement among basic-class students who used app A" are different conditional probabilities. To compare, first check whether the groups being compared have the same composition.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain to a friend who first thought "B is more effective" why the overall rate is higher for B while the class-by-class rates are higher for A, and how the comparison should be made.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.hint.0: Count which class most of the students who used A and the students who used B belong to, and compare.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.hint.1: Connect which class's students improve more easily with which app many of those students used.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Among the students who used A, ...
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you point out that the makeup of A users differs from that of B users?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say why comparing within the same class is fairer?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you link the reason the overall rate and the class rates differ into one sentence?
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.model.0: Basic-class students don't improve easily with either app, and many of them are concentrated in A, so A's overall rate went down. That is why you have to compare within the same class to see the effect of the app.
n-m-h3-prob-03.s.s2.model.1: Most of the students who used A are in the basic class, where it is hard to improve grades, so A looks worse if you only look at the overall rate. If you split by class and compare under the same conditions, A is higher.

n-m-h3-prob-04.title: Wearing Glasses and Joining a Club: Making a Table of Unrelated Traits
n-m-h3-prob-04.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-04.goal: Make several 2×2 tables in which two events are independent, and check how to read independence as "the rates within the groups are equal."
n-m-h3-prob-04.material: You will make a table counting the 60 students in a class by "whether they wear glasses" and "whether they joined a club."
n-m-h3-prob-04.thinking.0: Translating the meaning of independence into a table
n-m-h3-prob-04.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.prompt: The 60 students in a class were sorted by "whether they wear glasses" and "whether they joined a club." Which statement best describes what it means for these two to be independent?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether, among only the students who wear glasses, the proportion who joined is the same as the proportion who joined overall.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.hint.1: If they are independent, "knowing whether a student wears glasses does not change the probability of joining" must hold. Compare whether each choice says this.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.a: The number of students who wear glasses equals the number who do not.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.a: You read it as the group sizes being equal. Independence is about the rates within groups, not the sizes of the groups.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.b: The number of members among students who wear glasses equals the number of members among students who do not.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.b: You compared head counts. If the two groups have different sizes, the rates differ even when the head counts are equal.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.c: The proportion of members among students who wear glasses equals the proportion of members among students who do not.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.o.d: Every student who wears glasses joined, and every student who does not wear glasses did not join.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.r.d: You treated two traits that always appear together as independent. That is the strongest kind of dependence, where knowing one determines the other.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s1.explain: If the proportion who joined among students who wear glasses equals the proportion who joined among those who do not, then knowing whether a student wears glasses does not change the probability of joining. That is, P(join|glasses)=P(join), which means the same as P(glasses∩join)=P(glasses)P(join).
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.prompt: Make tables for the 60 students. Let a = number wearing glasses who joined, b = wearing glasses who did not join, c = not wearing glasses who joined, d = not wearing glasses who did not join. All four numbers must be natural numbers at least 1 with sum 60, glasses and joining must be independent, and the number of students wearing glasses must differ from the number of members. Enter 3 different tables.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number of students wearing glasses, x, and the number of members, y. If they are independent, the number a of students wearing glasses who joined must be x×y÷60.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose x and y so that a is an integer, then fill in the remaining b, c, d so the sum is 60, and check that the membership rates of the two groups are equal.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.ok.c1: All four numbers are natural numbers at least 1.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c, d must all be natural numbers at least 1.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the four numbers is not 60.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c3: They are not independent. Compare the membership rate of students who wear glasses with that of students who do not.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.ok.c4: The number of students wearing glasses differs from the number of members.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.fail.c4: The number of students wearing glasses equals the number of members.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.explain: (10,10,20,20): of the 20 students with glasses, 10 joined (1/2), and of the 40 without, 20 joined (1/2), so the rates are equal. In (5,15,10,30) both groups have a membership rate of 1/4, and in (12,18,12,18) both have 2/5. In (10,10,10,30) the rate is 1/2 for students with glasses but 1/4 for those without, so they are not independent. (15,15,15,15) is independent, but the number wearing glasses equals the number of members, so it does not meet condition 4.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of your tables, find and write the membership rate among students who wear glasses and among those who do not, and explain why that is evidence of independence.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: In your chosen table, first write the number of students with glasses and without glasses, then divide each group's number of members by it.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write the two rates side by side, compare whether they are equal, and then connect this to the meaning of independence.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., Among students who wear glasses, the membership rate is ...
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: For each of the two groups, did you find the rate by dividing the number of members by the number of students in that group?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect equal rates to the idea that wearing glasses does not change the probability of joining?
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.model.0: Of the 20 students with glasses, 10 joined, so the rate is 1/2, and of the 40 students without glasses, 20 joined, so it is also 1/2. Since the two rates are equal, knowing whether a student wears glasses does not change the probability of joining, so they are independent.
n-m-h3-prob-04.s.s2.because.model.1: Both the group that wears glasses and the group that does not have a membership rate of 50%. So whether a student wears glasses has no effect on the probability of joining, which means we can say they are independent.

n-m-h3-prob-05.title: Five Heads in a Row: Is Tails Due Now?
n-m-h3-prob-05.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-05.goal: Identify the misconception about probability after a streak of results, and then rephrase the same idea so a middle-school younger sibling can understand it.
n-m-h3-prob-05.material: Your younger sibling was flipping a fair coin and said, "Heads came up 5 times in a row! Isn't it about time for tails?" The coin is fair: heads and tails are equally likely. Your sibling is in 7th grade.
n-m-h3-prob-05.thinking.1: Choosing an explanation that fits the audience
n-m-h3-prob-05.thinking.2: Explaining it yourself in simple words
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.prompt: You flipped a fair coin and got heads 5 times in a row. Which statement about the probability of heads on the sixth flip is correct?
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the coin remembers past flips or tries to make up for them.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how what we are predicting differs between "when we don't know the first 5 flips" and "after the first 5 heads have already happened."
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.o.a: This coin tends to land heads, so the probability of heads is greater than 1/2.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.r.a: Even though the coin is fair, you thought the earlier results change the coin's nature.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.o.b: Heads has come up a lot, so it is now tails' turn, and the probability of heads is less than 1/2.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.r.b: You thought the earlier results must be "made up for." A coin does not remember earlier results and adjust to match them.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.o.c: Regardless of the results of the first 5 flips, the probability that the sixth flip is heads stays 1/2.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.o.d: The probability of 6 heads in a row is 1/64, so the probability of heads on the sixth flip is also 1/64.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.r.d: You mixed up the probability of predicting all six flips from the start with the probability of predicting one flip after the first five have already happened.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s1.explain: Each flip of a fair coin is independent, so even if we know the earlier results, the probability of heads on the sixth flip is 1/2. The probability 1/64 of 6 heads in a row is the value for predicting all six flips before flipping; under the condition that the first 5 heads have already happened, it is (1/64)÷(1/32)=1/2.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.prompt: You want to explain to your 7th-grade sibling "why the sixth flip is also 50-50 heads or tails." Choose the most appropriate explanation.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.hint.0: For each explanation, write in one line what your sibling would say next.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check separately whether the content is correct and whether your sibling can read and understand it.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.o.a: Since the events are independent, P(H6 | H1~H5) = P(H6) = 1/2.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.r.a: There are many symbols and terms, so it is hard for your sibling to follow. It is missing the step of rewording the same content in everyday language.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.o.b: A coin can't remember earlier results. You flip it fresh every time, so the sixth flip is also 50-50 heads or tails.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.o.c: If you flip enough times it eventually evens out to 50-50, so this time tails is a bit more likely.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.r.c: You read "it eventually evens out" as meaning the next flip makes up for the heads. It actually reinforces the wrong idea.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.o.d: Five in a row is really amazing. If the sixth is heads too, you should suspect this coin.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.r.d: This ignores the condition that the coin is fair. This explanation does not answer your sibling's misconception.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s2.explain: A good explanation rewords the same content in words the sibling knows. B puts the meaning of independence in simple words with "it doesn't remember" and "you flip it fresh every time"; A is correct but its symbols are hard; C reinforces the wrong idea; and D ignores the condition that the coin is fair.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.prompt: Your sibling asks back, "But the probability of 6 heads in a row is only 1/64. So if the sixth is heads too, that's really rare!" Answer in simple words so your sibling can understand. (Try not to use symbols or terms such as P( ) or "conditional.")
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write in one sentence "when" the probability 1/64 applies. Is it before flipping, or after five flips have come up?
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many flips are left now, and say the probability that this one flip is heads.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., 1/64 is ... The first five flips have already ...
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say when 1/64 is the probability (when predicting all six flips before flipping)?
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the probability now, with only the sixth flip left, is 1/2?
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain using only words your sibling knows?
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.model.0: 1/64 is the chance that all six flips are heads, figured out before you start flipping. Now the first 5 have already happened and only the sixth flip is left, so for that one flip, heads and tails are equally likely.
n-m-h3-prob-05.s.s3.model.1: The first five flips are already over, and the coin doesn't remember them. So the sixth flip is heads or tails with the same 1/2 chance. 1/64 is the chance of getting all six right ahead of time, so it is different from the situation now.

n-m-h3-prob-06.title: Multiples on Cards: Finding Independent Pairs
n-m-h3-prob-06.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-06.goal: Find pairs of multiple events that are independent on your own, and explain by counting that being relatively prime is not enough for independence.
