n-m-h3-prob-06.material: You draw one card from 20 cards numbered 1 to 20. Seunghyeon guessed that the event "a multiple of p" and the event "a multiple of q" would be independent whenever p and q are relatively prime.
n-m-h3-prob-06.thinking.2: Explaining a counterexample where numbers are relatively prime but not independent
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.prompt: You draw one card from 20 cards numbered 1 to 20. Let A be the event that a multiple of 3 is drawn and B the event that a multiple of 4 is drawn. What is the probability P(A∩B) that both events happen together?
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write out all the cards that are multiples of 3 and all the cards that are multiples of 4.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find which cards appear in both lists.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.o.a: 0: there is no card that is a multiple of both 3 and 4
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.r.a: You thought that because 3 and 4 are relatively prime, no cards overlap. But 12 is a multiple of both 3 and 4.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.r.c: You did not count the common multiples and used the value of 3×4 as the denominator. You did not use the fact that there are only 20 cards.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.o.d: 1/2: the proportion of cards that are multiples of 3 or multiples of 4
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.r.d: You found the union ("or"). What we want is "both."
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s1.explain: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 (6 cards), the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 (5 cards), and only one card, 12, is in both. So P(A∩B)=1/20, while P(A)P(B)=6/20×5/20=3/40. The two values differ, so A and B are not independent.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.prompt: For natural numbers p, q with 2 ≤ p < q ≤ 20, find and enter at least 3 different pairs (p, q) for which A = "a multiple of p" and B = "a multiple of q" are independent.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many of the 20 cards are multiples of p, multiples of q, and common multiples of p and q, and compare 20×(number of cards that are both) with (number of multiples of p)×(number of multiples of q).
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.hint.1: Start by counting small pairs by hand, and look for what the pairs that work have in common.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.fail.c1: They must be natural numbers with 2≤p<q≤20.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.fail.c2: They are not independent. Count the multiples of p, the multiples of q, and the cards that are both, and compare P(A∩B) with P(A)P(B).
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.explain: With 20 cards, the possible pairs are the five pairs (2,3), (2,5), (2,7), (2,9), (4,5). For example, (2,5) has 10 multiples of 2, 4 multiples of 5, and 2 multiples of 10, so 20×2=40=10×4 holds. (3,4) is relatively prime, yet 20×1=20 and 6×5=30, so it is not independent, and (2,4) gives 20×5=100 and 10×5=50, so it is not independent.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.prompt: p=3, q=4 are relatively prime (their only common divisor is 1), yet they are not independent. Show why they are not independent by counting, and say what is different from (2, 5), which is independent.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write how many of the 20 cards are multiples of 3, of 4, and of 12, and compute the product.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count the same quantities for (2, 5), compare, and look at whether 20 divides evenly by the common multiple.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., There are 6 multiples of 3, and the multiples of 4 are ...
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you count 6 multiples of 3, 5 multiples of 4, and 1 card that is both, and compare the two values?
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the same calculation works for (2,5)?
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid concluding that "relatively prime means independent"?
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.model.0: There are 6 multiples of 3, 5 multiples of 4, and only one card, 12, that is both. P(A∩B)=1/20, but P(A)P(B)=6/20×5/20=3/40, so they are not equal. For (2,5), the common multiple is 10 and 20 is a multiple of 10, so the number of cards fits exactly and the product holds.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.model.1: Only 12 overlaps, so P(A∩B) is one twentieth, but 6/20×5/20 is 3/40, so they differ. For 2 and 5, there are 2 multiples of 10 within 20, so 10×4=20×2 works, but for 3 and 4, 12 is not a divisor of 20, so it does not fit.
n-m-h3-prob-06.s.s2.because.model.2: There are 6 multiples of 3, 5 multiples of 4, and just one card, 12, that is both. If they were independent it should be 6×5÷20=1.5 cards, but it is 1, so it doesn't match. For (2,5), 10×4÷20=2 cards, a whole number, so it fits exactly.

n-m-h3-prob-07.title: The First Ball We Haven't Seen: What Is the Probability for the Second Ball?
n-m-h3-prob-07.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-07.goal: Check how probabilities change with conditions when information is revealed step by step, and understand that information learned later can also change the probability of an earlier draw.
n-m-h3-prob-07.material: You do the activity below with balls in a bag. Once a ball is taken out it is not put back, and every ball is equally likely to be drawn.
n-m-h3-prob-07.thinking.0: Splitting the unknown cases and combining them
n-m-h3-prob-07.thinking.1: Narrowing the sample space using what we learned
n-m-h3-prob-07.thinking.2: Distinguishing time order from the direction of information
n-m-h3-prob-07.prereq.0: Product of probabilities for drawing without replacement
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each stage, choose the probability using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, check whether there is something newly learned and whether it changes what the remaining balls are.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.hint.1: If there is a ball whose color you don't know, split into cases by color and add up the probabilities of the cases.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.info: An opaque bag contains 3 red balls and 5 blue balls (identical in shape). Mina took out one ball and hid it to the side without checking its color. Then she took one more ball out of the bag.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the probability that the second ball taken out is red?
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.after: If the probability that the hidden ball is red is 3/8, then the remaining red probability is 2/7, and if the probability that it is blue is 5/8, then the remaining red probability is 3/7. So (3/8)(2/7)+(5/8)(3/7)=21/56=3/8. If we don't know the first ball, the probability for the color of the second ball is the same as the original proportion.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 3/7: calculating as if the hidden ball was blue
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You calculated as if the hidden ball's color were fixed as blue. Right now we do not know that color.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 3/8: splitting into cases by the hidden ball's color and adding gives the same as the original proportion
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 2/7: calculating as if the hidden ball was red
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You calculated as if the hidden ball's color were fixed as red. Right now we do not know that color.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Cannot be determined: because we don't know the hidden ball's color
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You did not use the method of splitting into cases and combining them. Even without knowing the color, you can find it if you know the probability of each case.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.info: Mina opened the ball she had hidden, and it was a red ball. (The second ball has not been checked yet.)
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, what is the probability that the second ball taken out is red?
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.after: Now that we know the hidden ball is red, the remaining balls are 2 red and 5 blue, 7 in all. So the probability that the second ball is red drops to 2/7.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 3/7: there are 3 red balls among the remaining 7
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You knew the hidden ball was red but did not reflect that the number of red balls decreased.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 3/8: the original proportion stays the same
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You did not use the information from checking the hidden ball. When information increases, the makeup of the remaining balls changes.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 2/7: there are 2 red balls among the remaining 7
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.info: On another day, you do it again with the same bag. This time, with the first ball still hidden, you opened the second ball that was taken out next, and it was a red ball. The first ball has not been checked yet.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the probability that the first ball, the one hidden earlier, was red?
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.after: P(first red | second red) = P(both red)÷P(second red) = (3/8×2/7)÷(3/8) = 2/7. Knowing the second ball is red is calculated as if one red ball were removed, so the probability that the first ball is red also goes down from 3/8 to 2/7.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 2/7: if we know the second ball is red, the probability that the first ball is red goes down
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 3/8: the first ball was already drawn, so knowing the second ball does not change it
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You mistook time order for the direction of information. Information learned later can also change the probability of an earlier result.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 5/7: the second ball is red, so the first ball was probably blue
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The question asks for the probability that the first ball is red, but you gave the probability that it is blue. Check whether the two values add up to 1.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s1.reflect: When we had not seen any ball, the probability for the second ball was 3/8, the same as at the start, but once we knew the first ball it changed to 2/7. Also, learning about the ball drawn later changed the probability of the ball drawn earlier. Conditional probability is determined not by time order but by "what we know."
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.prompt: Explain to a friend why the probability that the second ball, taken out without knowing the color of the first ball, is red is 3/8. (This is the friend who said it cannot be calculated if you don't know the color of the first ball.)
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the case where the hidden ball is red and the case where it is blue separately, and find the probability that the second ball is red in each case.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.hint.1: Multiply by the probability of each case, add the two cases, and calculate what value comes out.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., When the hidden ball is red and when it is blue, ...
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you split into cases by the color of the first ball, or give a reason that they are equally likely?
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the process of multiplying and adding the probabilities of the cases to get 3/8?
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.model.0: If the hidden ball is red, the remaining red probability is 2/7, and if it is blue, it is 3/7. So multiplying by their probabilities 3/8 and 5/8 and adding gives (3/8)(2/7)+(5/8)(3/7)=3/8.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.model.1: If we don't know the first ball, then any one of the 8 balls is equally likely to be the one taken out second, so the probability that it is red is the original proportion, 3/8.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.model.2: If the hidden ball is red, the remaining red probability is 2/7, and if it is blue, it is 3/7. So 3/8×2/7+5/8×3/7=3/8.
n-m-h3-prob-07.s.s2.model.3: If we don't know the color of the hidden ball, the ball taken out second is the same as any ball picked at random, so the probability that it is red is the original proportion, 3/8.

n-m-h3-prob-08.title: Prize Money from an Interrupted Match: How Should We Split It?
n-m-h3-prob-08.topic: Probability: conditional probability, independence and dependence, Bayesian-style reasoning, setting up the sample space
n-m-h3-prob-08.goal: Sort out the information needed to find the probability of winning, and set up an equally likely sample space by assuming that a match that would end early is played to the end.
n-m-h3-prob-08.material: Team A and Team B were playing a match in which the first team to win 3 games takes all of the 80,000-won prize, but it was interrupted for some reason. So far Team A has 2 wins and Team B has 1 win. The two teams agreed to split the prize in proportion to "the probability that each team wins in the remaining games."
n-m-h3-prob-08.thinking.0: Telling needed information from unneeded information
n-m-h3-prob-08.thinking.1: Setting up an equally likely sample space
n-m-h3-prob-08.thinking.2: Explaining why an assumption does not change the result
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.prompt: Team A and Team B were playing a match in which the first team to win 3 games takes all of the 80,000-won prize, but it was interrupted. So far Team A has 2 wins and Team B has 1 win. The prize is to be split in proportion to each team's probability of winning. Choose all the information that is essential for finding these probabilities. (Nothing is known about the teams' skill levels.)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.hint.0: Remove each piece of information one at a time and think about whether the future winning probability could still be calculated without it.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write what you need in order to know how many more games each team must win to be champion.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.a: The order of the games won so far (whether it was A, B, A)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.r.a: You thought the order matters. The future winning probability depends on the current win counts and the remaining games; the order in which wins accumulated has no effect.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.b: The number of wins for each team so far (2 wins and 1 win)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.c: The number of wins needed to be champion (first to 3 wins)
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.d: The time the match has taken so far
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.r.d: Time has nothing to do with future wins and losses. Think about whether it is information that affects the winning probability.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.o.e: The chance that each team wins a single game
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s1.explain: The current win counts and the wins needed to be champion determine how many more games each team must win (A needs 1 game, B needs 2 games), and the per-game winning chance determines the probability of that happening. The order of wins and the time taken do not affect the remaining games, so they are not needed.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the two teams are equally likely to win a single game and the games do not affect one another. Find the probability that Team A wins the championship, and also write the prize money Team A should receive. Include in your solution which cases you counted.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write what must happen in the remaining games for Team A to win and for Team B to win.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.hint.1: Even if the match would end early, consider whether imagining that all the remaining games are played lets you make the cases equally likely.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you consider the cases where Team A wins and where Team B wins separately?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you choose the cases so that each one is equally likely?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you split the prize money using the probabilities?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.model.0: If we imagine playing both remaining games, the four outcomes (A,A),(A,B),(B,A),(B,B) are equally likely. For B to win, B must win both games, which is only (B,B), so B has 1/4 and A has 3/4. So A should receive 60,000 won and B 20,000 won.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s2.model.1: For B to win, B must win the remaining two games in a row, and that probability is 1/2×1/2=1/4. So the probability that A wins is 3/4, and A should receive 60,000 won of the 80,000-won prize.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.prompt: Minji said, "If A wins the next game the match ends, so it's not right to imagine playing both remaining games, because that's different from what would really happen." Which is the most appropriate response to Minji's statement?
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.hint.0: Find the probability of each of the three ways the real match could end, and check that they add up to 1.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.hint.1: If both remaining games are played, make a table showing who wins the championship for each of the four outcomes.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.a: Two more games are really played, so all four outcomes can happen.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.a: This explanation contradicts the fact that the match ends early. They do not actually play all of them.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.b: The number of games until the end must be the same for the prize to be split fairly.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.b: You based fairness on the number of games until the end. The standard is the probability of winning.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.c: It is just for convenience, so it does not matter as long as the value is right.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.r.c: You did not say why the value is right. There is a reason why it is fine to look at it this way.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.o.d: Games after the match is decided do not change the winning team, so the result is the same even if all are played.
n-m-h3-prob-08.s.s3.explain: If A wins the next game, A is the champion, and later games do not change the winner. So even if we assume both remaining games are played, "who wins the championship" does not change, and the four outcomes each become equally likely at 1/4, which makes counting easy. If we treat the three ways the real match ends ("A wins" with 1/2, "B wins then A wins" with 1/4, "B wins twice in a row" with 1/4) as equally likely, that is wrong.

n-m-h3-serieslim-01.title: If We Group the Terms, Is the Sum the Same?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.goal: By writing out partial sums yourself, check and explain that the convergence of a series with grouped terms does not let us conclude that the original series converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.material: Three friends are arguing about what the sum of the series 1−1+1−1+1−1+… is. Information is revealed one piece at a time. (The general term is (−1)^(n−1): 1 if n is odd, −1 if n is even.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.thinking.0: Revising your judgment each time new information appears
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.thinking.1: Judging the convergence of a series using partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.thinking.2: Sorting out which direction holds between the grouped series and the original series
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.prereq.1: Defining the sum of a series as the limit of its partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.prompt: At each stage, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.hint.0: When new information appears, reconsider whether the judgment you chose just before is still fine.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write out two different groupings and compare whether the same value comes out no matter how the terms are grouped.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Mina grouped two terms at a time and wrote (1−1)+(1−1)+(1−1)+…, so each parenthesis is 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you judge the sum of this series to be?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Depending on how the terms are grouped, both 0 and 1 came out. So you can see that it is too early to state the sum just because "I grouped it one way."
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is 0: because each group is 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You accepted the result of one grouping as the sum. This is the first judgment that comes to mind.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is 1: because leaving the first term 1 and grouping as 1+(−1+1)+(−1+1)+… gives 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You tried a different grouping and got a different value. But you could look more carefully at the fact that you immediately decided that value is the sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Too early to decide: we need to check whether the value is the same when we change the grouping
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You are suspecting that the result can change depending on how the terms are grouped.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Writing out the partial sums in order gives S_1=1, S_2=0, S_3=1, S_4=0, S_5=1, ….
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: A series is defined by the limit of its partial sums. Now what do you judge?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.after: The partial sums do not approach a single value, so this series diverges. Its sum is not determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It converges to 0: because S_2, S_4, … are all 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You looked only at the even-numbered partial sums. You missed that the odd-numbered ones are 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It converges to 1: because S_1, S_3, … are all 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You looked only at the odd-numbered partial sums. You missed that the even-numbered ones are 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It does not converge: because the partial sums alternate between 0 and 1 and do not approach a single value
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked at the behavior of all the partial sums and judged according to the definition of a limit.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.info: But the series 0+0+0+… that Mina made by grouping clearly converges to 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: From the fact that the grouped series converges, what can we say about the original series?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If the original series converges, the grouped series converges to the same value. But the converse does not hold, because the grouped series uses only S_2, S_4, ….
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The original series also converges, with the same sum: because we only grouped terms
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You applied the intuition that grouping keeps the sum unchanged in both directions.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Nothing can be determined: because the partial sums of the grouped series are only some of the original partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You pointed out that the grouped series uses only some of the original partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The sum of the original series is both 0 and 1: because each way of grouping has a sum
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You said a non-convergent series has two sums. A sum is defined as one limit of the partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s1.reflect: At first the calculation of 0 by grouping seemed plausible, but your judgment changed once you wrote the partial sums. Whether a series converges is decided not by how it is grouped but by the behavior of all the partial sums S_n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.prompt: Soyoung said, "Grouping with parentheses gave 0+0+0+…, so the sum of 1−1+1−1+… is 0." Write an explanation to send to Soyoung. Include how the partial sums of the original series behave and how the partial sums of the grouped series relate to the original partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4 yourself and note how the values change.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.hint.1: Point out which of the original partial sums are the partial sums of the grouped series (1−1)+(1−1)+….
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you actually check the values of the partial sums S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say which of the original partial sums the grouped series uses?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you consider whether "the grouped series converges" guarantees "the original series converges"?
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.0: The partial sums of the original series are 1, 0, 1, 0, …, alternating between 0 and 1 and not approaching a single value. So it has no sum. The partial sums of the grouped series pick out only some of them (the even-numbered ones), like S_2, S_4, …, so it just happens to come out as 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.1: The partial sums repeat 1,0,1,0 and do not converge. If we change the grouping to 1+(−1+1)+(−1+1)+…, it gives 1, so the value depends on the grouping. The grouped series being 0 has nothing to do with the sum of the original series.
n-m-h3-serieslim-01.s.s2.model.2: Soyoung, the original series' S_n is 1 for odd n and 0 for even n, so it has no limit (it diverges). Grouping with parentheses means looking only at S_2, S_4, …, which give 0, so it is no evidence that the original series converges.

n-m-h3-serieslim-02.title: Checking a Solution That Found the General Term from the Partial Sum Formula
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.goal: Learn that a_1 must be found separately when finding the general term from the partial sum S_n, correct the wrong solution, and check it using the sum lim S_n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.material: The sum of the first n terms of a series is S_n = 4 − 3·(1/2)^(n−1). Read Minjae's solution for finding the sum of this series. ((1/2)^(n−1) means one half to the power n−1.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.thinking.0: Finding the first line in the solution that goes wrong
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.thinking.1: Checking the range where the formula holds (n≥2)
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.thinking.2: Checking by another method (limit of partial sums)
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.thinking.3: Finding the condition under which the formula also holds at n=1
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.prereq.1: Formula for the sum of an infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minjae's solution that goes wrong.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.hint.0: Check line by line whether each line really follows from the previous one.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the condition (the range of n) used to obtain a formula is kept as it is in the next line.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.line.0: The sum of the series is lim S_n, and for n ≥ 2, a_n = S_n − S_(n−1).
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.line.2: Assuming this formula can also be used for n=1, set a_n = 3·(1/2)^(n−1) for all n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.line.3: This is an infinite geometric series with first term 3 and common ratio 1/2, so the sum is 3/(1−1/2) = 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s1.explain: It is line 3. S_n−S_(n−1) can be used only for n≥2, so whether the formula obtained also holds at n=1 must be checked separately. Here a_1=S_1=4−3=1, but plugging n=1 into the formula gives 3, which differs. The calculations in lines 1 and 2 are correct, and line 4 is a result that follows line 3.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.prompt: Correct Minjae's solution and find the sum of this series. Then find the first term a_1 directly, compare it with Minjae's value, and write why the sum changes.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.hint.0: Find the limit of S_n directly and compare it with the value Minjae got.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.hint.1: Plug into the formula to find a_1 from S_1, then compare it with the value you get by putting n=1 into Minjae's general-term formula.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether the formula obtained for n≥2 also holds at n=1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you double-check the sum with lim S_n?
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.model.0: a_1=S_1=4−3=1. But putting n=1 into 3·(1/2)^(n−1) gives 3, so a_1 is different. So a_1=1, and from n≥2 the term is 3·(1/2)^(n−1). The sum is 1+(3/2)/(1−1/2)=1+3=4, which also equals lim S_n=4.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.model.1: The first term is S_1=1, not the 3 from the general-term formula. From n=2 on, the first term is 3/2 and the common ratio is 1/2, so that part is 3/2÷(1/2)=3, and adding the 1 gives the sum 4.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.model.2: Taking the limit of S_n directly gives 4−0=4, and the 6 Minjae wrote is the value with 3 extra added because he took a_1 to be 3 by mistake. The actual a_1 is S_1=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s2.model.3: lim S_n=4. a_1=S_1=1, but Minjae took it to be 3. So the correct answer is 4, not 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.prompt: For each S_n below, choose the one for which the general-term formula obtained for n≥2 also holds as it is at n=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.hint.0: For each formula, find S_1 and compare it with the value you get by putting n=1 into the formula obtained from S_n−S_(n−1).
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.hint.1: For each formula, substitute different values of n into S_n and compare, and look for something in common among the formulas where the directly computed S_1 equals the value of the a_1 formula.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.r.a: This is Minjae's series. a_1=1 but the formula gives 3, so it does not match.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.r.b: a_1=S_1=1, but putting n=1 into the formula 2·(1/2)^(n−1) for n≥2 gives 2, so it does not match.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.r.c: a_1=S_1=3, and putting n=1 into the formula 3·(1/2)^(n−1) for n≥2 also gives 3, so it matches.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.r.d: a_1=S_1=7/2, but putting n=1 into the formula 3·(1/2)^n for n≥2 gives 3/2, so it does not match.
n-m-h3-serieslim-02.s.s3.explain: If putting n=0 into the S_n formula gives S_0=0 (c: 6−6=0), the formula also holds at n=1. For the others, S_0 is −2, −1, 2 respectively, so a_1 must be found separately.

n-m-h3-serieslim-03.title: The Common Ratios of Area and Perimeter When We Keep Drawing Squares
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.goal: Learn that when similar figures repeat, the common ratio of the areas differs from the common ratio of the perimeters, and write a message that lets a friend correct the mistake on their own.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.material: There is a square R1 with side length 8. Joining the midpoints of its sides makes a square R2, joining the midpoints of R2's sides makes R3, and this process is repeated endlessly. To find the sum of the areas and the sum of the perimeters of R1, R2, R3, …, Jiwon sent a friend the message below.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.thinking.0: Telling apart the ratio of lengths and the ratio of areas
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.thinking.1: Finding the common ratio that fits the quantity forming the sequence
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.thinking.2: Writing an explanation that helps a friend check on their own
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.prereq.0: Sum of an infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.prereq.2: Ratio of lengths and ratio of areas in similar figures
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Jiwon's message that contains something wrong.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the area and perimeter of R1 and of R2, and find R2÷R1 separately for each.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table of which common ratio was used for which quantity (area or perimeter) in each line.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.line.0: R1 has side 8, so its area is 64 and its perimeter is 32.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.line.1: Joining the midpoints makes the area exactly half each time, so the common ratio of the areas is 1/2, and the sum of the areas is 64/(1−1/2)=128.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.line.2: The perimeter is also of the same squares, so I can just use 1/2 as the common ratio,
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.line.3: and the sum of the perimeters is 32/(1−1/2)=64.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 4. A side of R2 is 1/√2 times a side of R1 (8÷√2), so the common ratio of the perimeters is 1/√2. The common ratio of the areas is its square, 1/2. Lines 1 and 2 are correct.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the checking methods that would help Jiwon discover the error on her own.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether, when she carries out each method, Jiwon runs into something that contradicts 64.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether the method uses information obtained independently of Jiwon's result.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.o.a: Check that it seems natural that the sum of perimeters 64 is half the sum of areas 128
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.r.a: Perimeter and area are quantities with different units. Comparing 128 and 64 does not check anything.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.o.b: Find the side length of R2 directly with the Pythagorean theorem and compare it with the side of R1
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.r.b: This is a way to check directly that the common ratio of the perimeters is the ratio of the side lengths.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.o.c: Since all squares are similar, set the similarity ratio equal to the ratio of areas
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.r.c: The similarity ratio is the ratio of lengths, and the ratio of areas is its square. Setting them equal is the cause of the error.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.o.d: Actually add up the perimeters of R1, R2, R3 and see whether they exceed 64
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.r.d: 32+22.6+16 already exceeds 70, which contradicts 64, the sum of a series whose terms are all positive.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s2.explain: B has her find the common ratio directly, and D lets her see the contradiction that the partial sum already exceeds Jiwon's sum of 64. A simply confirms the error, and C repeats the cause of the error.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.prompt: Write the message to send to Jiwon. (1) Explain why the common ratio of the perimeters is not 1/2, using the side length of the smaller square, (2) include one way she can check on her own, but (3) do not write the value of the completed sum of perimeters.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.hint.0: Draw a picture of what right triangle the side of R2 and the side of R1 form (hypotenuse and leg).
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write the relationship between the ratio of areas and the ratio of sides, then think about whether the same value is used for the perimeter as well.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you acknowledge the part Jiwon got right (the area)?
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the common ratio of the perimeters is not 1/2 using the ratio of lengths?
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you guide her toward an action to check, without giving her the answer?
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.model.0: You're right that the ratio of areas is 1/2. But the perimeter is a length, so its ratio is different. A side of the new square is half of the diagonal, so it gets shorter, to about 8÷√2, and the ratio of lengths is 1/√2. The ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of lengths, which is why it is 1/2. Find a side of R2 yourself and compare it with R1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.model.1: Jiwon, you did the area calculation well! But using 1/2 as the common ratio of the perimeters brought over the area's common ratio. The ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of lengths, so the ratio of perimeters is 1 over √2. Find a side of R2 with the Pythagorean theorem and compare it with 8, and if you add up the perimeters of R1, R2, R3, you can also see whether it exceeds your answer of 64.
n-m-h3-serieslim-03.s.s3.model.2: Area is in square units and perimeter is in length units, so their ratios differ. Use the square root of 2 to first find how many times a side of R1 a side of R2 is. Then use that value as the common ratio.

n-m-h3-serieslim-04.title: Is 0.999… a Little Less Than 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.goal: Explain, using the limit of a difference, that a limit can be the sum even if the partial sums never reach it, and construct another series with the same property.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.material: Two friends are arguing about whether 0.999… (with 9s repeating forever) equals 1. Yuna: "0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … are always less than 1 no matter how far you go, so 0.999… is less than 1." Dohyun: "0.999…=9/10+9/100+9/1000+…, which is an infinite geometric series with first term 9/10 and common ratio 1/10, so its sum is 1."
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.thinking.0: Sorting out whether a claim's evidence supports its conclusion
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.thinking.2: Making examples with the same property
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.prereq.0: Sum of an infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.prompt: Examine the two friends' statements and evidence, and choose the most appropriate judgment.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check separately whether Yuna's evidence is true and whether her conclusion follows from that evidence.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write what the sum of a series is defined as, and compare whether Dohyun's calculation matches that definition.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.a: Dohyun is right: the sum of a series is the limit of its partial sums, and the partial sums get arbitrarily close to 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.a: You judged according to the definition of a sum (the limit of the partial sums). You also see that Yuna's evidence does not lead to her conclusion.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.b: The sum is not determined: because the partial sums keep changing forever and cannot have a single value
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.b: You confused the partial sums continuing to change with not converging. Even if they change, the series converges if they approach a single value.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.c: Yuna is right: no partial sum equals 1, so 0.999… differs from 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.c: You carried a property of each partial sum over directly to the limit. The limit is not one of the partial sums.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.o.d: Both are right: 0.999… is less than 1 by an arbitrarily small amount, but in calculations it is treated as 1
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.r.d: You said a positive difference from 1 remains, and also said it equals 1. Among real numbers, two numbers are the same only if their difference is 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s1.explain: The sum of a series is the limit of the partial sums S_n. Here S_n=1−(1/10)^n and the limit is 1, so 0.999…=1. Yuna's evidence is true, but from "all S_n are less than 1" it does not follow that "lim S_n is less than 1" (in the limit it becomes ≤).
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.prompt: Yuna's statement "no matter up to which n you add, the partial sum is less than 1" is true. Yet her conclusion is wrong. Explain the reason using 1−S_n, the value of 1 minus the partial sum S_n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write S_1, S_2, S_3 and write each one's difference from 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.hint.1: Connect how that difference behaves as n grows with what the sum of the series is determined as the limit of.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you express 1−S_n as a formula in n?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect that value approaching 0 with the sum being 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that the limit can be 1 even though the partial sums never reach 1?
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.0: 1−S_n=1/10^n is always greater than 0, so it is true that S_n is less than 1. But as n grows, 1/10^n gets arbitrarily close to 0, so the limit of S_n is 1, and since the sum of a series is that limit, 0.999…=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.1: No partial sum ever reaches 1, but 1−S_n=(1/10)^n converges to 0. The sum of a series is the limit of its partial sums, so it is 1. Even if every partial sum is less than 1, the limit can be 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s2.model.2: Every S_n is less than 1, but the difference 0.00…01 becomes arbitrarily small as n grows, so the limit is 1, and therefore 0.999…=1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.prompt: Make a series with the same property yourself. Enter two infinite geometric series a + ar + ar² + … with first term a and common ratio r whose sum is 1 and all of whose partial sums are less than 1, using different common ratios. (You may enter decimals.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.hint.0: First write what equation must hold between a and r for the sum to be 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compute S_1 and S_2 to check what sign r must have for all the partial sums to be less than 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.ok.c1: The absolute value of the common ratio is less than 1, so it converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.fail.c1: |r|<1 does not hold, so this is not a convergent series with sum 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.ok.c3: All terms are positive, so the partial sums are less than 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.fail.c3: The common ratio is not positive, so a partial sum could exceed 1.
n-m-h3-serieslim-04.s.s3.explain: If a=1−r and 0<r<1, the partial sum S_n=1−r^n is always less than 1 but its limit is 1. a=0.9, r=0.1 is exactly 0.999…. If r is negative, a=1−r>1, so the first partial sum already exceeds 1.

n-m-h3-serieslim-05.title: When x Is 0, Is the Sum of the Series Given by the Same Formula?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.goal: For a geometric series whose common ratio changes with x, examine the range where the sum formula applies, and explain that calculating separately at x=0 shows the sum differs at that point.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.material: For a real number x, let f(x)=x²+x²/(1+x²)+x²/(1+x²)²+x²/(1+x²)³+…. (It is a series with first term x² in which each next term is multiplied by 1/(1+x²).) Information is revealed one piece at a time.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.thinking.0: Revising your judgment as information increases
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.thinking.1: Checking the condition for applying the formula (first term ≠ 0)
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.thinking.2: Testing by substituting the boundary value directly
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.prereq.0: Sum of an infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.prompt: At each stage, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, check again whether the formula you used earlier still applies as it is.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.hint.1: Substitute x=0 directly and write what the first few terms are.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What formula do you expect f(x) to be for every real number x?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.after: x²/(1−1/(1+x²))=1+x² is a formula obtained after canceling. Remember that there is an x for which the canceled x² is 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You extended a formula that fits two points to all x. This is the first judgment that comes to mind.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: f(x)=1+x², but the x for which the common ratio is unusual must be examined separately
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You are doubting whether the results at two points apply to every x.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: f(x)=x²+1/x²: because another formula could also fit the two values
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: At x=1 it gives 2 and at x=2 it gives 4.25, so it does not fit one of the two values. You did not substitute to check the formula.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Now consider the case x=0. Substitute x=0 directly into the defining formula of f.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.after: f(0)=0. Even if the common ratio is 1, if the first term is 0 then every partial sum is 0, so it converges to 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 1: because we can put x=0 into the formula 1+x²
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You applied the formula obtained for x≠0 to x=0 as it is.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 0: because every term is 0, so all partial sums are 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You started from the definition and calculated the partial sums directly.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is not determined: because the common ratio is 1, so it diverges
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought that a common ratio of 1 always diverges. You missed the case where the first term is 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.info: To summarize, f(x)=1+x² if x≠0, and f(0)=0 if x=0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which statement is correct about the limit of f(x) as x→0 and the continuity at x=0?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.after: Each term is continuous, but the sum f is broken at x=0. For an infinite sum, "if each term is continuous, the sum is continuous" does not always hold.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The limit is 1 and f(0)=0, so f is not continuous at x=0
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You judged continuity by comparing the limit value and the function value.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Each term is a continuous function, so the sum f is continuous for all x
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You applied a property that holds for finite sums to an infinite sum as it is.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Both the limit and f(0) are 0, so f is continuous at x=0
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You did not check where the formula 1+x² for x≠0 goes as x→0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s1.reflect: At first you wanted to use the formula that fits two points for all x, but your judgment changed when you checked the condition x²≠0 used in the cancellation. When using a formula, you must test directly at a boundary value whether the conditions under which the formula holds apply in this case.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.prompt: Each term x²/(1+x²)^n is a continuous function of x. Write what f(0) is at x=0, and how it differs from the formula 1+x² for x≠0, with the reason.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute x=0 directly into the defining formula of f and write the first few terms.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.hint.1: When using the sum formula for a geometric series, check whether there is a case where the divisor becomes 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you actually substitute x=0 and write the first few terms?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you consider whether the formula obtained for x≠0 can be used at x=0?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that even if each term is continuous, the sum may not be continuous?
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.model.0: If x=0, every term is 0²/1^n=0, so f(0)=0. But if x≠0, f(x)=1+x², so near x=0 its values are close to 1. So the limit 1 differs from f(0)=0, and f is discontinuous at x=0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.model.1: Substituting x=0 gives a common ratio of 1, but every term from the first is 0, so the sum is 0. This differs from 1, which is what you get by putting 0 into 1+x², and f is broken at x=0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.model.2: The formula 1+x² is used only for x≠0. If x=0, all the terms are 0 so the sum is 0, and that differs from 1+0²=1, so the function is not connected at that point.
n-m-h3-serieslim-05.s.s2.model.3: If x=0, the common ratio becomes 1 so the formula cannot be used, and every term is 0, so f(0)=0. That differs from 1, which you get by putting 0 into 1+x².

n-m-h3-serieslim-06.title: An Infinite Geometric Series Whose First Term Is Greater Than Its Sum
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.goal: Make an example of an infinite geometric series with sum 6 whose first term is greater than 6, and explain how the sign of the common ratio makes the partial sums go above and below the sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.material: Suppose the infinite geometric series a + ar + ar² + … with first term a and common ratio r has sum 6. It is easy to think, "The sum is 6, so the first term must be less than 6."
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.thinking.0: Making examples that satisfy the conditions yourself to find a pattern
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.thinking.1: Verifying the size relationship between the sum and partial sums with cases
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.thinking.2: Drawing a general property from the examples
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.prereq.0: Sum of an infinite geometric series a/(1−r)
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.prompt: Make an infinite geometric series with sum 6 and first term a greater than 6, and also choose an n (a natural number from 1 to 9) for which the partial sum S_n of that series is greater than 6. Enter a, r, n. Make three with different (r, n). (S_n is the sum from the first term through the nth term.)
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.hint.0: First write what equation holds between a and r for the sum to be 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.hint.1: After choosing r from that equation, check whether a is greater than 6, and if not, change the sign or size of r.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.hint.2: With your chosen r, calculate S_1, S_2, S_3 directly and pick the n for which it is greater than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.var.n: n for which S_n is greater than 6
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.ok.c1: The absolute value of the common ratio is less than 1, so it converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.fail.c1: |r|<1 does not hold, so this series has no sum.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.ok.c3: The first term is greater than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.fail.c3: The first term is not greater than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.ok.c4: At this n, S_n=6(1−r^n) is greater than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.fail.c4: At this n, S_n is not greater than 6. Calculate S_1, S_2, S_3 directly and compare them with 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s1.explain: Since a=6(1−r), a>6 requires r<0. Then S_n=6(1−r^n), so for S_n to be greater than 6 we need r^n<0, that is, n must be odd. For example, if a=9 and r=−1/2, then S_1=9 and S_3=6(1+1/8)=6.75 are greater than 6, and S_2=4.5 is less. r=−1 is not allowed because |r|<1 fails, and a=8, r=−1/2 has sum 8/1.5≈5.33.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything that must hold for an infinite geometric series with sum 6 and first term greater than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.hint.0: Organize what the examples you made in the previous step have in common in a table.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate S_1, S_2, S_3 for your examples and compare whether each is greater or less than 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.o.a: S_2 is always greater than 6, like S_1
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.r.a: S_1 is greater than 6, but the second term is negative, so S_2 becomes smaller than S_1. In the example a=9, r=−1/2, S_2=4.5.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.o.b: All terms are positive and keep decreasing
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.r.b: For the first term to exceed the sum, some term must be negative. If all terms are positive, the sum cannot be smaller than the first term.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.r.c: The common ratio is negative and the first term is positive, so the second term ar is negative.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.o.d: Partial sums greater than 6 and partial sums less than 6 alternate
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.r.d: S_n=6(1−r^n) and r<0, so the sign of r^n alternates, and S_n−6=−6r^n alternates in sign as well.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s2.explain: Since r<0, the second term is negative, and in S_n=6−6r^n the sign of the difference from 6, −6r^n, alternates. So S_2 is less than 6, and it is also impossible for all the terms to be positive.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain why an infinite geometric series with sum 6 can have a first term greater than 6. Include how the partial sum S_n being greater or less than 6 depends on n.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.hint.0: Using one of the examples you made above, calculate S_1, S_2, S_3 and compare them with 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write S_n in terms of a and r, and think about the sign of its difference from the sum 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate S_1, S_2, S_3 for the example you made?
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the sign of the common ratio with the behavior of the partial sums?
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare with the case where all terms are positive?
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.model.0: If the common ratio is negative, the signs of the terms alternate. If the first term is greater than 6, S_1 is greater than 6, and the second term is negative, so S_2 becomes less than 6. In this way the partial sums go up and down alternately around 6 while getting closer to 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.model.1: A sum of 6 does not mean the first term must be less than 6. If r is negative, S_n=6(1−r^n), so when n is odd it is above 6 and when n is even it is below 6. So it goes up and down while converging to 6.
n-m-h3-serieslim-06.s.s3.model.2: Only when the terms are positive are the partial sums less than the sum. If the common ratio is negative, the partial sums repeatedly go above 6 and come back down, so the first term can be greater than the sum.

n-m-h3-serieslim-07.title: When Does the Sum Series of Two Series Converge?
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.goal: Sort out the combinations in which the convergence of Σ(a_n+b_n) is determined by whether Σa_n and Σb_n converge and those in which it is not determined, and construct a counterexample.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.material: There are two infinite series Σa_n and Σb_n, and you want to know whether the series Σ(a_n+b_n), formed by adding them term by term, converges or diverges. Depending on what you know, it is sometimes determined and sometimes not.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.thinking.1: Showing the undetermined cases with counterexamples
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.thinking.2: Stating the conditions under which an operation rule holds
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.prereq.1: Sum and constant multiples of convergent series
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information that determine, as a single answer, whether Σ(a_n+b_n) converges or diverges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, think of two different pairs a_n, b_n that fit it and see whether the sum series gives the same result.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether adding or subtracting a convergent series can make a divergent series converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.a: The sum of two convergent series converges, so it is determined as a single answer.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.b: If a_n=b_n=1 it diverges, but if a_n=1, b_n=−1 the sum series converges, so it is not determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.c: Subtracting the convergent Σa_n leaves Σb_n, so if the sum series converged, Σb_n would have to converge too; hence the sum series diverges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.o.d: a_n and b_n both converge to 0
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.r.d: If a_n=b_n=1/n the sum series diverges, and if a_n=1/n², b_n=1/n² it converges. It is not determined.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s1.explain: If both converge, the sum series converges, and if only one converges, the sum series diverges (because if it converged, Σb_n=Σ(a_n+b_n)−Σa_n would have to converge too). If both diverge, or if the terms go to 0, that alone does not determine it.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.prompt: Show a case with insufficient information. Let a_n=p·r^n, b_n=q·r^n (p≠0, q≠0, |r|≥1); then Σa_n and Σb_n both diverge. Enter p, q, r twice, with different r, so that Σ(a_n+b_n) converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write a_n+b_n grouped in terms of r^n, then think about what the coefficient must be for that series to converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find a way to make the coefficient 0 while keeping the condition that neither p nor q is 0.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The general terms of Σa_n and Σb_n are not 0, so each diverges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p or q is 0, so that series does not diverge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.ok.c2: |r|≥1, so the general term does not go to 0, and each diverges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.ok.c3: a_n+b_n=(p+q)r^n=0, so the sum series converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.fail.c3: (p+q)r^n is not 0, so the sum series diverges as well.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s2.explain: Since a_n+b_n=(p+q)r^n, if p+q=0 every term is 0, so the sum series converges to 0. But if p≠0 and |r|≥1, a_n and b_n do not go to 0, so each diverges. With p=q=1 the sum series also diverges, and with |r|<1 each series converges.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.prompt: Explain why the statement "if Σa_n and Σb_n both diverge, then Σ(a_n+b_n) also diverges" is wrong. Use the example from the previous step, and also write the condition needed when splitting the series of sums into the sum of two series.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write out a_n+b_n for the example you entered in the previous step.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether each part must have a value when the sum is split.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate a_n+b_n yourself for the example in the previous step?
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the condition needed for splitting?
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say what can happen when two divergent series are combined?
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.0: Even if both diverge, like Σa_n with p·r^n and Σb_n with −p·r^n, adding them makes every term 0, so it converges. So when both diverge, whether the sum series converges is not determined. To split the sum into Σa_n+Σb_n, each must converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.1: There is a counterexample. If a_n=2^n and b_n=−2^n, each diverges, but a_n+b_n=0, so the sum series converges to 0. So Σ(a_n+b_n)=Σa_n+Σb_n can be used only when both series converge.
n-m-h3-serieslim-07.s.s3.model.2: The sum of two divergent series can converge by cancellation (1 and −1 add to 0), or diverge if they have the same sign. So before splitting, you must first check that each series converges.

n-m-h3-serieslim-08.title: Using a Partial Sum Table to Decide Which Calculation Is Right
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.topic: Series: partial sums and infinite geometric series
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.goal: Filter out a wrong claim using the numerical values of partial sums, find the sum of a telescoping series by identifying exactly which terms remain, and generalize when the gap changes.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.material: Two friends give different values for the sum of the series 1/(1·3) + 1/(2·4) + 1/(3·5) + … + 1/(n(n+2)) + …. Jiho: "The terms cancel front and back, so the sum is 1/2." Seoa: "The sum is 3/4." Using a calculator, the partial sums S_n came out as S_1=0.333, S_2=0.458, S_3=0.525, S_4=0.567, S_5=0.595.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.thinking.2: Changing the form (partial fractions) to reveal the structure
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.thinking.3: Extending the pattern to a different gap
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.prereq.1: Sum of a series = limit of partial sums
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the judgment that you can state most reliably from the partial sum table alone.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.hint.0: If all terms are positive, check whether the partial sums only increase or can also decrease.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the values in the table with the two claims' values and see whether one has already been exceeded.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.o.a: Seoa is right: the partial sums keep increasing and are approaching 3/4
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.r.a: You concluded 3/4 just from the fact that the values in the table increase. They could be increasing toward other values too.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.o.b: Jiho is wrong: the partial sums only increase, and S_3 has already exceeded 1/2
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.r.b: You used the fact that all terms are positive, so S_n does not decrease, to rule out 1/2.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.o.c: Jiho is right: the partial sums seem to be moving around 1/2
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.r.c: From S_3 on, they have already exceeded 1/2. You did not read the table to the end.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.o.d: From the table alone, we cannot judge either Jiho or Seoa
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.r.d: Even if we cannot determine what the sum is, we can rule out 1/2.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s1.explain: All terms are positive, so S_n only increases. S_3=0.525 is already greater than 1/2, so the sum cannot be 1/2. Seoa's 3/4 cannot be confirmed from the table alone, so we have to find it directly.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.prompt: Use 1/(n(n+2))=½(1/n−1/(n+2)) to write S_n, write exactly which terms remain after the others cancel, and find the sum of the series. Also write why those terms remain.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.hint.0: Expand the parentheses, line up the first 5 or 6 terms in one row, and draw lines through the pairs that cancel.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many terms remain uncancelled.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you actually expand and write out the first few terms?
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say why two terms remain?
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you find the sum using the limit of S_n?
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.model.0: In S_n=½{(1−1/3)+(1/2−1/4)+(1/3−1/5)+…}, from 1/3 on each term cancels two places later, and the initial 1 and 1/2 and the final −1/(n+1) and −1/(n+2) remain. S_n=½(1+1/2−1/(n+1)−1/(n+2)) and the limit is ½·3/2=3/4.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.model.1: The terms are two places apart, so the first two terms, 1 and 1/2, have no partners to cancel with. The last two terms go to 0 as n→∞, so the sum is ½(1+½)=3/4.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.model.2: Since S_n=½(3/2−1/(n+1)−1/(n+2)), it converges to 3/4 as n grows. Because the first two terms 1 and 1/2 remain, 3/2 rather than 1 goes inside the parentheses.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s2.model.3: The leading 1 and 1/2 are left uncancelled. Sum 3/4
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.prompt: If we use the same method on the series 1/(1·4) + 1/(2·5) + 1/(3·6) + … + 1/(n(n+3)) + …, what is the sum?
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.hint.0: First find the formula that writes 1/(n(n+3)) as a difference of two fractions.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.hint.1: When the difference is 3 places, count how many leading terms remain uncancelled.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.r.a: This is the case where only the leading 1 remains. With gap 3, the first 3 terms remain.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.r.b: This is the case where only the first two terms remain. With gap 3, three terms remain.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.r.d: This is the case where the first four terms remain. The number of remaining terms is 3, the same as the gap.
n-m-h3-serieslim-08.s.s3.explain: If the gap is k, then 1/(n(n+k))=(1/k)(1/n−1/(n+k)) and the first k terms 1, 1/2, …, 1/k remain. The sum is (1/k)(1+1/2+…+1/k). For k=2 it is 3/4, and for k=3 it is 11/18.

n-m-h3-vec-01.title: Checking a Solution for the Range of k That Gives an Obtuse Angle
n-m-h3-vec-01.goal: Find and fix the first wrong line in a solution that turned the condition for an obtuse angle into the sign of the dot product, and decide whether the same check is needed for the acute-angle condition.
n-m-h3-vec-01.material: This is Dain's solution for the range of real numbers k such that the angle between the two vectors a=(1, 2) and b=(k, −1) is obtuse. (k is a real number, θ is read "theta," −1 is "negative one," and a·b is read "a dot b.")
n-m-h3-vec-01.thinking.0: Finding the first line in the solution that goes wrong
n-m-h3-vec-01.thinking.1: Distinguishing the direction of "if" and "therefore" (necessary and sufficient)
n-m-h3-vec-01.thinking.2: Checking special cases on the boundary
n-m-h3-vec-01.prereq.0: Components and dot product of plane vectors
n-m-h3-vec-01.prereq.1: Relationship between the dot product and the angle between two vectors a·b=|a||b|cosθ
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Dain's solution that goes wrong.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether each line necessarily follows from the previous one, or whether it is a statement whose converse must be checked separately.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write the range of θ for which cosθ<0, from 0° to 180°, including the endpoints.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.line.1: If the angle is obtuse, then cosθ<0 and |a|, |b| are positive, so a·b<0.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.line.2: Conversely, if a·b<0 then the angle is obtuse, so the only condition for an obtuse angle is a·b<0.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the range of k is k < 2.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s1.explain: It first goes wrong at line 3. Line 2 states only one direction: "if the angle is obtuse, then a·b<0." Line 3 carried over the opposite direction ("if a·b<0, then the angle is obtuse") as it is, but a·b<0 includes every case where θ is greater than 90° and at most 180°, so 180° (parallel in exactly opposite directions) is included too. Lines 4 and 5 follow line 3, so the conclusion is off. The calculation in line 1 is correct.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.prompt: Fix the wrong line and write the correct range of k. Then, if there is a value to remove from the range, write that value and explain what the two vectors look like then.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.hint.0: First find the k for which b is a real multiple of a (parallel vectors).
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.hint.1: For that k, write the sign of a·b and the directions of the two vectors side by side and compare.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., a·b<0, but it includes cases where ..., so ...
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you find the value of k for which b is parallel to a?
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: At that value, did you check both the sign of a·b and the size of the angle?
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you say in one sentence why "a·b<0" and "obtuse angle" are not the same statement?
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.model.0: For b to be parallel to a, from (k, −1)=λ(1, 2) we get λ=−1/2 and k=−1/2. Then a·b=−5/2 is negative, but b points in exactly the opposite direction of a, so the angle is 180° and not obtuse. So the range is k<2, k≠−1/2.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.model.1: If a·b<0 then 90°<θ≤180°, so 180° is mixed in. When k=−1/2, b=(−1/2, −1)=−(1/2)a, so they are parallel in opposite directions. Removing that value, k<2 and k is not −1/2.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: You may also write it in symbols as k<−1/2 or −1/2<k<2.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.prompt: Using the same method, the range of m for which the angle between a=(1, 2) and c=(m, 4) is acute was solved with "a·c>0." Choose one value that must be checked separately or removed from the range.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.hint.0: First find the value of m for which c is a positive real multiple of a.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether that m is among the values satisfying a·c>0.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.r.a: m=−8 is the value where a·c=0, which the ">" sign already excludes. It is not a new value to check.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.r.b: This choice examines whether, among the values with a·c>0, there is a case where c becomes parallel to a in the same direction.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.r.c: c=(8, 4) is not parallel to a. It is an ordinary value giving an acute angle.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.r.d: c=(−2, 4) has a·c>0 and is not parallel to a. It is an ordinary value giving an acute angle.
n-m-h3-vec-01.s.s3.explain: If a·c=m+8>0, then m>−8. Among these, the case where c=(m, 4) is parallel to a=(1, 2) in the same direction is c=2a, that is, m=2, and then the angle is 0°, which is not acute. So m>−8, m≠2. For an obtuse angle, the exactly opposite direction (180°) slips in at the boundary, and for an acute angle, the same direction (0°) does.

n-m-h3-vec-02.title: What Do We Need to Know to Find the Distance Between a Point and a Plane?
n-m-h3-vec-02.goal: Sort out which information is sufficient and which is insufficient to determine the distance from a point to a plane, explain the insufficient cases with counterexamples, and then set up an actual plane equation and find the distance.
n-m-h3-vec-02.material: You want to find the distance from the point P(1, 1, 1) in space to a plane α. Suppose each piece of information below is given about the plane α separately. (A normal vector is a vector perpendicular to the plane. Coordinates are read as (x, y, z).)
n-m-h3-vec-02.thinking.0: Distinguishing necessary information from sufficient information
n-m-h3-vec-02.thinking.1: Explaining with counterexamples why information is insufficient
n-m-h3-vec-02.thinking.2: Setting up the equation of a plane from three points
n-m-h3-vec-02.prereq.0: Equation of a plane ax+by+cz+d=0 and normal vectors
n-m-h3-vec-02.prereq.1: Distance between a point and a plane
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.prompt: Among the following pieces of information, choose all those for which, if only that is given, the distance from P to α is determined as a single value.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, picture how many planes could satisfy it.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.hint.1: If you can find two planes with different distances, that information is insufficient.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.r.a: Planes through two points can be rotated about the line through them, so there are infinitely many. The distance is not determined.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.o.b: One point on α and a normal vector of α
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.r.b: The point fixes the plane's position and the normal vector fixes its tilt. You noticed that this is information that determines the plane uniquely.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.r.c: A normal vector tells only the tilt of the plane. There are infinitely many parallel planes with the same normal vector.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.o.d: Three points on α that are not on one line
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.r.d: Three points not on one line determine a plane uniquely. Once the plane is determined, so is the distance.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.o.e: Three points on α that are on one line
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.r.e: If the three points are on one line, it is effectively information about just a line, so the plane is not determined.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s1.explain: For the distance to be determined as a single value, the plane α must be uniquely determined. A plane is determined by "a point and a normal vector" or by "three points not on one line." Two different points or three points on one line leave infinitely many planes, and a normal vector alone leaves infinitely many parallel planes.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.prompt: The information "only a normal vector of α is given" does not determine the distance. Explain by giving an example of two planes that have the same normal vector but different distances from P.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write two equations of planes whose normal vector is (0, 0, 1).
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find the distance from the point P to each of the two planes and compare them.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Even if the normal vectors are the same, ...
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the equations of the two planes concretely?
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the distance from P to each plane and show that they differ?
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you explain it with the words "same tilt, different position"?
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.model.0: Even if the normal vector is the same, (1, 0, 0), the planes x=2 and x=5 are different parallel planes. Their distances from P(1, 1, 1) are 1 and 4, which differ.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.model.1: There are infinitely many parallel planes with the same normal vector, and their positions differ. For example, z=0 and z=3 have the same normal, but their distances from P come out different, 1 and 2.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.model.2: The planes z=0 and z=3, with normal (0,0,1), are at distances 1 and 2 from the point P(1,1,1).
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s2.model.3: The planes z=1 and z=4 have the same normal vector (0,0,1). Their distances from P are 0 and 3, so they differ.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.prompt: Suppose α passes through the three points A(1, 0, 0), B(0, 2, 0), C(0, 0, 3). Choose the distance from P(1, 1, 1) to α.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.hint.0: Use the fact that the three points lie on the coordinate axes to set up the plane's equation first, and check by substituting the three points.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check that the denominator in the distance formula is the magnitude of the normal vector.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.r.a: You probably used the squared value 49 in the denominator instead of the normal vector's magnitude √(36+9+4)=7.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.r.b: You set up the plane as 6x+3y+2z=6, got 6+3+2−6=5, and divided by the normal's magnitude 7.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.r.c: You probably did not subtract the plane's constant term 6 from the substituted value 6+3+2.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.r.d: You probably mistook the intercepts 1, 2, 3 for coefficients and set up the plane as something like x+2y+3z=1.
n-m-h3-vec-02.s.s3.explain: The three points have x-intercept 1, y-intercept 2, z-intercept 3, so the plane is x/1+y/2+z/3=1, that is, 6x+3y+2z−6=0. The distance from P is |6+3+2−6|/√(36+9+4)=5/7.

n-m-h3-vec-03.title: If the Direction Vectors Are Parallel, Are the Lines the Same?
n-m-h3-vec-03.goal: Sort out what evidence from the direction vectors and points of two lines is enough to decide whether they are the same line, and check for yourself a case where the evidence is insufficient.
n-m-h3-vec-03.material:
Three lines in space are written with parameters t and s. (t and s are real numbers. l₁ is read "l one," and (2, −1, 1) is the vector with components 2, −1, 1.)
l₁: (x, y, z) = (1, 0, 2) + t(2, −1, 1)
l₂: (x, y, z) = (3, −1, 3) + s(−4, 2, −2)
l₃: (x, y, z) = (3, −1, 4) + s(−4, 2, −2)
Mina, Hajun, Seoyun, and Dohyun made the following claims about the relationship between l₁ and l₂.
n-m-h3-vec-03.thinking.0: Judging the connection between claims and evidence
n-m-h3-vec-03.thinking.1: Checking whether lines are the same even when the expressions differ
n-m-h3-vec-03.thinking.2: Distinguishing necessary conditions from sufficient conditions
n-m-h3-vec-03.prereq.0: Vector equation (parametric form) of a line in space
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.prompt: Among the four people's claims about l₁ and l₂, choose the claim whose reasoning has no gaps.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.hint.0: First check what number you multiply one direction vector by to get the other.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.hint.1: Then substitute the coordinates of the point l₂ passes through into the formula for l₁ and see whether a suitable t exists.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.o.a: Mina: The direction vectors (2, −1, 1) and (−4, 2, −2) are not equal, so l₁ and l₂ are different lines.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the fact that the direction vectors are not the same expression. When determining a line, a direction vector can be written with a different length and direction (sign).
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.o.b: Hajun: The direction vectors (2, −1, 1) and (−4, 2, −2) are parallel, so l₁ and l₂ are the same line.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.r.b: The conclusion is right but the reasoning is insufficient. Lines whose direction vectors are merely parallel may be different parallel lines.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.o.c: Seoyun: The direction vectors (2, −1, 1) and (−4, 2, −2) are not parallel, so l₁ and l₂ are skew.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.r.c: (−4, 2, −2) is −2 times (2, −1, 1), so they are parallel. You did not even check the calculation of whether they are parallel.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.o.d: Dohyun: The direction vectors are parallel and the point (3, −1, 3) that l₂ passes through is on l₁, so the two lines are the same line.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.r.d: The directions are the same and they share a point, so the lines coincide. Both conditions were checked as evidence.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s1.explain: (−4, 2, −2)=−2(2, −1, 1), so the direction vectors are parallel. Also, putting t=1 into l₁ gives (3, −1, 3), so the point of l₂ is on l₁. If the directions are parallel and one point coincides, the lines are the same. Parallel direction vectors alone are not enough, and the direction vectors not being the same expression does not mean the lines are different.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.prompt: This time, compare l₃ (point (3, −1, 4), direction vector (−4, 2, −2)) with l₁. Decide whether the two lines are the same, and write the reasoning for your decision along with your calculation.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.hint.0: Match the x and y coordinates of l₃'s point (3, −1, 4) to the formula for l₁ and find t.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.hint.1: Use that t to calculate the z coordinate as well and compare it with l₃'s point.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., The direction vector of l₃ is ... and the point of l₃ is ...
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you first check that the direction vectors are parallel?
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you substitute l₃'s point into l₁'s formula and compare all three coordinates?
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that "lines can have parallel directions without being the same line"?
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.model.0: The direction vector of l₃ is −2 times that of l₁, so they are parallel. But if we put l₃'s point (3, −1, 4) into l₁, x and y give t=1, and then z=3, which differs from 4, so the point is not on l₁. So they are parallel but not the same line.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s2.model.1: Even with the same direction, we can't say they are the same line. From (1+2t, −t, 2+t)=(3, −1, 4), the first two equations give t=1 but the third gives t=2, a contradiction. The point is not on l₁, so they are different parallel lines.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.prompt: Choose the relationship between the line l₄: (x, y, z) = (5, −2, 4) + u(−6, 3, −3) and l₁.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.hint.0: First find the multiple relationship between the direction vectors.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.hint.1: Substitute l₄'s point into l₁'s formula to check whether it is on l₁.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.o.a: It is parallel to l₁ but a different line
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.r.a: You checked only that the direction vectors are parallel and did not check whether the point is on l₁.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.o.b: It is the same line as l₁
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.r.b: This choice checked both that the direction vectors are parallel and that the point is on l₁.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.o.c: It meets l₁ at exactly one point
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.r.c: Two lines with parallel direction vectors cannot meet at exactly one point. If they meet, they coincide; otherwise they do not meet.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.r.d: Two lines with parallel direction vectors cannot be skew. Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting.
n-m-h3-vec-03.s.s3.explain: (−6, 3, −3)=−3(2, −1, 1), so they are parallel. Putting t=2 into l₁ gives (5, −2, 4), so l₄'s point is on l₁. Therefore l₄ is the same line as l₁. The same line can be expressed with any choice of point and direction vector.

n-m-h3-vec-04.title: Is the Angle Between Two Lines the Same as the Angle Between Their Direction Vectors?
n-m-h3-vec-04.goal: Understand the difference between the angle between direction vectors and the angle between lines by revising your judgment as information is added, and use the correct formula for the angle between lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.material: You want to find the angle θ between two lines l and m in the coordinate plane. Information is revealed one piece at a time. (u·v is read "u dot v," |u| is the magnitude of u, and √5 is read "root 5.")
n-m-h3-vec-04.thinking.0: Revising your judgment when new information appears
n-m-h3-vec-04.thinking.1: Checking whether the value is the same even if the direction vector is chosen differently
n-m-h3-vec-04.thinking.2: Explaining why the absolute value is needed
n-m-h3-vec-04.prereq.0: Dot product of plane vectors and the angle between them
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each stage, choose a judgment using only what you know so far.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, check whether the earlier judgment still holds.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.hint.1: For the same line, choose the opposite direction vector, do the same calculation, and compare the results.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.info: You chose u=(1, 2) as the direction vector of line l and v=(1, −3) as the direction vector of line m. Calculating gives u·v=−5, |u|=√5, |v|=√10.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you judge the angle θ between the two lines?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The angle between u and v has cos = −1/√2, that is, 135°. But it has not yet been confirmed whether this value can be taken as the angle between the two lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You transferred the angle between the two vectors directly to the angle between the lines. This is the first judgment that comes to mind.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We need to check further whether this value really describes the angle between the lines, and whether it is the same if the direction vectors are chosen differently
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You recalled that a direction vector is not a single fixed value for each line.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Since the dot product is negative, we can only say the two lines are not perpendicular
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You said only that they are not perpendicular. You did not determine the size of the angle.
