n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Even if you take −v=(−1, 3) as the direction vector of line m instead of v, it is the same line m.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the angle between u and −v, and what does this tell us about the angle θ between the lines?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The angle between u and v is 135°, and the angle between u and −v is 45°. Even for the same two lines, the value changes depending on how the direction vector is chosen. When two lines meet, angles of 45° and 135° form, so we need a convention for which one to call the angle between the lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: u·(−v)=5 and cos=1/√2, so it is 45°. For the same lines, two angles, 135° and 45°, come out, so the signed dot product alone does not determine the angle between the lines
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You directly checked that the value changes depending on how the direction vector is chosen.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Getting 45° is a calculation mistake, and 135° is correct
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Changing to −v reverses the sign of the dot product, so cos becomes +1/√2; this is not a mistake.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: u·(−v)=5 and the angle is 45°, so the earlier 135° was wrong and the angle between the lines is 45°
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You were right that 45° comes out, but you missed that both 135° and 45° came from the same two lines. We need a convention for which one to take as the angle between the lines.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.info: We agree that the angle θ between two lines is the one of the two kinds of angles formed where they meet (45° and 135°) that is not larger, that is, the one with 0°<θ≤90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which formula always gives θ no matter how the direction vectors are chosen?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.after: |u·v|=5, so cosθ=5/(√5·√10)=1/√2 and θ=45°. The angle between lines must be found with a formula that takes the absolute value of the dot product, so that the same value comes out no matter how the direction vectors are chosen.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The sign changes depending on the choice of direction vector, so it may not fit the convention that θ is between 0° and 90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Using the absolute value of the dot product gives the same value even if a direction vector is reversed, and cosθ≥0, so θ is at most 90°.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is right only when −v is used; if it is chosen the other way the sign differs, so it is not a formula that is always right.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you transferred the angle between direction vectors directly to the angle between the lines, but your judgment changed when the information was added that even the same line has direction vectors in two opposite directions. The angle between lines must be a quantity that does not change with the sign of the direction vector, so we find it by taking the absolute value of the dot product.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.prompt: The direction vector of line p is (2, 1) and the direction vector of line q is (1, −3). Find the value of cosθ for the angle θ between the two lines, and write in one sentence why the formula needs an absolute value.

n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.hint.1: Do the same calculation with (−1, 3), the reverse of the direction vector (1, −3), and compare the results.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., cosθ = ... The absolute value is needed because ...

n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you compare what angle comes out if you use the dot product as it is when it is negative?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you connect the reason for the absolute value to "how the direction vector is chosen"?
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.model.0: (2, 1)·(1, −3) = −1 and the magnitudes are √5 and √10, so cosθ = |−1|/(√5·√10) = 1/(5√2) ≈ 0.14. If we reverse the direction vector, the sign of the dot product changes, so we need the absolute value for the angle between the lines to be determined uniquely.
n-m-h3-vec-04.s.s2.model.1: The dot product is −1 and |p|=√5, |q|=√10, so cosθ=1/√50=√2/10. We use the absolute value because we agreed that the angle between two lines is at most 90°, and we want the same value no matter how the direction vectors are chosen.

n-m-h3-vec-05.title: Making a Line That Does Not Meet a Plane
n-m-h3-vec-05.goal: Do not think of the condition for a line not meeting a plane as a single condition on the direction vector; also account for the case where the line lies in the plane, and make examples.
n-m-h3-vec-05.material: In space there is a plane α: x + y − 2z = 0. You want to make a line l through the point (p, 1, 1) with direction vector (a, b, c) so that it does not meet α. (l is read "el," p is an integer, and the direction vector (a, b, c) is the vector with components a, b, c.)
n-m-h3-vec-05.thinking.0: Making examples that satisfy the conditions yourself
n-m-h3-vec-05.thinking.1: Checking the boundary between parallel and contained
n-m-h3-vec-05.thinking.2: Determining the position of a line relative to a plane with two conditions
n-m-h3-vec-05.prereq.0: Equation of a line and equation of a plane in space
n-m-h3-vec-05.prereq.1: Normal vector of a plane and the dot product
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose (p, a, b, c) so that the line l: (x, y, z) = (p, 1, 1) + t(a, b, c) does not meet the plane α: x + y − 2z = 0. p, a, b, c are integers and (a, b, c) must not be the zero vector. So that direction vectors in the same direction are not repeated, the greatest common divisor of a, b, c must be 1, and either a>0 or (a=0 and b>0). Make three examples with different direction vectors.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.hint.0: First decide what relationship the direction vector and the plane's normal vector must have for the line to be parallel to the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.hint.1: After making one example, also check whether a point on the line is on the plane.

n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.var.b: y-component b of the direction vector
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.var.c: z-component c of the direction vector

n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.fail.c1: p, a, b, c must be integers with absolute value at most 50.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.ok.c2: The direction vector is not the zero vector, its greatest common divisor is 1, and the sign condition holds too.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.fail.c2: The direction vector must not be the zero vector, its greatest common divisor must be 1, and either a>0 or (a=0 and b>0).
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.ok.c3: The direction vector is perpendicular to the plane's normal vector.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.fail.c3: Check the relationship between the direction vector and the plane's normal vector (1, 1, −2) so that the line's direction is parallel to the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.ok.c4: The point on the line is not on the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.fail.c4: Check whether the line fails to meet the plane at even a single point, and whether the point (p, 1, 1) on the line is on the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.explain: The plane's normal vector is (1, 1, −2). For a line not to meet the plane, its direction vector must be perpendicular to the normal vector, so a+b−2c=0. But that alone might leave the line contained in the plane. If the point (p, 1, 1) on the line is on the plane (p+1−2=0, that is, p=1), the whole line lies in the plane. So p≠1 is needed as well.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.prompt: Explain why you cannot use a direction vector satisfying a+b−2c=0 when p=1.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.hint.0: When p=1, substitute the coordinates of the point the line passes through into the plane's equation.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.hint.1: Think about what happens to the other points on the line when the direction vector condition is also used.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.placeholder: e.g., If p=1, a point on the line ...
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate whether the point (1, 1, 1) on the line is on the plane x+y−2z=0 when p=1?
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Can you say why the direction vector condition alone does not guarantee "does not meet"?
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.model.0: If p=1, the point (1, 1, 1) that the line passes through is on the plane. And if the direction is also parallel to the plane, every point on the line is on the plane, so the line is contained in the plane. Then it doesn't fail to meet the plane; it meets it at infinitely many points.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s1.because.model.1: If p=1, (1,1,1) satisfies the plane x+y−2z=0, so a point on the line is on the plane. The direction vector is perpendicular to the normal, so the whole line lies in the plane, which makes it contained rather than parallel.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose the relationship between the line m: (x, y, z) = (1, 0, 0) + t(0, 1, 1) and the plane β: y − z = 0.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.hint.0: First calculate the dot product of the direction vector and the plane's normal vector.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute the coordinates of the point the line passes through into the plane's equation.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.r.a: You probably did not check whether the dot product of the direction vector and the normal vector (0, 1, −1) is 0.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.o.b: It is parallel and does not meet
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.r.b: You probably checked only that the direction is parallel to the plane and did not check whether the point on the line is on the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.o.c: The line lies in the plane
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.r.c: This choice checked that the direction vector is perpendicular to the normal and that the point (1, 0, 0) on the line is on the plane.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.o.d: The line is perpendicular to the plane
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.r.d: If the direction vector is perpendicular to the normal vector, the line is parallel to the plane. For it to be perpendicular to the plane, the direction vector must be parallel to the normal vector.
n-m-h3-vec-05.s.s2.explain: The dot product of the direction vector (0, 1, 1) and the normal vector (0, 1, −1) is 0, so the line is parallel to the plane. Also, the point (1, 0, 0) satisfies y−z=0, so it is on the plane. Therefore the line lies in the plane.

n-m-h3-vec-06.title: Explaining the Dot Product to a Younger Sibling Who Doesn't Know Cosine Yet
n-m-h3-vec-06.goal: Explain the meaning of the dot product (a single number expressing how much two vectors point in the same direction) to an audience that doesn't know cosine, by changing the situation.
n-m-h3-vec-06.material: Jisu explained the dot product of vectors to her 7th-grade younger sibling like this: "The dot product of two vectors a and b is |a||b|cosθ. You just multiply the components and add, and it's 0 if they're perpendicular." Her sibling hasn't learned cos yet, so asked back, "But what is the dot product?" (|a| is the magnitude of a, θ is read "theta," and cos is cosine.)
n-m-h3-vec-06.thinking.0: Changing the wording to fit the audience
n-m-h3-vec-06.thinking.1: Moving the meaning into a situation
n-m-h3-vec-06.thinking.2: Explaining the opposite-direction and perpendicular cases too
n-m-h3-vec-06.prereq.0: Definition of the dot product and the angle between two vectors
n-m-h3-vec-06.prereq.1: Sign of the dot product and the perpendicularity condition
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the sentence that best explains the meaning of the dot product in words your sibling can understand.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.hint.0: First tell whether each sentence says the result of the dot product is a number or a vector.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.hint.1: Test each sentence one at a time for when the two vectors point the same way, are perpendicular, and point in opposite directions.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.o.a: The dot product is a single number that shows how much one vector points in the same direction as the other, taking their sizes into account.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.r.a: This explanation captures all the properties of the dot product: it is larger the more the directions agree, 0 when perpendicular, and negative when they point opposite ways.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.o.b: The dot product is a calculation that multiplies the components of two vectors with each other to make a new vector. The result is also an arrow.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.r.b: The result of the dot product is not a vector but a single number. You mixed up the method of calculation with the kind of result.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.o.c: The dot product is the product of the sizes of the two vectors. It gives the same value no matter which way the two arrows point.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.r.c: The dot product's value depends on the angle between the two vectors. This explanation ignores direction.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.o.d: The dot product is a value that tells you the angle between two vectors in degrees. If they are at a right angle, you get 90.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.r.d: The dot product is not the angle itself. At a right angle the dot product is 0, not 90.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s1.explain: The dot product is a single number that depends on both the sizes of the two vectors and the angle between them. It gets larger the more similar the directions are, is 0 when perpendicular, and is negative when they point opposite ways. A mistook the result for a vector, B ignored direction, and D confused it with the angle itself.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.prompt: Now write the explanation to send to your sibling yourself. (1) Explain it with the scene of pulling a sled with a rope, (2) compare pulling in the same direction as the sled goes with pulling perpendicular (upward), and (3) do not use words like cos, θ, or projection.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.hint.0: First picture the case where the direction the sled goes and the direction the rope pulls are the same.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.hint.1: Then think about how much is used for going forward when the rope's pull is at a right angle to the direction of motion.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., When you pull a sled with a rope, ...
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you change to a scene your sibling can understand (a sled, a cart, etc.)?
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the same direction, a slanted direction, and the perpendicular case?
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you put "how much is used in the same direction" into words instead of a formula?
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.model.0: When you pull a sled with a rope, if the rope is in the same direction the sled goes, all your force goes into moving forward. If the rope is slanted, only part of the force is used, and if you pull straight up toward the sky, none of it goes into moving forward, so it's 0. The dot product is a single number that tells how much of the force is used in the direction it goes.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.model.1: When you push a cart, it goes best when you push in the same direction it's heading. If the direction is a little off, it goes less well, and if you push sideways at a right angle, it does nothing to help the cart go forward, so it's 0. The dot product is a number for how much two arrows point the same way.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.model.2: If you pull the rope upward, none of it is used to go forward, so it's 0. If it's exactly in the direction the sled goes, all the force is used.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s2.model.3: If you pull straight in the direction the sled goes, all the force is used, and if it's slanted, only part is used. At a right angle, it's 0.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.prompt: Your sibling asked, "Then what's a scene where the dot product is negative?" Choose the appropriate one in the sled scene.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.hint.0: For the same direction, perpendicular, and opposite direction, write whether each helps or hinders going forward.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the sign of the dot product connects to how much it helps.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.o.a: When the rope pulls in exactly the direction the sled goes
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.r.a: In the same direction, the dot product is the largest positive number.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.o.b: When the rope is pulled upward at a right angle
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.r.b: At a right angle, the dot product is 0.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.o.c: When the rope pulls opposite to the direction the sled goes
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.r.c: If it points in the opposite direction, it hinders going forward, so the dot product is negative.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.o.d: When the rope pulls slantedly in the same general direction the sled goes
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.r.d: In a slanted direction toward the same side, the dot product is positive and the angle is less than 90°.
n-m-h3-vec-06.s.s3.explain: The dot product becomes a larger positive number the more two vectors point toward the same side, is 0 when perpendicular, and is negative when they point to opposite sides. In the sled scene, pulling the opposite way hinders going forward, so it corresponds to a negative value.

n-m-h3-vec-07.title: If No Two Planes Are Parallel, Do the Three Planes Meet at One Point?
n-m-h3-vec-07.goal: Check a prediction about the positions of three planes with a counterexample you make yourself, and explain the structure that the counterexample has.
n-m-h3-vec-07.material: Consider three different planes. A friend said that if no two of the planes are parallel, the three planes always meet at a single point. The two planes x=0 and y=0 are not parallel, and they meet in a line. (x=0 is read "x equals 0," and ax+by+cz=d is the equation of a plane.)
n-m-h3-vec-07.thinking.0: Testing a prediction with examples you make yourself
n-m-h3-vec-07.thinking.1: Finding the conditions for making a counterexample
n-m-h3-vec-07.thinking.2: Explaining positions using the arrangement of the lines of intersection
n-m-h3-vec-07.prereq.0: Equation of a plane and normal vector
n-m-h3-vec-07.prereq.1: Line of intersection of two planes
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of your friend's statement?
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.hint.0: First find the line where the planes x=0 and y=0 meet.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether what they have in common changes depending on how the third plane meets that line.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.o.a: It is not always true. There are cases where the three planes have no common point
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.r.a: This judgment also considered the relationship between the line where two planes meet and the third plane.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.o.b: It is always true. Planes that are not parallel meet, so three planes also meet at one point
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.r.b: Two planes meeting pair by pair and three planes having a common point are different things.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.o.c: It is not always true. But there are only two cases: meeting at a point or along a line
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.r.c: You did not examine the case with no common point. Think about the case where the third plane is parallel to the line of intersection of the first two.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.o.d: It is always true. Three planes fail to meet only when two of them are parallel
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that did not directly check whether there can be no common point even without parallel planes.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s1.explain: The planes x=0 and y=0 meet in the z-axis. The result depends on whether or not the third plane meets this line. Even if no two of the three planes are parallel, they may have no common point. Check whether this is true by making an example yourself.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.prompt: There are the planes x=0 and y=0. Choose a third plane ax + by + cz = d so that no two of the three planes are parallel and the three planes have no common point. a, b, c, d are real numbers. Make three different planes.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.hint.0: First figure out where the line where the planes x=0 and y=0 meet is.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what shape the equation must have so that no point on that line satisfies the third plane.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The third plane is not parallel to the plane x=0.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The third plane is parallel to the plane x=0. Check whether the normal vector (a, b, c) is parallel to (1, 0, 0).
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The third plane is not parallel to the plane y=0.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The third plane is parallel to the plane y=0. Check whether the normal vector (a, b, c) is parallel to (0, 1, 0).
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.ok.c3: There is no point that all three planes pass through.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.fail.c3: There is a point that all three planes pass through. Check whether a point on the line where the planes x=0 and y=0 meet is on the third plane.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s2.explain: The planes x=0 and y=0 meet in the z-axis. If the third plane passes through even one point on the z-axis, the three planes have a common point. Substituting a point (0, 0, z) on the z-axis gives cz=d, and for no z to satisfy this we need c=0 and d≠0. Also, a and b must be nonzero for the plane not to be parallel to x=0 and y=0.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.prompt: Taking one of the planes you made as an example, explain why the three planes meet two at a time but have no common point among all three.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write what happens when you substitute a point on the line made by x=0 and y=0 into the plane you made.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how the three lines formed where the planes meet two at a time are related to one another.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The line where x=0 and y=0 meet is ..., and the third plane ...

n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.model.0: Take x+y=1, for example. x=0 and y=0 meet in the z-axis, but x+y=1 is parallel to the z-axis, and a point on the z-axis has x+y=0, so it cannot satisfy this plane. No two planes are parallel, but there is no point common to all three.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.model.1: The three lines of intersection of the planes are all lines parallel to the z-axis. Like the three side faces of a triangular prism, the planes meet two at a time, but there is no point that all three pass through together.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.model.2: x+y=1 is parallel to the z-axis. Putting a point (0,0,z) on the z-axis into it gives 0=1, which is impossible, so there is no point common to the three planes.
n-m-h3-vec-07.s.s3.model.3: The z-axis is parallel to the third plane, so they do not meet. So the planes meet two at a time, but there is no point where all three meet together.
